# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis

If you are about to make a new document and this session offers Claude's own docs (a Docs connector, docs skill or Docs artifact type), and the user has neither named Word/.docx/.dotx, asked for tracked changes, nor supplied a .docx/.dotx file to change or use as a template, make the document there instead. It exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to make a Word file. A .docx/.dotx given only as source material does not count as supplied. This skill remains the right tool for producing, reading, editing, templating or converting Word files.

A `.docx` is a ZIP archive of XML files. Choose your approach by task:

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Create** a new document | Write a `docx` (npm) script — see gotchas below |
| **Edit** an existing document | `unzip` → edit `word/document.xml` → `zip` (docx-js cannot open existing files) |
| **Read** content | `pandoc -t markdown file.docx` |

> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.

## Creating with docx-js — gotchas

`docx` is preinstalled — do not run `npm install` first; write the script and `require('docx')` directly. Only if that require fails: `npm install docx`. The model knows the API; these are the footguns:

- **Page size defaults to A4.** For US Letter set `page: { size: { width: 12240, height: 15840 } }` (DXA; 1440 = 1″).
- **Landscape:** pass portrait dimensions and `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE` — docx-js swaps width/height internally.
- **Tables need dual widths:** set `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on every cell, both in `WidthType.DXA` (PERCENTAGE breaks in Google Docs). Column widths must sum to the table width.
- **Table shading:** use `ShadingType.CLEAR`, never `SOLID` (renders black).
- **Lists:** never insert `•` literally; use a `numbering` config with `LevelFormat.BULLET`.
- **`ImageRun` requires `type:`** (`"png"`, `"jpg"`, …).
- **`PageBreak` must be inside a `Paragraph`.**
- **Never use `\n`** — use separate `Paragraph` elements.
- **Headings:** style every level you use (`title`, `heading1`, `heading2`…) in `styles.default`: `heading1: { run: { font: "Arial", size: 32, bold: true }, paragraph: { spacing: { before: 240, after: 120 }, keepNext: true } }`. Every level needs its own font (even with a document default), `before` and `after` (even if 0) and `keepNext`: the built-in styles set none of them.
- **TOC:** headings must use built-in `HeadingLevel.*`; custom heading styles need `outlineLevel` set or they won't appear.
- **Don't use a table as a horizontal rule** — use a paragraph bottom border instead.
- **Dot-leader / right-aligned-on-same-line:** use `PositionalTab` (`alignment: PositionalTabAlignment.RIGHT`, `leader: PositionalTabLeader.DOT`) inside a `TextRun`, not literal `.` or space padding.

## Verify the output

After writing a `.docx`, render it and look at it:

```bash
zip -d output.docx '*/' >/dev/null || true   # drop the ZIP's folder entries: Word has refused a file that has them when opened through a cloud co-editing service
python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf output.docx
pdftoppm -jpeg -r 100 output.pdf page
ls page-*.jpg   # then Read the images
```

`pdftoppm` zero-pads page numbers to the width of the page count (`page-01.jpg`…`page-12.jpg`).

## Editing existing documents

Legacy `.doc` files must be converted first: `python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx file.doc`.

```bash
unzip -q doc.docx -d unpacked/
find unpacked -type l -delete   # strip symlink entries — docx from external parties is untrusted
python scripts/merge_runs.py unpacked/   # coalesce fragmented runs so text is findable
# edit unpacked/word/document.xml in place — do NOT reformat or pretty-print
(cd unpacked && rm -f ../out.docx && zip -XrD ../out.docx .)
python scripts/office/validate.py out.docx --original doc.docx   # XSD checks; --auto-repair fixes common issues
# redlining? add --author "<the name you redlined under>" to check every edit is tracked
```

Word splits text across many `<w:r>` runs (revision ids, spell-check markers), so a phrase you can see in the document often doesn't exist as a contiguous string in the XML. `merge_runs.py` merges adjacent identically-formatted runs in `word/document.xml` without changing content or rendering; it also accepts a `.docx` directly (`python scripts/merge_runs.py doc.docx -o merged.docx`).

**Tracked changes:** when redlining, validate with `--author "<the name you redlined under>"` (needs `--original`) — it reports any text you changed without a `<w:ins>`/`<w:del>` around it, which is easy to do by accident and invisible in the accepted view. Wrap runs in `<w:ins>`/`<w:del>` with `w:id`, `w:author`, `w:date` attributes. Inside `<w:del>`, the text element is `<w:delText>`, not `<w:t>`. A deleted paragraph mark (`<w:pPr><w:rPr><w:del w:id=".." w:author=".." w:date=".."/></w:rPr></w:pPr>`) means "merge this paragraph into the next" — so deleting a paragraph outright is that plus a `<w:del>` around every run. The `<w:del/>` must come before the rPr's other children; their order is schema-enforced.

To produce a clean copy with all tracked changes accepted: `python scripts/accept_changes.py in.docx out.docx`.

Accepting a deleted paragraph mark should join that paragraph to the one below it, so a paragraph whose runs are *all* deleted vanishes. Word does this; `accept_changes.py` and `pandoc --track-changes=accept` don't always. Both fail the same way — they strip the deleted text but leave the emptied paragraph behind, which reads as a stray empty bullet when it was auto-numbered:

- `pandoc --track-changes=accept` never joins the paragraphs.
- `accept_changes.py` (LibreOffice) joins them correctly, except when the deleted paragraph is followed by an empty spacer paragraph.

An empty bullet in either view is an artifact of that view, not a defect in the document. Check paragraph deletions in the XML.

## Comments

Comments require six cross-linked files. Use the helper — directory mode when you'll also be editing `document.xml` (saves an unzip/rezip cycle), `.docx`-direct mode otherwise:

```bash
# Against an already-unpacked directory (preferred when also placing markers)
python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ "Fees & expenses cap is too low"
python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ "Agreed" --parent 0

# Against a .docx directly
python scripts/comment.py contract.docx "This cap is too low" -o annotated.docx
```

The script writes `comments.xml`, `commentsExtended.xml`, `commentsIds.xml`, `commentsExtensible.xml`, the relationships, and the content-type overrides. Comment IDs are auto-assigned. It then prints the `<w:commentRangeStart>`/`<w:commentRangeEnd>`/`<w:commentReference>` snippet to add to `word/document.xml` so the comment anchors to specific text — until you place those markers, the comment exists but is not visible.

## Dependencies

`docx` (npm, preinstalled — install only if `require('docx')` fails) · `pandoc` · LibreOffice (`soffice`) · `pdftoppm` (Poppler)

78	| **D06** | Technical Support, SLA & Update Governance | **Built** | Response times, severity tiers, patching cadence, EOL policy, and the false-positive cost regime (quarterly service credits). |
79	| **D07** | Comprehensive Master Contract | **Built** | Federal guidelines, data security, indemnities, limitation of liability, insurance, export control, audit rights, dispute resolution. |
80	| **D08** | Master Licensing & Liability | **Built — but it is a commercial annex, not an instrument to sign** | Licensing structure, tier bands, workable corridor economics, performance component. D08 explains the money; **D07 and D02 are what a customer executes.** Where D08 and either of them differ, they govern and D08 is corrected. |
81	| **D09** | Data Processing & Security Addendum (DPA) | **Built** | The security schedule: data residency, security controls, incident notification (72h), retention, subprocessor register, audit rights. |
82	| **D10** | Subprocessor & Third-Party Component Register | **Built** | Zero subprocessors. One runtime dependency (numpy, BSD-3). Restates the supply-chain gaps. **Incorporated by reference in D02 §11, D07 §3.4, D13 §8 and B04 §7 — now exists.** |
83	| **D11** | Mutual NDA | **Built** | Needed *before* D02. Often overlooked and always needed first. |
84	| **D12** | Regulatory Status & Safety-Critical Function Statement | **Built** | Single annex stating this is not a certified safety appliance, is not a substitute for required inspection, and relieves the Railroad of no regulatory obligation. Identical language across B01, C02, D02, D07, D08. See §III.1. |
85	| **D13** | IP Ownership & Escrow Schedule | **Built** | Definitive statement of what transfers and when. Records the five-year retention decision. Escrow releases the **running version only**, insolvency-triggered, operability never ownership. Includes contributor assignment requirement. |
86	| **D14** | Operating Model & Liability Boundary | **Built** | Who installs, operates, supports and staffs. Separates operational liability (largely removed by responsible self-install) from product liability (retained regardless). Sets representational discipline. |
87	
88	### E. Forms — the executable instruments
89	
90	Contracts say what the rules are. **Forms are how the rules are actually applied, one event at a time.** Every form is one purpose, one signatory, one stated consequence for silence.
91	
92	| ID | Form | Status | Purpose |
93	|---|---|---|---|
94	| **F00** | Forms Register & Documentation Policy | **Built** | The index, the seven documentation rules, and the rule that governs the others: *if no form exists for what you are about to do, create the form first.* Rule 7 separates a fill-in blank from an unmade decision. |
95	| **F01** | Site Readiness & Survey Questionnaire | **Built** | Pre-deployment site assessment: detector, compute, network, people, existing systems. |
96	| **F02** | Configuration Attestation | **Built** | The Customer's IT Director certifies the installation. **Establishes the Commissioning Date and starts the pilot clock.** The single most important form in the docket. |
97	| **F03** | Change Order | **Built** | The only mechanism by which scope, price or schedule may change on an executed Order. 8-hour tolerance for minor change. |
98	| **F04** | Travel Pre-Approval Request | **Built** | Written approval before any billable travel. Records what we will and will not do on site. |
99	| **F05** | Payment Terms Schedule | **Built** | What is paid, when, and how. Includes the invoicing-discipline rules and the non-suspension commitment. |
100	| **F06** | Deliverable Acceptance | **Built** | Acceptance, acceptance-with-notes, or specific non-conformity. **Silence past 10 Business Days is acceptance.** |
101	| **F07** | Travel & Expense Claim | **Built** | Reimbursement at actual cost, no markup, with cap reconciliation. |
102	| **F08** | Reviewer Certification Application | **Built** | Application, assessment, certification, and revocation. **Currently the authoritative certification record** until the signed registry is built. |
103	| **F09** | Advisory Disposition Record | **Built** | The human decision, recorded. The most legally significant record the Platform produces. Discloses the append-only gap in Part 7. |
104	| **F10** | Security Incident Notification | **Built** | 72-hour Supplier notice, 24-hour Customer notice, RCA, and regulatory hand-off. |
105	| **F11** | Site Visit Report | **Built** | What we observed, **and what we declined to do.** Part 4 records every boundary event. |
106	| **F12** | Formal Notice | **Built** | Termination, breach, cure, non-renewal, conversion election. Delivery method determines effectiveness. |
107	| **F13** | Data Export & Transition Certificate | **Built** | What the Customer gets when it ends, in specific files, with reconciliation. |
108	
109	---
110	
111	## Part III — Loopholes identified, and current status
112	
113	These are the gaps that most often go wrong in rail technology contracts specifically. Status markers show which are now closed by a built document and which remain open work.
114	
115	### 1. The safety-critical disclaimer paradox — the biggest one
116	
117	**Status: CLOSED** — D12 built. The decision-support framing is now fixed in D12 §§1–2, and D12 §9 makes it controlling over every other document.
118	
119	Our claim is that we prevent derailments. Our inevitable limitation-of-liability clause will say we do not guarantee detection. **Put together, those two statements are a contradiction that a plaintiff's lawyer will find in ten minutes.**
120	
121	The resolution is not to weaken either. It is to define the product precisely: AxiomDynamics is a **decision-support system** that presents a ranked, physics-derived risk assessment to a **qualified human reviewer**. The Railroad retains the operating decision. That framing must be *identical* in B01, C02, D02, D07 and D08 — same words, same scope. If the technical annex calls it a "detection system" and the contract calls it "decision support," we have manufactured our own liability.
122	
123	**Add: D12 — Regulatory Status & Safety-Critical Function Statement.** A single annex that states, unambiguously, that this is not a certified safety appliance, is not a substitute for FRA-required inspection, and does not relieve the Railroad of any regulatory obligation. This protects both parties and is the document that makes the disclaimer credible rather than self-serving.
124	
125	### 2. Data ownership vs. model improvement
126	
127	**Status: CLOSED** — D13 §3 separates ownership explicitly. Default position is no cross-customer learning, which under AD-1 is structurally true rather than merely promised.
128	
129	The standard clause — "Railroad owns its data" — is insufficient. The Railroad will ask: *if you train on our data, and the model improves, do we own the improvement? Do our competitors benefit?* Left unanswered, this stalls the deal at legal review every time.
130	
131	**Add to D07/D09:** explicit separation of (a) Railroad's raw and derived operating data — owned by Railroad; (b) AxiomDynamics' models, weights, rules and source — owned by AxiomDynamics, including improvements derived from Railroad data; (c) a licence back to the Railroad for its own data in usable form on termination. Also state plainly whether cross-customer learning occurs — and if it does, that it is aggregated and non-attributable.
132	
133	### 3. The "who pays for the false positive" gap
134	
135	**Status: CLOSED** — D06 §4 defines a quarterly service credit schedule tied to measured false-positive rate, capped at the platform fee, excluding detector-data causes and consequential damages.
136	
137	A false stop on a Class I main line costs train-hours, crew-hours, and network knock-on. **Nothing in the current documents says who bears the cost when we are wrong.** A railroad's counsel will ask this in the first meeting. If we have no answer, they will assume we bear it.
138	
139	> **Note on the false-positive figure.** Earlier internal drafts cited "<0.1% false positives" as a marketing claim. **That figure was never measured and has been withdrawn from the client-facing docket** — D06 §4 now sets a measurement regime with no target, and A2 states no target. Claiming a rate before measuring it, in the same docket that promises a credit when the rate is high, is the contradiction a plaintiff would build a case on.
140	
141	**Add to D06/D08:** a defined false-positive cost regime — for example, a service credit schedule tied to verified false-positive volume, capped, and explicitly excluding consequential damages. This converts an unbounded risk into a bounded, priced one.
142	
143	### 4. Detector data rights and the integration dependency
144	
145	**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §6 allocates the warranty in three parts: Railroad warrants its detector hardware; Supplier warrants its processing; neither warrants the other's domain. The Configuration Attestation plus detector maintenance records plus processing logs determine which domain a failure falls in.
146	
147	We integrate with the Railroad's existing wayside detectors. Who warrants that the detector data is accurate? Who is liable if the HBD feeding us is miscalibrated and we therefore miss a defect?
148	
149	**Add to D07:** a clear allocation. The Railroad warrants that detector hardware is maintained per its own standards and AAR recommended practice; AxiomDynamics warrants its processing of that data. **Neither party warrants the other's equipment.** Silence here is dangerous in both directions.
150	
151	### 5. Rollover cliff — the commercial trap in D05
152	
153	**Status: CLOSED** — D05 built. 90-day conversion election window; 50% pilot licence credit ($90K); three-year price lock (Years 1–3 at 0% increase, Year 4+ capped at 5%/yr); defined exit if declined; Year 1 termination for convenience at 60 days with no penalty.
154	
155	If the pilot converts on day 366 at full production price with no credit for pilot fees, the Railroad's internal ROI calculation changes shape at conversion and the deal dies at the CFO's desk, not the lawyer's. **D05 must specify: pilot fee credit, price protection for the first production term, a conversion window, and a defined outcome if they decline** — including whether they keep any data or reports produced during the pilot.
156	
157	### 6. Certification liability — an unnoticed exposure
158	
159	**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §16. Certification evidences completion of the curriculum and creates no liability for a Certified Reviewer's act or omission; the Railroad is solely responsible for its personnel.
160	
161	C02 certifies the Railroad's personnel. **If we certify someone and they then make a consequential error, are we liable for the certification?** This is a real and commonly-missed exposure in any product that trains its customer's staff. D07 must state that certification evidences competency against our curriculum, not a guarantee of individual performance, and that the Railroad retains employment and supervision responsibility.
162	
163	### 7. The air-gap representation problem
164	
165	**Status: CLOSED** — B05 verified against code: zero outbound calls. D09 §3.2 and D07 §7.1 both state it contractually. All four supply-chain gaps (dependency pinning, hash verification, SBOM and signed release artefacts — see B04 §7 and D09 §4.4) are disclosed in D09 §4.4 rather than papered over.
166	
167	We tell customers "on-premise, air-gap capable." If the product requires *any* outbound network call — licence check, telemetry, update ping — that representation is false, and it is the kind of false that surfaces during a security audit in month three.
168	
169	**B05 must be written by someone looking at the actual code, not the marketing.** Then D07 must match B05 exactly. If we need a licence server, say so and design the offline activation path; do not claim air-gap and then require a phone-home.
170	
171	### 8. Cyber incident notification
172	
173	**Status: CLOSED** — D09 §6. 72-hour Supplier-to-Railroad notification, 24-hour Railroad-to-Supplier for discovered vulnerabilities, defined reportable incident, 30-day root-cause analysis, and joint review. D07 §7.5 carries the same window in the master contract.
174	
175	Rail is now explicitly in scope for transportation-sector cyber risk. D09 must include a **breach notification window** (typically 72 hours), the notification channel, and what constitutes a reportable incident. Absent this, the Railroad's CISO will block the deployment regardless of what procurement agreed.
176	
177	### 9. Personnel security and background checks
178	
179	**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §7.7. Supplier personnel with access to Platform IP are subject to background verification; Supplier personnel require no access to Railroad systems at all, which is the structural answer. Railroad-specific screening on any on-site visit is accommodated.
180	
181	Railroad IT will ask whether our engineers have background checks, and whether they will accept the Railroad's. Especially relevant given federal hazmat and security-sensitive rail requirements.
182	
183	### 10. Export control and sanctions
184	
185	**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §13. Mutual compliance, denied-party confirmation, no encryption beyond OS and standard libraries, no re-export without authorisation.
186	
187	Even a domestic-only deployment can raise export-control questions if any component or engineer is foreign-sourced. Cheap to address in D07, expensive to discover later.
188	
189	### 11. Missing: escrow
190	
191	**Status: CLOSED** — D13 §4. Insolvency-triggered, running-version deposit, operability never ownership.
192	
193	If AxiomDynamics ceases to exist, can the Railroad keep operating? A **source code escrow** agreement (triggered on insolvency or cessation of support) is the standard answer and is often the clause that lets a sole-source vendor be approved at all. Given that this is a company selling to organisations that plan in decades, expect this question.
194	
195	### 12. Transition and exit assistance
196	
197	**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §15.6. On termination for any reason except Railroad's uncured breach, 90 days at no charge: data export, transition assistance, final configuration statement. D09 §5 on retention and deletion.
198	
199	What does the Railroad get on termination — data export format, a defined assistance period, and a prohibition on our retaining copies. Must be specified, not implied.
200	
201	---
202	
203	## Part IV — Precedence and construction
204	
205	To prevent the loophole where a technical annex contradicts the master contract:
206	
207	1. **D07 Comprehensive Master Contract** governs generally.
208	2. **D02 Master Pilot Agreement** governs during the pilot term, where it conflicts with D07.
209	3. **D09 Data Processing & Security Addendum** governs on data protection and security matters.
210	4. **D03 MSA** governs structure, ordering, and change control across all orders.
211	5. **D04 SOW** governs scope of work and deliverables for that specific order.
212	6. **A2 Rate Card** governs price. **Where any document's fee differs from A2, A2 wins.**
213	7. **B-series technical annexes** are descriptive and do not create warranties unless D07 expressly incorporates them.
214	8. **F-series forms** are administrative. Where a form conflicts with an agreement, the agreement governs. A form records an event; it does not vary a term.
215	9. Where a B-series document describes a capability that D07 disclaims, **the disclaimer governs and the annex must be corrected** — this is a drafting error to be fixed, not a gap to be argued.
216	
217	That rule 9 is the one that keeps this docket honest over time. Rule 6 is the one that keeps the numbers honest.
218	
219	---
220	
221	## Part V — Build status at a glance
222	
223	**Built — 36 Markdown documents plus one Excel model and one HTML one-pager (38 artifacts):** A1 ROI calculator (`.xlsx`) · **A2 rate card** · B01 blueprint · **B02 flow map** · **B03 one-page brief** · B04 tech stack · B05 data flow · C01 deployment SOP · C02 certification & assessment · **D01 preface & checklist** · D02 pilot agreement · **D03 MSA** · **D04 SOW templates** · D05 rollover mechanics · D06 support & SLA · D07 master contract · D08 licensing · D09 DPA · **D10 component register** · D11 NDA · D12 regulatory status · D13 IP & escrow · D14 operating model · **F00–F13 forms (14)** · this index.
224	
225	**Not yet built — 0.** Every document identified in Part II now exists.
226	
227	**All twelve identified contractual loopholes are closed.** That is a statement about the *documents*: every gap listed in Part III now has a clause that closes it. **It is not a statement that the build matches them** — four controls remain unbuilt, and they are listed in Part VI. A docket that claimed both would be claiming something the code does not support, which is the exact failure this index exists to prevent.
228	
229	**The agreement layer is complete.** A customer can be taken from first conversation to executed order, through pilot, through conversion, through support, through termination, using only documents in this docket. Nothing in that chain requires an improvised document.
230	
231	**Next by value:** nothing in the docket. The remaining work is not documentary — it is the four unbuilt controls in Part VI, the Phase 0 pre-signature items (LLC, EIN, insurance, bank, USPTO), and counsel review of the agreement layer. **A docket with no gaps in its index is a docket that has stopped being honest with itself; the gaps that remain are in the code and in the company formation, not in these documents.**
232	
233	**Deferred by decision:** E-series assurance documents (evidence registry, air-gap media chain of custody, DR/RTO/RPO, continuous compliance, records retention, RACI) — gaps identified in library reconciliation but not needed for a BNSF pilot; candidates for Phase 2.
234	
235	**Internal, moved to `assets/`:** carrier dossiers, library reconciliation, IP strategy.
236	
237	**Architectural decisions locked (B01):** fully on-premise edge, zero outbound network — **both built**. Signed certification registry and append-only disposition ledger — **design decided, not yet built; see Part VI.**
238	
239	> That distinction is the whole point of this index. A locked decision is a decision. It is not a delivered control, and the two must never be written in one sentence without the difference stated.
240	
241	**Commercial decision locked (D13):** AxiomDynamics retains all IP; escrow grants operability only on insolvency.
242	
243	---
244	
245	## Part VI — Known gaps between the docket and the build
246	
247	These are disclosed rather than hidden, and they are tracked here so the docket cannot drift ahead of the code without someone noticing.
248	
249	| Gap | Where disclosed | Consequence while open |
250	|---|---|---|
251	| **No detector ingest path at all** — no endpoint accepts a Railroad payload; signals are generated from physics equations on synthetic traces | B01 §7 gap #5 · **B02 §2** · **B03 status block** | **The largest gap in this table.** Every demonstration number is a demonstration of the method, not of the Railroad's data. The validation chain (schema, timestamp, plausibility) is designed and not built. |
252	| Disposition ledger **overwrites** rather than appends | B01 §7 gap #2 · D09 §4.4 · **F09 Part 7** | The ledger is a record, not an audit trail. Do not represent it as tamper-evident. |
253	| Certification registry is **local accounts**, no cryptographic verification | B01 §7 gap #1 · D09 §4.4 · **F08 Part 1** | Manual control via F08 is the substitute. A reviewer can self-assert a cert ID. |
254	| No SBOM artefact in releases | D09 §4.4 · **D09 §7.2** | Customer cannot independently verify the dependency chain. Target Q1 2027. |
255	| No hash pinning of dependencies | D09 §4.4 | A compromised package index could serve malware. Target Q1 2027. |
256	| No signed release artefacts | D09 §4.4 · **D09 §7.3** | A release archive could be substituted. Target Q2 2027. |
257	| Licence scope enforced **by contract only**, not by the software | D02 §6 · D05 §5.2 | Nothing technically prevents a second site. Scope is an obligation, not a control. |
258	| Insurance limit is **$2M, not $5M** | D07 §10.1 · D03 §9 | Stated honestly with a step-up commitment. Certificates must match the clause. |
259	
260	**The rule for this table:** a gap moves from here to closed only when the code changes, and the entries in B01, D09, F08 and F09 are amended in the same commit. Documenting a fix that was not made is the exact failure this docket was built to prevent.
261	
262	---
263	
264	*This docket index is a working structure, not a legal opinion. Every document in Part II under D must be reviewed by qualified counsel in the relevant jurisdiction before execution. Nothing here constitutes legal advice.*
265

# AxiomDynamics — Master Brief Docket
## Docket Index & Document Map

**Classification:** Client-facing. Reviewed by both parties' counsel.
**Purpose:** a single, uniform set of documents that defines the entire relationship between AxiomDynamics and the Railroad — from technical architecture through pilot execution through multi-year licensing — so that legal, IT, safety and procurement are all reading the same instrument.

**The principle behind this docket:** one service, one set of terms, no parallel side-letters. Every document in here must reconcile with every other. Where two documents could conflict, **the precedence ladder in Part IV of this document governs** — D02 contains no precedence clause of its own, and an index that points at a clause that does not exist is the same dangling-reference failure it exists to prevent. This exists to close the single most common loophole in rail technology contracts: a technical annex that promises something the master agreement disclaims.

---

## Part I — The relationship, in one sequence

```
PREFACE / DELIVERABLES CHECKLIST  (D01)
        ↓
BLUEPRINT OF THE BUILD  (B01–B05)
  flow map · infographic · tech stack · architecture
        ↓
SELF-DEPLOYMENT SOP  (C01)
  granular steps for the Railroad's own IT team
        ↓
CERTIFICATION & ROLE-BASED ASSESSMENT  (C02)
  who is trained, what they must prove, how they are certified
        ↓
MASTER PILOT AGREEMENT  (D02)
  the entry contract — scoped, time-boxed, reversible
        ↓
MASTER LICENSING & LIABILITY  (D08)
  what a licence is, what it costs, who bears what risk
        ↓
PILOT → YoY LICENSING ROLLOVER  (D05)
  how pilot converts to production without renegotiation
        ↓
TECH SUPPORT & RELEASE GOVERNANCE  (D06)
  updates, patching, CVE response, version policy
        ↓
COMPREHENSIVE MASTER CONTRACT  (D07)
  federal guidelines, data security, all limitations
```

| **F13** | Data Export & Transition Certificate | **Built** | What the Customer gets when it ends, in specific files, with reconciliation. |

---

## Part III — Loopholes identified, and current status

These are the gaps that most often go wrong in rail technology contracts specifically. Status markers show which are now closed by a built document and which remain open work.

### 1. The safety-critical disclaimer paradox — the biggest one

**Status: CLOSED** — D12 built. The decision-support framing is now fixed in D12 §§1–2, and D12 §9 makes it controlling over every other document.

Our claim is that we prevent derailments. Our inevitable limitation-of-liability clause will say we do not guarantee detection. **Put together, those two statements are a contradiction that a plaintiff's lawyer will find in ten minutes.**

The resolution is not to weaken either. It is to define the product precisely: AxiomDynamics is a **decision-support system** that presents a ranked, physics-derived risk assessment to a **qualified human reviewer**. The Railroad retains the operating decision. That framing must be *identical* in B01, C02, D02, D07 and D08 — same words, same scope. If the technical annex calls it a "detection system" and the contract calls it "decision support," we have manufactured our own liability.

**Add: D12 — Regulatory Status & Safety-Critical Function Statement.** A single annex that states, unambiguously, that this is not a certified safety appliance, is not a substitute for FRA-required inspection, and does not relieve the Railroad of any regulatory obligation. This protects both parties and is the document that makes the disclaimer credible rather than self-serving.

### 2. Data ownership vs. model improvement

**Status: CLOSED** — D13 §3 separates ownership explicitly. Default position is no cross-customer learning, which under AD-1 is structurally true rather than merely promised.

The standard clause — "Railroad owns its data" — is insufficient. The Railroad will ask: *if you train on our data, and the model improves, do we own the improvement? Do our competitors benefit?* Left unanswered, this stalls the deal at legal review every time.

**Add to D07/D09:** explicit separation of (a) Railroad's raw and derived operating data — owned by Railroad; (b) AxiomDynamics' models, weights, rules and source — owned by AxiomDynamics, including improvements derived from Railroad data; (c) a licence back to the Railroad for its own data in usable form on termination. Also state plainly whether cross-customer learning occurs — and if it does, that it is aggregated and non-attributable.

### 3. The "who pays for the false positive" gap

**Status: CLOSED** — D06 §4 defines a quarterly service credit schedule tied to measured false-positive rate, capped at the platform fee, excluding detector-data causes and consequential damages.

A false stop on a Class I main line costs train-hours, crew-hours, and network knock-on. **Nothing in the current documents says who bears the cost when we are wrong.** A railroad's counsel will ask this in the first meeting. If we have no answer, they will assume we bear it.

> **Note on the false-positive figure.** Earlier internal drafts cited "<0.1% false positives" as a marketing claim. **That figure was never measured and has been withdrawn from the client-facing docket** — D06 §4 now sets a measurement regime with no target, and A2 states no target. Claiming a rate before measuring it, in the same docket that promises a credit when the rate is high, is the contradiction a plaintiff would build a case on.

**Add to D06/D08:** a defined false-positive cost regime — for example, a service credit schedule tied to verified false-positive volume, capped, and explicitly excluding consequential damages. This converts an unbounded risk into a bounded, priced one.

### 4. Detector data rights and the integration dependency

**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §6 allocates the warranty in three parts: Railroad warrants its detector hardware; Supplier warrants its processing; neither warrants the other's domain. The Configuration Attestation plus detector maintenance records plus processing logs determine which domain a failure falls in.

We integrate with the Railroad's existing wayside detectors. Who warrants that the detector data is accurate? Who is liable if the HBD feeding us is miscalibrated and we therefore miss a defect?

**Add to D07:** a clear allocation. The Railroad warrants that detector hardware is maintained per its own standards and AAR recommended practice; AxiomDynamics warrants its processing of that data. **Neither party warrants the other's equipment.** Silence here is dangerous in both directions.

### 5. Rollover cliff — the commercial trap in D05

**Status: CLOSED** — D05 built. 90-day conversion election window; 50% pilot licence credit ($90K); three-year price lock (Years 1–3 at 0% increase, Year 4+ capped at 5%/yr); defined exit if declined; Year 1 termination for convenience at 60 days with no penalty.

If the pilot converts on day 366 at full production price with no credit for pilot fees, the Railroad's internal ROI calculation changes shape at conversion and the deal dies at the CFO's desk, not the lawyer's. **D05 must specify: pilot fee credit, price protection for the first production term, a conversion window, and a defined outcome if they decline** — including whether they keep any data or reports produced during the pilot.

### 6. Certification liability — an unnoticed exposure

**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §16. Certification evidences completion of the curriculum and creates no liability for a Certified Reviewer's act or omission; the Railroad is solely responsible for its personnel.

C02 certifies the Railroad's personnel. **If we certify someone and they then make a consequential error, are we liable for the certification?** This is a real and commonly-missed exposure in any product that trains its customer's staff. D07 must state that certification evidences competency against our curriculum, not a guarantee of individual performance, and that the Railroad retains employment and supervision responsibility.

### 7. The air-gap representation problem

**Status: CLOSED** — B05 verified against code: zero outbound calls. D09 §3.2 and D07 §7.1 both state it contractually. All four supply-chain gaps (dependency pinning, hash verification, SBOM and signed release artefacts — see B04 §7 and D09 §4.4) are disclosed in D09 §4.4 rather than papered over.

We tell customers "on-premise, air-gap capable." If the product requires *any* outbound network call — licence check, telemetry, update ping — that representation is false, and it is the kind of false that surfaces during a security audit in month three.

**B05 must be written by someone looking at the actual code, not the marketing.** Then D07 must match B05 exactly. If we need a licence server, say so and design the offline activation path; do not claim air-gap and then require a phone-home.

### 8. Cyber incident notification

**Status: CLOSED** — D09 §6. 72-hour Supplier-to-Railroad notification, 24-hour Railroad-to-Supplier for discovered vulnerabilities, defined reportable incident, 30-day root-cause analysis, and joint review. D07 §7.5 carries the same window in the master contract.

Rail is now explicitly in scope for transportation-sector cyber risk. D09 must include a **breach notification window** (typically 72 hours), the notification channel, and what constitutes a reportable incident. Absent this, the Railroad's CISO will block the deployment regardless of what procurement agreed.

### 9. Personnel security and background checks

**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §7.7. Supplier personnel with access to Platform IP are subject to background verification; Supplier personnel require no access to Railroad systems at all, which is the structural answer. Railroad-specific screening on any on-site visit is accommodated.

Railroad IT will ask whether our engineers have background checks, and whether they will accept the Railroad's. Especially relevant given federal hazmat and security-sensitive rail requirements.

### 10. Export control and sanctions

**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §13. Mutual compliance, denied-party confirmation, no encryption beyond OS and standard libraries, no re-export without authorisation.

Even a domestic-only deployment can raise export-control questions if any component or engineer is foreign-sourced. Cheap to address in D07, expensive to discover later.

### 11. Missing: escrow

**Status: CLOSED** — D13 §4. Insolvency-triggered, running-version deposit, operability never ownership.

If AxiomDynamics ceases to exist, can the Railroad keep operating? A **source code escrow** agreement (triggered on insolvency or cessation of support) is the standard answer and is often the clause that lets a sole-source vendor be approved at all. Given that this is a company selling to organisations that plan in decades, expect this question.

### 12. Transition and exit assistance

**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §15.6. On termination for any reason except Railroad's uncured breach, 90 days at no charge: data export, transition assistance, final configuration statement. D09 §5 on retention and deletion.

What does the Railroad get on termination — data export format, a defined assistance period, and a prohibition on our retaining copies. Must be specified, not implied.

---

## Part IV — Precedence and construction

To prevent the loophole where a technical annex contradicts the master contract:

1. **D07 Comprehensive Master Contract** governs generally.
2. **D02 Master Pilot Agreement** governs during the pilot term, where it conflicts with D07.
3. **D09 Data Processing & Security Addendum** governs on data protection and security matters.
4. **D03 MSA** governs structure, ordering, and change control across all orders.
5. **D04 SOW** governs scope of work and deliverables for that specific order.
6. **A2 Rate Card** governs price. **Where any document's fee differs from A2, A2 wins.**
7. **B-series technical annexes** are descriptive and do not create warranties unless D07 expressly incorporates them.
8. **F-series forms** are administrative. Where a form conflicts with an agreement, the agreement governs. A form records an event; it does not vary a term.
9. Where a B-series document describes a capability that D07 disclaims, **the disclaimer governs and the annex must be corrected** — this is a drafting error to be fixed, not a gap to be argued.

That rule 9 is the one that keeps this docket honest over time. Rule 6 is the one that keeps the numbers honest.

---

## Part V — Build status at a glance

**Built — 36 Markdown documents plus one Excel model and one HTML one-pager (38 artifacts):** A1 ROI calculator (`.xlsx`) · **A2 rate card** · B01 blueprint · **B02 flow map** · **B03 one-page brief** · B04 tech stack · B05 data flow · C01 deployment SOP · C02 certification & assessment · **D01 preface & checklist** · D02 pilot agreement · **D03 MSA** · **D04 SOW templates** · D05 rollover mechanics · D06 support & SLA · D07 master contract · D08 licensing · D09 DPA · **D10 component register** · D11 NDA · D12 regulatory status · D13 IP & escrow · D14 operating model · **F00–F13 forms (14)** · this index.

**Not yet built — 0.** Every document identified in Part II now exists.

**All twelve identified contractual loopholes are closed.** That is a statement about the *documents*: every gap listed in Part III now has a clause that closes it. **It is not a statement that the build matches them** — four controls remain unbuilt, and they are listed in Part VI. A docket that claimed both would be claiming something the code does not support, which is the exact failure this index exists to prevent.

**The agreement layer is complete.** A customer can be taken from first conversation to executed order, through pilot, through conversion, through support, through termination, using only documents in this docket. Nothing in that chain requires an improvised document.

**Next by value:** nothing in the docket. The remaining work is not documentary — it is the four unbuilt controls in Part VI, the Phase 0 pre-signature items (LLC, EIN, insurance, bank, USPTO), and counsel review of the agreement layer. **A docket with no gaps in its index is a docket that has stopped being honest with itself; the gaps that remain are in the code and in the company formation, not in these documents.**

**Deferred by decision:** E-series assurance documents (evidence registry, air-gap media chain of custody, DR/RTO/RPO, continuous compliance, records retention, RACI) — gaps identified in library reconciliation but not needed for a BNSF pilot; candidates for Phase 2.

**Internal, moved to `assets/`:** carrier dossiers, library reconciliation, IP strategy.

**Architectural decisions locked (B01):** fully on-premise edge, zero outbound network — **both built**. Signed certification registry and append-only disposition ledger — **design decided, not yet built; see Part VI.**

> That distinction is the whole point of this index. A locked decision is a decision. It is not a delivered control, and the two must never be written in one sentence without the difference stated.

**Commercial decision locked (D13):** AxiomDynamics retains all IP; escrow grants operability only on insolvency.

---

## Part VI — Known gaps between the docket and the build

These are disclosed rather than hidden, and they are tracked here so the docket cannot drift ahead of the code without someone noticing.

| Gap | Where disclosed | Consequence while open |
|---|---|---|
| **No detector ingest path at all** — no endpoint accepts a Railroad payload; signals are generated from physics equations on synthetic traces | B01 §7 gap #5 · **B02 §2** · **B03 status block** | **The largest gap in this table.** Every demonstration number is a demonstration of the method, not of the Railroad's data. The validation chain (schema, timestamp, plausibility) is designed and not built. |
| Disposition ledger **overwrites** rather than appends | B01 §7 gap #2 · D09 §4.4 · **F09 Part 7** | The ledger is a record, not an audit trail. Do not represent it as tamper-evident. |
| Certification registry is **local accounts**, no cryptographic verification | B01 §7 gap #1 · D09 §4.4 · **F08 Part 1** | Manual control via F08 is the substitute. A reviewer can self-assert a cert ID. |
| No SBOM artefact in releases | D09 §4.4 · **D09 §7.2** | Customer cannot independently verify the dependency chain. Target Q1 2027. |
| No hash pinning of dependencies | D09 §4.4 | A compromised package index could serve malware. Target Q1 2027. |
| No signed release artefacts | D09 §4.4 · **D09 §7.3** | A release archive could be substituted. Target Q2 2027. |
| Licence scope enforced **by contract only**, not by the software | D02 §6 · D05 §5.2 | Nothing technically prevents a second site. Scope is an obligation, not a control. |
| Insurance limit is **$2M, not $5M** | D07 §10.1 · D03 §9 | Stated honestly with a step-up commitment. Certificates must match the clause. |

**The rule for this table:** a gap moves from here to closed only when the code changes, and the entries in B01, D09, F08 and F09 are amended in the same commit. Documenting a fix that was not made is the exact failure this docket was built to prevent.

---

*This docket index is a working structure, not a legal opinion. Every document in Part II under D must be reviewed by qualified counsel in the relevant jurisdiction before execution. Nothing here constitutes legal advice.*

D07 must state that certification evidences competency against our curriculum, not a guarantee of individual performance, and that the Railroad retains employment and supervision responsibility.
162	
163	### 7. The air-gap representation problem
164	
165	**Status: CLOSED** — B05 verified against code: zero outbound calls. D09 §3.2 and D07 §7.1 both state it contractually. All four supply-chain gaps (dependency pinning, hash verification, SBOM and signed release artefacts — see B04 §7 and D09 §4.4) are disclosed in D09 §4.4 rather than papered over.
166	
167	We tell customers "on-premise, air-gap capable." If the product requires *any* outbound network call — licence check, telemetry, update ping — that representation is false, and it is the kind of false that surfaces during a security audit in month three.
168	
169	**B05 must be written by someone looking at the actual code, not the marketing.** Then D07 must match B05 exactly. If we need a licence server, say so and design the offline activation path; do not claim air-gap and then require a phone-home.
170	
171	### 8. Cyber incident notification
172	
173	**Status: CLOSED** — D09 §6. 72-hour Supplier-to-Railroad notification, 24-hour Railroad-to-Supplier for discovered vulnerabilities, defined reportable incident, 30-day root-cause analysis, and joint review. D07 §7.5 carries the same window in the master contract.
174	
175	Rail is now explicitly in scope for transportation-sector cyber risk. D09 must include a **breach notification window** (typically 72 hours), the notification channel, and what constitutes a reportable incident. Absent this, the Railroad's CISO will block the deployment regardless of what procurement agreed.
176	
177	### 9. Personnel security and background checks
178	
179	**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §7.7. Supplier personnel with access to Platform IP are subject to background verification; Supplier personnel require no access to Railroad systems at all, which is the structural answer. Railroad-specific screening on any on-site visit is accommodated.
180	
181	Railroad IT will ask whether our engineers have background checks, and whether they will accept the Railroad's. Especially relevant given federal hazmat and security-sensitive rail requirements.
182	
183	### 10. Export control and sanctions
184	
185	**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §13. Mutual compliance, denied-party confirmation, no encryption beyond OS and standard libraries, no re-export without authorisation.
186	
187	Even a domestic-only deployment can raise export-control questions if any component or engineer is foreign-sourced. Cheap to address in D07, expensive to discover later.
188	
189	### 11. Missing: escrow
190	
191	**Status: CLOSED** — D13 §4. Insolvency-triggered, running-version deposit, operability never ownership.
192	
193	If AxiomDynamics ceases to exist, can the Railroad keep operating? A **source code escrow** agreement (triggered on insolvency or cessation of support) is the standard answer and is often the clause that lets a sole-source vendor be approved at all. Given that this is a company selling to organisations that plan in decades, expect this question.
194	
195	### 12. Transition and exit assistance
196	
197	**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §15.6. On termination for any reason except Railroad's uncured breach, 90 days at no charge: data export, transition assistance, final configuration statement. D09 §5 on retention and deletion.
198	
199	What does the Railroad get on termination — data export format, a defined assistance period, and a prohibition on our retaining copies. Must be specified, not implied.
200	
201	---
202	
203	## Part IV — Precedence and construction
204	
205	To prevent the loophole where a technical annex contradicts the master contract:
206	
207	1. **D07 Comprehensive Master Contract** governs generally.
208	2. **D02 Master Pilot Agreement** governs during the pilot term, where it conflicts with D07.
209	3. **D09 Data Processing & Security Addendum** governs on data protection and security matters.
210	4. **D03 MSA** governs structure, ordering, and change control across all orders.
211	5. **D04 SOW** governs scope of work and deliverables for that specific order.
212	6. **A2 Rate Card** governs price. **Where any document's fee differs from A2, A2 wins.**
213	7. **B-series technical annexes** are descriptive and do not create warranties unless D07 expressly incorporates them.
214	8. **F-series forms** are administrative. Where a form conflicts with an agreement, the agreement governs. A form records an event; it does not vary a term.
215	9. Where a B-series document describes a capability that D07 disclaims, **the disclaimer governs and the annex must be corrected** — this is a drafting error to be fixed, not a gap to be argued.
216	
217	That rule 9 is the one that keeps this docket honest over time. Rule 6 is the one that keeps the numbers honest.
218	
219	---
220	
221	## Part V — Build status at a glance
222	
223	**Built — 36 Markdown documents plus one Excel model and one HTML one-pager (38 artifacts):** A1 ROI calculator (`.xlsx`) · **A2 rate card** · B01 blueprint · **B02 flow map** · **B03 one-page brief** · B04 tech stack · B05 data flow · C01 deployment SOP · C02 certification & assessment · **D01 preface & checklist** · D02 pilot agreement · **D03 MSA** · **D04 SOW templates** · D05 rollover mechanics · D06 support & SLA · D07 master contract · D08 licensing · D09 DPA · **D10 component register** · D11 NDA · D12 regulatory status · D13 IP & escrow · D14 operating model · **F00–F13 forms (14)** · this index.
224	
225	**Not yet built — 0.** Every document identified in Part II now exists.
226	
227	**All twelve identified contractual loopholes are closed.** That is a statement about the *documents*: every gap listed in Part III now has a clause that closes it. **It is not a statement that the build matches them** — four controls remain unbuilt, and they are listed in Part VI. A docket that claimed both would be claiming something the code does not support, which is the exact failure this index exists to prevent.
228	
229	**The agreement layer is complete.** A customer can be taken from first conversation to executed order, through pilot, through conversion, through support, through termination, using only documents in this docket. Nothing in that chain requires an improvised document.
230	
231	**Next by value:** nothing in the docket. The remaining work is not documentary — it is the four unbuilt controls in Part VI, the Phase 0 pre-signature items (LLC, EIN, insurance, bank, USPTO), and counsel review of the agreement layer. **A docket with no gaps in its index is a docket that has stopped being honest with itself; the gaps that remain are in the code and in the company formation, not in these documents.**
232

234	
235	**Internal, moved to `assets/`:** carrier dossiers, library reconciliation, IP strategy.
236	
237	**Architectural decisions locked (B01):** fully on-premise edge, zero outbound network — **both built**. Signed certification registry and append-only disposition ledger — **design decided, not yet built; see Part VI.**
238	
239	> That distinction is the whole point of this index. A locked decision is a decision. It is not a delivered control, and the two must never be written in one sentence without the difference stated.
240	
241	**Commercial decision locked (D13):** AxiomDynamics retains all IP; escrow grants operability only on insolvency.
242	
243	---
244	
245	## Part VI — Known gaps between the docket and the build
246	
247	These are disclosed rather than hidden, and they are tracked here so the docket cannot drift ahead of the code without someone noticing.
248	
249	| Gap | Where disclosed | Consequence while open |
250	|---|---|---|
251	| **No detector ingest path at all** — no endpoint accepts a Railroad payload; signals are generated from physics equations on synthetic traces | B01 §7 gap #5 · **B02 §2** · **B03 status block** | **The largest gap in this table.** Every demonstration number is a demonstration of the method, not of the Railroad's data. The validation chain (schema, timestamp, plausibility) is designed and not built. |
252	| Disposition ledger **overwrites** rather than appends | B01 §7 gap #2 · D09 §4.4 · **F09 Part 7** | The ledger is a record, not an audit trail. Do not represent it as tamper-evident. |
253	| Certification registry is **local accounts**, no cryptographic verification | B01 §7 gap #1 · D09 §4.4 · **F08 Part 1** | Manual control via F08 is the substitute. A reviewer can self-assert a cert ID. |
254	| No SBOM artefact in releases | D09 §4.4 · **D09 §7.2** | Customer cannot independently verify the dependency chain. Target Q1 2027. |
255	| No hash pinning of dependencies | D09 §4.4 | A compromised package index could serve malware. Target Q1 2027. |
256	| No signed release artefacts | D09 §4.4 · **D09 §7.3** | A release archive could be substituted. Target Q2 2027. |
257	| Licence scope enforced **by contract only**, not by the software | D02 §6 · D05 §5.2 | Nothing technically prevents a second site. Scope is an obligation, not a control. |
258	| Insurance limit is **$2M, not $5M** | D07 §10.1 · D03 §9 | Stated honestly with a step-up commitment. Certificates must match the clause. |

################ project-logs/chat-1/SUMMARY.md ################
# Chat-1 — Summary

**Thread:** the original AxiomDynamics build conversation, resumed across three
raw session logs.
**Span:** 2026-11-08 04:24 → 2026-11-10 03:00 (per the transcript index produced
at the end of chat-1).

> **What this file is.** A distillation, written at the close of chat-1. The
> conversation itself — 2,527 turns — was extracted into readable transcripts and
> **those files were lost** when the sandbox was destroyed (see
> `../README.md`). This summary is therefore the only surviving record of chat-1,
> and it is a judgement about what mattered, not a transcript. Read it knowing
> that.

---

## What chat-1 built

The project began from a Master Build & Rollout prompt that set the physics-first
philosophy: named physical models, rolling per-axle z-scores, kinematics from
`E_k = ½mv²`, acoustics against the standard bearing defect-frequency equations —
explicitly *not* black-box ML and *not* fixed absolute alarm thresholds. That
philosophy was never varied, at the user's standing instruction: **"we will keep
this same concept throughout."**

From there, chat-1 built the Master Brief Docket: the A-series commercial
documents (ROI model, rate card), B-series technical (blueprint, flow map,
infographic, stack disclosure, data residency), C-series deployment (self-deploy
SOP, certification), D-series contractual (D01–D14), and the F-series forms
(F00–F13).

Commits that reached GitHub, in order: `d05501f` (D14), `e8a08fc` (D13),
`7c47aa6` (D12/D11/D02), `96e058c` (D07/C01/C02), `b9aa4a8` (D05/D06/D09, 12
loopholes closed, 16/30 built), `cf2e6ba` (Q7: F00–F13, A2, D03, D04, D01, D10,
two-pass consistency audit), `33ccc7e` (B02/B03, build status reconciled),
`de9b245` (B02/B03 corrected to disclose no detector ingest path).

## What chat-1 caught

The corrections matter more than the builds, because they are the pattern chat-2
inherits:

- **The detector ingest path was drawn as built.** B02 and B03 showed a flow from
  detector to edge inference; no endpoint accepts a Railroad payload. Corrected in
  `de9b245`. This is the largest gap in the docket and it was found by checking a
  diagram against the code, not by reading the diagram.
- **D09 §4.3 promised an SBOM that §4.4 listed as a gap** — in the same document,
  six lines apart. Corrected to state the negative plainly.
- **D07 §15.4 contradicted D03 §12.1** on convenience termination. Both cannot be
  right; the position was made consistent.
- **D08 is a commercial annex, not an instrument to sign.** Relabelled so nobody
  executes it.

## What chat-1 decided

- **A2 governs price across the entire docket.** Where any other document's fee
  differs from A2, A2 wins.
- **D07 and D02 are what a customer executes.** D08 explains the money; it is not
  a contract.
- **Texas law is the working expectation** for venue — recorded as an expectation,
  not a term.
- **The document precedence order in D00 Part IV governs** conflicts between
  documents.

## What chat-1 left open

1. **The A2/D08 arithmetic pass** — not re-derived since `cf2e6ba`.
2. **D07 §14.3 venue** — pointed at an Order signature-block field that no Order
   template contains. (Found at the very end of chat-1; rebuilt in chat-2.)
3. **D09 signed-release language** — existed only as a §4.4 gap row, never stated
   affirmatively. (Closed in chat-2 as §7.3.)
4. **The F00 blank-versus-decision distinction** — a blank and an unmade decision
   were written identically. (Closed in chat-2 as Rule 7.)
5. **Q6 — entity formation and support boundary.** Written at the close of
   chat-1, lost with the sandbox, rebuilt in chat-2.

## The pattern worth carrying forward

Nearly every bad citation in chat-1 came from writing a claim from memory and
checking it afterwards. The worst defect in the project came from the same habit
applied to a diagram: it looked right, so nobody checked whether it was true.

**Verify against the file, then write.**

# Transcripts

Conversation records for the project.

## What is here

| File | Turns | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| `2026-11-09-chat-2.md` | 256 | chat-2, from the first line to the point of extraction |
| `raw/2026-11-09-chat-2.jsonl` | 780 events | the unprocessed session log, 1.6 MB |

The `.md` is the readable version: every user and assistant turn in order. Tool
calls are recorded inline so you can see what was run; tool *output* — command
results, file listings, screenshots — is omitted, because it is bulk without
being conversation.

The `.jsonl` in `raw/` is the source. Don't edit it. It is what the `.md` was
derived from, so if the extraction ever looks wrong, the raw file is the answer.

## What is NOT here, and cannot be

**Chat-1 — the original build conversation — is lost.**

It ran from 2026-11-08 04:24 to 2026-11-10 03:00 and covered 2,527 turns across
three raw session logs. Chat-1 did extract those into readable transcripts. They
were written into a sandbox whose storage was destroyed when the session ended,
and they never reached this repository. The raw logs they came from were in the
same place and went with them.

There is no copy. No archive, no mirror, no cache. `project-logs/chat-1/SUMMARY.md`
is the only surviving record of that conversation, and it is a distillation — a
judgement about what mattered, not the conversation itself.

**This is why it will not happen again:** every session from chat-2 forward is
extracted and committed at the end of the session it belongs to, raw log included.
Nothing is left in sandbox storage to be lost.

## Reproducing an extraction

The raw log lives at
`.claude/projects/session/<session-id>.jsonl` inside the session's mounted
folder. The extractor keeps only `user` and `assistant` events, drops sidechains
and system reminders, and writes them in order. It is a small script and easy to
rewrite if needed; the point is that the **raw file is committed**, so the
conversation survives even if the extractor does not.

# AxiomDynamics — Working Tree

Two folders, one rule.

## The classification rule

> **If a customer could read it, it goes in `client-assets/`. If it is about us — our strategy, our weaknesses, our playbook, our research — it goes in `assets/`.**

This is not a filing preference. `client-assets/` is presumed forwardable to a Class I railroad's legal and procurement teams. Anything sitting there may be attached to an email without a second thought. Anything in `assets/` may not.

That rule was violated with the first three carrier dossiers, which contained our competitive strategy, our assessment of which carriers are buyable and which are not, and our judgement about a customer's negotiating position. Moved to `assets/market-intel/carrier-dossiers/`.

## `client-assets/` — forwardable

One deliverable: the **Master Brief Docket**. A uniform contract-and-architecture set reviewed by both parties' counsel. Index and document register in `MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/D00-DOCKET-INDEX.md`.

```
client-assets/
└── MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/
    ├── D00-DOCKET-INDEX.md            docket map, precedence rules, gap analysis
    ├── A1-ROI-MODEL/                  Excel business case + build script
    └── D08-MASTER-LICENSING-AND-LIABILITY.md
```

Docket parts: commercial model (A), build blueprint for the Railroad's IT (B), deployment and certification (C), legal contract stack (D).

## `assets/` — internal only

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `market-intel/carrier-dossiers/` | BNSF; UP/NS; CN/CPKC network dossiers |
| `external-pilot-cost-structure-and-licensing-model.md` | Internal copy of the commercial model |

## Current build state

**Built:** ROI model (A1), licensing model (D08, commercial grade — needs conversion to contract language), docket index (D00).

**Highest value next:** NDA (D11), tech stack disclosure (B04), master pilot agreement (D02).

**Deliberately not built:** the earlier `04-pilot-proposal` narrative — superseded by D02 as a legal instrument.

## Standing constraints

- Nothing in `assets/` may be forwarded. Nothing in `client-assets/` may contain internal assessment.
- Every legal document in the docket requires review by qualified counsel before execution.
- Carrier dossiers require re-verification before use — the UP/NS merger is live and the facts move.

################ ROOT README ################
# AxiomDynamics — Physics-First Predictive Maintenance (Demo)

A small web app for freight-rail predictive maintenance built on three
named physical models instead of black-box ML or fixed alarm thresholds:

1. **Thermodynamics** — wheel-bearing temperature rate-of-change, flagged
   with a rolling z-score against each axle's own recent baseline, instead
   of a fixed absolute alarm. Also computes the legacy check correctly:
   real hot-bearing detectors alarm on temperature **above ambient**, not
   a flat number (see "East Palestine" note below).
2. **Peer comparison** — a robust median/MAD z-score against (a) this
   axle's own detector-pass history and (b) every other axle in the fleet
   right now, so a reading is judged against what's normal for it and for
   its peers, not in isolation.
3. **Kinematics** — coasting distance/energy from `E_k = 1/2 m v^2` plus
   grade and resistance terms, integrated numerically, to predict whether
   a car will stop or run away on a given grade.
4. **Acoustics** — FFT vibration analysis against the standard
   rolling-element bearing defect-frequency equations (BPFO, BPFI, BSF,
   FTF), to flag a specific defect frequency standing out above the noise
   floor, rather than a generic "weird sound" classifier.
5. **Same-axle left/right differential** — standard hot-bearing practice
   alongside the ambient-relative check: the two journals on one axle
   share load path and speed, so a large gap between them (independent of
   either journal's absolute level) points at a one-sided defect.
6. **Executive ROI panel** (`backend/roi.py`, `GET /api/roi`) — fleet
   mission-ready %, net estimated benefit, mean-time-to-detect vs. legacy,
   and open review counts, shown as a KPI strip at the top of the
   dashboard, built on real cited derailment cost data (see "ROI research"
   below) blended with clearly-labeled modeling assumptions where no
   public figure exists.
7. **Human reviewer disposition** — each Ghost Warrant has a real
   disposition workflow (`POST /api/warrant/{advisory_id}/disposition`):
   a named reviewer with a certification ID records Concur & Dispatch,
   Escalate, Override/Downgrade, or Reject Sensor Hardware. This is not
   decorative — it's what makes "a human is in the loop" an actual
   recorded action instead of a claim in a README. (In-memory only in
   this demo; resets on restart.)
7. **Evidence fusion → Predictive Ghost Warrants** — no single signal can
   trigger the top severity tier by itself. `backend/warrants.py` only
   escalates to **URGENT REVIEW** when at least two independent signal
   types agree; a lone signal (even a critical one) is capped at
   **REVIEW**. Every warrant carries a SHA-256 hash of its evidence for a
   tamper-evident audit trail, and severity tiers are named
   INFORMATIONAL / REVIEW / URGENT REVIEW specifically so they can't be
   mistaken for an operational alarm level — this system never issues a
   stop-train or braking instruction.

Every number in the dashboard traces back to an equation in
`backend/physics.py` — read that file's docstrings for the exact formulas
and their sources. Nothing here is a trained model or a mystery black box.

## Why this design, not just "AI predicts failures"

This isn't arbitrary. [NTSB testimony on the Feb 3, 2023 East Palestine,
OH derailment](https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/Documents/East%20Palestine%20Ohio%20Board%20Meeting%20Summary%20with%20Amendments.pdf)
found the failed bearing read 253°F above a 10°F ambient at the final
detector before critical alarm — by then it was in its final stage of
mechanical failure. [FRA Safety Advisory 2023-01](https://railroads.dot.gov/sites/fra.dot.gov/files/2023-02/(Safety%20Advisory%202023-01%20%20Posting%20on-line%20022823).pdf)
and its supplements, issued because of that derailment, call out the
specific gaps this design targets: single-point checks with no trend
history, inconsistent thresholds across detectors, and no standard
practice for comparing a reading against a bearing's own history or its
peers. The demo fleet includes a unit (U3) deliberately modeled on that
night's cold-ambient conditions, specifically to show the gap between a
legacy point-in-time check and a trend/peer-aware one on the same data.

## Why no FastAPI / Chart.js / npm install

This was deliberately built on nothing but the Python standard library
(`http.server`) plus `numpy` for FFT/array math, and plain Canvas/JS on the
frontend with zero CDN dependencies. That's not a style preference — it's
the actual deployment story for an air-gapped wayside/dispatch environment,
where IT will not approve installing a dependency tree on a live network.
Run it with:

```bash
pip install numpy   # only dependency; skip if numpy is already present (sqlite3 is in the Python stdlib)
cd axiomdynamics-app
python3 -m backend.main
```

Then open **http://127.0.0.1:8420/** in a browser. Click any row in the
Fleet table to see that axle's thermodynamics, acoustics, and kinematics
detail charts.

## What's real and what's simulated

There is no freely downloadable, public, real-time rail wayside sensor
dataset (the datasets that exist, like CWRU's bearing set, are generic
motor-test-rig data behind a university host, not rail axle data — and
this build environment had no outbound internet access to fetch anything
anyway). So `backend/simulate.py` generates synthetic sensor traces **from
the same physics equations in `physics.py`**, with documented fault
conditions injected (a bearing-wear friction ramp for the thermal fault, an
injected BPFO-frequency harmonic for the acoustic fault). Every constant
used (bearing geometry, thermal mass, radial load, etc.) is called out in
that file as "representative," not pulled from a specific OEM spec.

To point this at real sensor data later, replace the three `generate_*`
functions in `simulate.py` with loaders that return the same shapes
(`times, temps_f` / `t, signal, defect_freqs, shaft_hz`) — `physics.py` and
`main.py` don't care where the samples came from.

## ROI research: real bearing-failure derailment costs

The ROI panel's cost figures come from two real, cited cost tiers rather
than an invented "average cost per derailment" (no such standardized
public figure exists — FRA tracks accident counts and causes, not a
normalized dollar average).

**Tier 1 — contained bearing/wheelset failure, no hazmat release:**
a BNSF bearing-related derailment with $5,000,000 in reported damage
([NTSB](https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/accidentreports/reports/rab1712.pdf)),
and a separate BNSF derailment with $13,500,000 in reported damage,
explicitly excluding lading and environmental remediation costs
([NTSB docket](https://data.ntsb.gov/Docket/Document/docBLOB?FileExtension=.PDF&FileName=BNSF%20Equipment%20Incident%20Report-Redacted.PDF&ID=40457595)).
These two figures bracket the $5.0M–$13.5M range used as the "contained"
tier.

**Tier 2 — catastrophic failure with hazmat release:** the Feb 3, 2023
East Palestine, OH derailment (Norfolk Southern, not BNSF, but the same
wheel-bearing failure mode this product targets) cost over $310 million
in a federal EPA/DOJ settlement
([DOJ](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/united-states-reaches-over-310-million-settlement-norfolk-southern-address-harms-caused-east)),
a separate $600 million personal-injury class settlement paid fully by
Norfolk Southern
([AP](https://apnews.com/article/east-palestine-derailment-norfolk-southern-gatx-oxyvinyls-2d5110bf096ec3524f3092999bee3060)),
and a cumulative cost reported to have exceeded $1 billion by mid-2024
([KTEN](https://www.kten.com/story/49275631/east-palestine-train-derailment-has-now-cost-norfolk-southern-1-billion)).

**What's an assumption, not a citation:** there is no published base rate
for what fraction of missed bearing defects progress to a catastrophic
event versus stay contained. `backend/roi.py` uses a conservative 2%
placeholder (`P_CATASTROPHIC_GIVEN_MISSED_DEFECT`) and blends the two
sourced tiers into one expected-cost figure. Replace that probability —
and the inspection-cost and detection-time constants, which are also
unsourced placeholders — with your own numbers, or a pilot customer's
real safety/cost data, before this supports an actual business case.

## One important caveat on the kinematics module

The coasting model assumes **no brake or throttle input at all** for as
long as you let it run. On a steep enough descending grade it will show
the car accelerating toward a terminal velocity that a real train would
never actually reach, because crews brake well before that. Read a
"will accelerate on this grade" result as *"this axle needs braking input
to control speed here,"* not as a forecast of what a train will actually
do — it's a decision-support signal, not a crystal ball.

## Project layout

```
backend/
  physics.py    the three physics modules (thermo / kinematics / acoustics)
  simulate.py   synthetic fleet + sensor trace generator
  main.py       stdlib HTTP server, routes, static file serving
frontend/
  index.html, style.css, app.js   dashboard UI, vanilla JS canvas charts
tests/
  test_physics.py   correctness tests for every formula
  run_tests.py      stdlib-only test runner (use this if pytest isn't installed)
```

## Running the tests

```bash
python3 tests/run_tests.py     # no pytest needed
# or, if you have pytest:
pytest tests/
```

## API routes

- `GET /api/fleet` — summary status for every axle
- `GET /api/alerts` — combined predictive alerts, most severe first
- `GET /api/unit/{id}/thermo` — temperature series + z-score sweep + alerts
- `GET /api/unit/{id}/acoustics` — FFT spectrum + defect frequency matches
- `GET /api/unit/{id}/kinematics` — coasting profile for that axle's car
- `GET /api/roi` — fleet-wide executive KPI summary (mission-ready %, net
  estimated benefit, mean-time-to-detect, open reviews)
- `POST /api/warrant/{advisory_id}/disposition` — record a reviewer's
  disposition (`{"reviewer_name", "cert_id", "disposition"}`, where
  disposition is one of `concur_dispatch`, `escalate`,
  `override_downgrade`, `reject_sensor`). Persisted in `axiom.db`
  (SQLite, stdlib `sqlite3`, survives a restart).

## Deploying to Render (free tier)

This gets you a real `https://your-app-name.onrender.com` URL anyone can
open without installing anything. Render needs your code in a git repo it
can pull from (GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket) — if this folder isn't a git
repo yet:

```bash
cd axiomdynamics-app
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
```

Then push it to a new GitHub repo (create one at github.com/new, then
follow the push instructions it gives you).

**Option A — Blueprint (uses the included `render.yaml`):**
1. Go to [render.com](https://render.com) and sign up / log in.
2. Dashboard → **New** → **Blueprint**.
3. Connect your GitHub account and select this repo.
4. Render reads `render.yaml` and fills everything in automatically —
   review and click **Apply**.

**Option B — Manual web service (if you skip the Blueprint):**
1. Dashboard → **New** → **Web Service** → connect this repo.
2. Runtime: **Python 3**.
3. Build command: `pip install -r requirements.txt`
4. Start command: `python -m backend.main`
5. Add an environment variable: `AXIOM_HOST` = `0.0.0.0`
6. Instance type: **Free**.
7. Click **Create Web Service**.

Either way, Render builds and deploys automatically, then gives you a
public URL (first load on the free tier can take ~30-60s if the instance
had spun down from inactivity — that's normal, not a bug).

**Important caveat — reviewer dispositions won't persist on Render's free
tier.** Free-tier instances have an ephemeral filesystem: it spins down
after inactivity and loses any local file changes, including `axiom.db`.
Dispositions you record will survive until the instance sleeps, then
reset. This is fine for a demo; for a real pilot, upgrade to a paid Render
plan with a persistent disk, or point `AXIOM_DB_PATH` at a managed
database instead of local SQLite.

# AxiomDynamics — Physics-First Predictive Maintenance (Demo)

A small web app for freight-rail predictive maintenance built on three
named physical models instead of black-box ML or fixed alarm thresholds:

1. **Thermodynamics** — wheel-bearing temperature rate-of-change, flagged
   with a rolling z-score against each axle's own recent baseline, instead
   of a fixed absolute alarm. Also computes the legacy check correctly:
   real hot-bearing detectors alarm on temperature **above ambient**, not
   a flat number (see "East Palestine" note below).
2. **Peer comparison** — a robust median/MAD z-score against (a) this
   axle's own detector-pass history and (b) every other axle in the fleet
   right now, so a reading is judged against what's normal for it and for
   its peers, not in isolation.
3. **Kinematics** — coasting distance/energy from `E_k = 1/2 m v^2` plus
   grade and resistance terms, integrated numerically, to predict whether
   a car will stop or run away on a given grade.
4. **Acoustics** — FFT vibration analysis against the standard
   rolling-element bearing defect-frequency equations (BPFO, BPFI, BSF,
   FTF), to flag a specific defect frequency standing out above the noise
   floor, rather than a generic "weird sound" classifier.
5. **Same-axle left/right differential** — standard hot-bearing practice
   alongside the ambient-relative check: the two journals on one axle
   share load path and speed, so a large gap between them (independent of
   either journal's absolute level) points at a one-sided defect.
6. **Executive ROI panel** (`backend/roi.py`, `GET /api/roi`) — fleet
   mission-ready %, net estimated benefit, mean-time-to-detect vs. legacy,
   and open review counts, shown as a KPI strip at the top of the
   dashboard, built on real cited derailment cost data (see "ROI research"
   below) blended with clearly-labeled modeling assumptions where no
   public figure exists.
7. **Human reviewer disposition** — each Ghost Warrant has a real
   disposition workflow (`POST /api/warrant/{advisory_id}/disposition`):
   a named reviewer with a certification ID records Concur & Dispatch,
   Escalate, Override/Downgrade, or Reject Sensor Hardware. This is not
   decorative — it's what makes "a human is in the loop" an actual
   recorded action instead of a claim in a README. (In-memory only in
   this demo; resets on restart.)
7. **Evidence fusion → Predictive Ghost Warrants** — no single signal can
   trigger the top severity tier by itself. `backend/warrants.py` only
   escalates to **URGENT REVIEW** when at least two independent signal
   types agree; a lone signal (even a critical one) is capped at
   **REVIEW**. Every warrant carries a SHA-256 hash of its evidence for a
   tamper-evident audit trail, and severity tiers are named
   INFORMATIONAL / REVIEW / URGENT REVIEW specifically so they can't be
   mistaken for an operational alarm level — this system never issues a
   stop-train or braking instruction.

Every number in the dashboard traces back to an equation in
`backend/physics.py` — read that file's docstrings for the exact formulas
and their sources. Nothing here is a trained model or a mystery black box.

## Why this design, not just "AI predicts failures"

This isn't arbitrary. [NTSB testimony on the Feb 3, 2023 East Palestine,
OH derailment](https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/Documents/East%20Palestine%20Ohio%20Board%20Meeting%20Summary%20with%20Amendments.pdf)
found the failed bearing read 253°F above a 10°F ambient at the final
detector before critical alarm — by then it was in its final stage of
mechanical failure. [FRA Safety Advisory 2023-01](https://railroads.dot.gov/sites/fra.dot.gov/files/2023-02/(Safety%20Advisory%202023-01%20%20Posting%20on-line%20022823).pdf)
and its supplements, issued because of that derailment, call out the
specific gaps this design targets: single-point checks with no trend
history, inconsistent thresholds across detectors, and no standard
practice for comparing a reading against a bearing's own history or its
peers. The demo fleet includes a unit (U3) deliberately modeled on that
night's cold-ambient conditions, specifically to show the gap between a
legacy point-in-time check and a trend/peer-aware one on the same data.
