(`http.server`) plus `numpy` for FFT/array math, and plain Canvas/JS on the
frontend with zero CDN dependencies. That's not a style preference — it's
the actual deployment story for an air-gapped wayside/dispatch environment,
where IT will not approve installing a dependency tree on a live network.

```bash
python3 -m backend.main
```

Then open **http://127.0.0.1:8420/** in a browser. Click any row in the
Fleet table to see that axle's thermodynamics, acoustics, and kinematics
detail charts.

## What's real and what's simulated

There is no freely downloadable, public, real-time rail wayside sensor
dataset (the datasets that exist, like CWRU's bearing set, are generic
motor-test-rig data behind a university host, not rail axle data — and
this build environment had no outbound internet access to fetch anything
anyway). So `backend/simulate.py` generates synthetic sensor traces **from
the same physics equations in `physics.py`**, with documented fault
conditions injected (a bearing-wear friction ramp for the thermal fault, an
injected BPFO-frequency harmonic for the acoustic fault). Every constant
used (bearing geometry, thermal mass, radial load, etc.) is called out in
that file as "representative," not pulled from a specific OEM spec.

functions in `simulate.py` with loaders that return the same shapes
(`times, temps_f` / `t, signal, defect_freqs, shaft_hz`) — `physics.py` and
`main.py` don't care where the samples came from.

## ROI research: real bearing-failure derailment costs

The ROI panel's cost figures come from two real, cited cost tiers rather
than an invented "average cost per derailment" (no such standardized
public figure exists — FRA tracks accident counts and causes, not a
normalized dollar average).

a BNSF bearing-related derailment with $5,000,000 in reported damage
([NTSB](https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/accidentreports/reports/rab1712.pdf)),
and a separate BNSF derailment with $13,500,000 in reported damage,
explicitly excluding lading and environmental remediation costs
([NTSB docket](https://data.ntsb.gov/Docket/Document/docBLOB?FileExtension=.PDF&FileName=BNSF%20Equipment%20Incident%20Report-Redacted.PDF&ID=40457595)).
These two figures bracket the $5.0M–$13.5M range used as the "contained"
tier.

**Tier 2 — catastrophic failure with hazmat release:** the Feb 3, 2023
East Palestine, OH derailment (Norfolk Southern, not BNSF, but the same
wheel-bearing failure mode this product targets) cost over $310 million
in a federal EPA/DOJ settlement
([DOJ](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/united-states-reaches-over-310-million-settlement-norfolk-southern-address-harms-caused-east)),
a separate $600 million personal-injury class settlement paid fully by
Norfolk Southern
([AP](https://apnews.com/article/east-palestine-derailment-norfolk-southern-gatx-oxyvinyls-2d5110bf096ec3524f3092999bee3060)),
and a cumulative cost reported to have exceeded $1 billion by mid-2024
([KTEN](https://www.kten.com/story/49275631/east-palestine-train-derailment-has-now-cost-norfolk-southern-1-billion)).

3	
4	Three independent, named-physical-law analysis modules. Each one is a
5	deliberate upgrade over a specific legacy practice in freight rail wayside

11	                    absolute threshold (e.g. 170F). That misses a bearing
12	                    that is heating rapidly but hasn't crossed the line yet.
13	                    Here we track dT/dt (Newton's-law-of-cooling-consistent)
14	                    and flag when the *rate* is a statistical outlier
15	                    (z-score) against that axle's own recent baseline.
16	
17	2. kinematics       Coasting distance/energy prediction from first
18	                    principles: KE = 1/2 m v^2, plus grade (gravity) and
19	                    resistance (rolling + aerodynamic drag) work terms,
20	                    integrated numerically.
21	
22	3. acoustics        FFT-based bearing defect detection using the standard
23	                    rolling-element bearing defect-frequency equations
24	                    (BPFO, BPFI, BSF, FTF) from vibration analysis, not a
25	                    generic "listen for weird noise" model.

27	None of this is mystical. Every function below names the textbook equation

34	from dataclasses import dataclass, field
35	from typing import List, Dict, Optional, Tuple

39	# ===========================================================================
40	# 1. THERMODYNAMICS: rate-of-change (z-score) bearing temperature alerting
41	# ===========================================================================

44	def rolling_rate_of_change(temps_f: np.ndarray, times_s: np.ndarray, window: int = 5) -> np.ndarray:
45	    """
46	    dT/dt in degrees F per minute, via backward finite difference over a
47	    trailing `window` of samples. First `window` samples are NaN (no history
48	    yet).
49	    """
50	    temps_f = np.asarray(temps_f, dtype=float)
51	    times_s = np.asarray(times_s, dtype=float)
52	    n = len(temps_f)
53	    rates = np.full(n, np.nan)
54	    for i in range(window, n):
55	        dt_s = times_s[i] - times_s[i - window]
56	        if dt_s <= 0:
57	            continue
58	        dtemp = temps_f[i] - temps_f[i - window]
59	        rates[i] = dtemp / (dt_s / 60.0)
60	    return rates
61	
62	
63	@dataclass
64	class ThermoAlert:
65	    index: int
66	    time_s: float
67	    temp_f: float
68	    rate_f_per_min: float
69	    zscore: float
70	    severity: str  # "watch" | "warning" | "critical"
71	
72	
73	def zscore_sweep(
74	    temps_f: np.ndarray,
75	    times_s: np.ndarray,
76	    window: int = 10,
77	    baseline_window: int = 36,
78	    z_watch: float = 2.5,
79	    z_warning: float = 3.5,
80	    z_critical: float = 5.0,
81	    min_rate_f_per_min: float = 0.4,
82	) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, List[ThermoAlert]]:
83	    """
84	    Compute rolling rate-of-change, then a rolling z-score of that rate
85	    against its own trailing baseline (mean/std over `baseline_window`
86	    prior samples). Flags a point when the current rate is an outlier
87	    relative to *that axle's own recent behavior* -- this is what lets the
88	    same logic work on a cold Montana morning and a hot Arizona afternoon
89	    without separate hand-tuned thresholds.
90	
91	    `min_rate_f_per_min` suppresses alerts on essentially-flat traces where
92	    the z-score is mathematically large but physically meaningless (e.g.
93	    std is near zero so any tiny wobble looks like infinity sigma).
94	
95	    Returns (rates, zscores, alerts).
96	    """
97	    rates = rolling_rate_of_change(temps_f, times_s, window=window)
98	    n = len(rates)
99	    zscores = np.full(n, np.nan)
100	    alerts: List[ThermoAlert] = []
101	
102	    for i in range(window + baseline_window, n):
103	        baseline = rates[i - baseline_window:i]
104	        baseline = baseline[~np.isnan(baseline)]
105	        if len(baseline) < max(5, baseline_window // 2):
106	            continue
107	        mu = float(np.mean(baseline))
108	        sigma = float(np.std(baseline))
109	        if sigma < 1e-6:
110	            sigma = 1e-6
111	        z = (rates[i] - mu) / sigma
112	        zscores[i] = z
113	
114	        if rates[i] < min_rate_f_per_min:
115	            continue
116	        if z >= z_critical:
117	            severity = "critical"
118	        elif z >= z_warning:
119	            severity = "warning"
120	        elif z >= z_watch:
121	            severity = "watch"
122	        else:
123	            continue
124	        alerts.append(
125	            ThermoAlert(
126	                index=i,
127	                time_s=float(times_s[i]),
128	                temp_f=float(temps_f[i]),
129	                rate_f_per_min=float(rates[i]),
130	                zscore=float(z),
131	                severity=severity,
132	            )
133	        )
134	    return rates, zscores, alerts

138	    temp_f: float,
139	    ambient_f: float,
140	    warning_delta_f: float = 115.0,
141	    critical_delta_f: float = 170.0,

144	    Legacy hot-bearing detector (HBD) logic, modeled as actually deployed:
145	    alarms are set on temperature ABOVE AMBIENT, not an absolute number.
146	    This matches the real-world mechanism in the NTSB account of the
147	    February 3, 2023 East Palestine, OH derailment -- the bearing that
148	    failed read 253F above an ambient of 10F at the final detector before
149	    critical alarm, i.e. the absolute temperature (~263F) is not the
150	    number the system was actually checking; the DELTA against that
151	    night's cold ambient is.
152	
153	    This function exists specifically so the dashboard can show, side by
154	    side, what a legacy point-in-time absolute/delta check would have said
155	    versus what the z-score rate-of-change sweep (above) says from the
156	    same data -- the core of the product's argument.
157	    """
158	    delta_f = temp_f - ambient_f

160	        legacy_status = "critical"
161	    elif delta_f >= warning_delta_f:
162	        legacy_status = "warning"
163	    else:
164	        legacy_status = "normal"
165	    return {
166	        "temp_f": temp_f,
167	        "ambient_f": ambient_f,
168	        "delta_f": delta_f,
169	        "critical_delta_f": critical_delta_f,
170	        "legacy_status": legacy_status,
171	    }

175	class PeerZScoreResult:
176	    index: int
177	    time_s: float
178	    value: float
179	    median_peer: float
180	    mad_peer: float
181	    robust_z: float
182	    severity: str  # "normal" | "watch" | "warning" | "critical"
183	
184	
185	def robust_mad_zscore(
186	    value: float,
187	    peer_population: np.ndarray,
188	    z_watch: float = 2.5,
189	    z_warning: float = 3.5,
190	    z_critical: float = 5.0,
191	) -> PeerZScoreResult:
192	    """
193	    Robust (outlier-resistant) z-score of a single reading against a peer
194	    population, using median and MAD (median absolute deviation) instead
195	    of mean/std:
196	
197	        Z = (x - median(P)) / (1.4826 * MAD(P))
198	
199	    The 1.4826 constant scales MAD to be a consistent estimator of the
200	    standard deviation under a normal distribution, so this Z is
201	    comparable to an ordinary z-score but isn't dragged around by one or
202	    two extreme peer readings the way mean/std would be.
203	
204	    `peer_population` can be ANY comparable population -- this same axle's
205	    history across past detector passes, a fleet-wide cohort of the same
206	    bearing type, or a route/environmental cohort (same line, similar
207	    ambient conditions) -- the math doesn't care which; the caller decides
208	    what "peer" means for a given comparison.
209	    """
210	    peer_population = np.asarray(peer_population, dtype=float)
211	    peer_population = peer_population[~np.isnan(peer_population)]
212	    if len(peer_population) == 0:
213	        return PeerZScoreResult(0, 0.0, value, value, 0.0, 0.0, "normal")
214	
215	    median_p = float(np.median(peer_population))
216	    mad_p = float(np.median(np.abs(peer_population - median_p)))
217	    scaled_mad = 1.4826 * mad_p
218	    if scaled_mad < 1e-6:
219	        scaled_mad = 1e-6
220	    z = (value - median_p) / scaled_mad
221	
222	    az = abs(z)
223	    if az >= z_critical:
224	        severity = "critical"
225	    elif az >= z_warning:
226	        severity = "warning"
227	    elif az >= z_watch:
228	        severity = "watch"
229	    else:
230	        severity = "normal"
231	
232	    return PeerZScoreResult(
233	        index=0, time_s=0.0, value=float(value),
234	        median_peer=median_p, mad_peer=mad_p, robust_z=float(z), severity=severity,
235	    )
236	
237	
238	def same_axle_differential_alarm(
239	    temp_left_f: float,
240	    temp_right_f: float,
241	    critical_diff_f: float = 95.0,
242	) -> Dict[str, object]:
243	    """
244	    Same-axle left/right journal temperature differential check, standard
245	    industry hot-bearing practice alongside the ambient-relative check
246	    above: the two journals on one axle should run close to each other,
247	    since they share the same axle, same speed, same load path. A large
248	    gap between them points at ONE side failing specifically (e.g. a
249	    spalled race on just that journal), independent of what the ambient-
250	    relative absolute check says -- a bearing could be running hot on both
251	    sides from heavy load/high ambient (not necessarily a defect) while
252	    still showing a small, healthy differential; conversely a modest
253	    absolute temperature with a large differential is a red flag.
254	
255	    This is deliberately a DIFFERENT signal from ambient_relative_alarm
256	    and zscore_sweep -- it's checking symmetry, not absolute level or
257	    trend -- which is why it's tracked as its own independent piece of
258	    evidence in the fusion/corroboration layer (see warrants.py).
259	    """
260	    diff_f = abs(temp_left_f - temp_right_f)
261	    status = "critical" if diff_f >= critical_diff_f else "normal"
262	    return {
263	        "temp_left_f": temp_left_f,
264	        "temp_right_f": temp_right_f,
265	        "diff_f": diff_f,
266	        "critical_diff_f": critical_diff_f,
267	        "status": status,
268	    }
269	
270	
271	# ===========================================================================
272	# 2. KINEMATICS: coasting distance / energy from E_k = 1/2 m v^2
273	# ===========================================================================
274	
275	G = 9.80665  # m/s^2, standard gravity
276	
277	
278	def kinetic_energy_j(mass_kg: float, velocity_mps: float) -> float:
279	    """E_k = 1/2 m v^2, in joules."""
280	    return 0.5 * mass_kg * velocity_mps**2
281	
282	
283	@dataclass
284	class CoastResult:
285	    times_s: List[float]
286	    velocities_mps: List[float]
287	    distances_m: List[float]
288	    kinetic_energy_j: List[float]
289	    stop_distance_m: Optional[float]
290	    stop_time_s: Optional[float]
291	    will_accelerate_on_grade: bool
292	
293	
294	def coasting_profile(
295	    mass_kg: float,
296	    velocity0_mps: float,
297	    grade_percent: float,
298	    rolling_resistance_coeff: float = 0.0020,
299	    drag_coeff_area_m2: float = 6.0,
300	    air_density_kgm3: float = 1.225,
301	    dt_s: float = 0.5,
302	    max_time_s: float = 1800.0,
303	) -> CoastResult:
304	    """
305	    Numerically integrates the equation of motion for a coasting (throttle
306	    off, no braking) train on a constant grade:
307	
308	        m * dv/dt = F_grade - F_roll - F_drag
309	
310	        F_grade = m * G * sin(theta)              (positive = downgrade helps)
311	        F_roll  = rolling_resistance_coeff * m * G  (Davis-equation style term)
312	        F_drag  = 0.5 * air_density * drag_coeff_area_m2 * v^2
313	
314	    grade_percent follows railroad convention (feet of rise per 100 feet of
315	    track, e.g. 1.0 = a 1% grade). Positive = climbing, negative = descending.
316	
317	    This answers the dispatcher-relevant question "if this train goes to
318	    idle right now, how far does it roll and does it need to brake, or will
319	    the grade make it accelerate instead" -- useful for both fuel strategy
320	    and for flagging a car that is coasting abnormally short/far versus its
321	    predicted profile (which can itself be an early mechanical signal, e.g.
322	    excess rolling resistance from a dragging brake shoe).
323	    """
324	    theta = math.atan(grade_percent / 100.0)
325	    # Signed so that a positive result ACCELERATES the train: climbing
326	    # (theta > 0) decelerates it (gravity pulls back), descending
327	    # (theta < 0) accelerates it (gravity pulls forward).
328	    a_grade_signed = -G * math.sin(theta)
329	    f_roll_per_kg = rolling_resistance_coeff * G  # always opposes motion
330	
331	    v = velocity0_mps
332	    d = 0.0
333	    t = 0.0
334	    times, vels, dists, kes = [0.0], [v], [0.0], [kinetic_energy_j(mass_kg, v)]
335	
336	    # At v=0, drag is zero, so this tells us whether gravity alone (on a
337	    # descending grade) already beats rolling resistance: if so the train
338	    # will speed up while coasting rather than need braking, converging on
339	    # a terminal velocity once drag grows enough to balance it.
340	    will_accelerate = a_grade_signed > f_roll_per_kg
341	
342	    stop_distance_m = None
343	    stop_time_s = None
344	
345	    while t < max_time_s:
346	        drag_per_kg = 0.5 * air_density_kgm3 * drag_coeff_area_m2 * v * v / mass_kg
347	        a = a_grade_signed - f_roll_per_kg - drag_per_kg
348	        v_new = v + a * dt_s
349	        if v_new <= 0 and not will_accelerate:
350	            # Linear interpolation to the exact stop instant within this step.
351	            frac = v / (v - v_new) if (v - v_new) != 0 else 1.0
352	            d += v * (frac * dt_s) + 0.5 * a * (frac * dt_s) ** 2
353	            t += frac * dt_s
354	            v = 0.0
355	            stop_distance_m = d
356	            stop_time_s = t
357	            times.append(t)
358	            vels.append(v)
359	            dists.append(d)
360	            kes.append(0.0)
361	            break
362	
363	        d += v * dt_s + 0.5 * a * dt_s**2
364	        v = max(v_new, 0.0) if not will_accelerate else v_new
365	        t += dt_s
366	        times.append(t)
367	        vels.append(v)
368	        dists.append(d)
369	        kes.append(kinetic_energy_j(mass_kg, v))
370	
371	        if will_accelerate and v > velocity0_mps * 3:
372	            # Safety cutoff: profile has clearly diverged (runaway on grade),
373	            # stop simulating further -- the point (needs intervention) is made.
374	            break
375	
376	    return CoastResult(
377	        times_s=times,
378	        velocities_mps=vels,
379	        distances_m=dists,
380	        kinetic_energy_j=kes,
381	        stop_distance_m=stop_distance_m,
382	        stop_time_s=stop_time_s,
383	        will_accelerate_on_grade=will_accelerate,
384	    )
385	
386	
387	# ===========================================================================
388	# 3. ACOUSTICS: FFT bearing-defect detection
389	# ===========================================================================
390	
391	
392	def bearing_defect_frequencies(
393	    shaft_hz: float,
394	    n_balls: int,
395	    ball_diameter_mm: float,
396	    pitch_diameter_mm: float,
397	    contact_angle_deg: float = 0.0,
398	) -> Dict[str, float]:
399	    """
400	    Standard rolling-element bearing characteristic defect frequencies
401	    (Hz), as used throughout industrial vibration analysis (see e.g. SKF /
402	    Timken bearing diagnostics literature):
403	
404	        BPFO = (n/2) * f_r * (1 - (d/D) cos(theta))   outer race defect
405	        BPFI = (n/2) * f_r * (1 + (d/D) cos(theta))   inner race defect
406	        BSF  = (D/2d) * f_r * (1 - (d/D)^2 cos^2(theta))  ball (rolling element) defect
407	        FTF  = (f_r/2) * (1 - (d/D) cos(theta))        cage (fundamental train) frequency
408	
409	    where f_r is the shaft rotation frequency (Hz), n is the number of
410	    rolling elements, d is ball diameter, D is pitch diameter, theta is the
411	    contact angle.
412	
413	    shaft_hz for a rail axle is derived from train speed and wheel diameter:
414	    f_r = v / (pi * wheel_diameter).
415	    """
416	    d_over_D = ball_diameter_mm / pitch_diameter_mm
417	    cos_t = math.cos(math.radians(contact_angle_deg))
418	    bpfo = (n_balls / 2.0) * shaft_hz * (1 - d_over_D * cos_t)
419	    bpfi = (n_balls / 2.0) * shaft_hz * (1 + d_over_D * cos_t)
420	    bsf = (pitch_diameter_mm / (2.0 * ball_diameter_mm)) * shaft_hz * (1 - (d_over_D * cos_t) ** 2)
421	    ftf = (shaft_hz / 2.0) * (1 - d_over_D * cos_t)
422	    return {"BPFO": bpfo, "BPFI": bpfi, "BSF": bsf, "FTF": ftf}
423	
424	
425	def axle_shaft_hz(speed_mps: float, wheel_diameter_m: float) -> float:
426	    """Shaft rotation frequency f_r = v / (pi * wheel_diameter)."""
427	    if wheel_diameter_m <= 0:
428	        return 0.0
429	    return speed_mps / (math.pi * wheel_diameter_m)
430	
431	
432	def fft_spectrum(signal: np.ndarray, sample_rate_hz: float) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
433	    """
434	    One-sided amplitude spectrum via real FFT. Returns (freqs_hz, magnitude).
435	    """
436	    signal = np.asarray(signal, dtype=float)
437	    n = len(signal)
438	    window = np.hanning(n)
439	    spectrum = np.fft.rfft(signal * window)
440	    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(n, d=1.0 / sample_rate_hz)
441	    magnitude = np.abs(spectrum) / n
442	    return freqs, magnitude
443	
444	
445	@dataclass
446	class DefectPeakResult:
447	    label: str
448	    target_hz: float
449	    found: bool
450	    peak_hz: Optional[float]
451	    peak_magnitude: Optional[float]
452	    noise_floor: float
453	    sigma_above_noise: float
454	
455	
456	def detect_defect_peak(
457	    freqs: np.ndarray,
458	    magnitude: np.ndarray,
459	    target_hz: float,
460	    label: str,
461	    tolerance_hz: float = 3.0,
462	    sigma_threshold: float = 4.0,
463	) -> DefectPeakResult:
464	    """
465	    Looks for a spectral peak within `tolerance_hz` of a theoretical defect
466	    frequency (BPFO/BPFI/BSF/FTF, or a harmonic of one) and checks whether
467	    it stands `sigma_threshold` standard deviations above the broadband
468	    noise floor (noise floor estimated from the whole spectrum excluding a
469	    guard band around the target). This is a standard "spectral kurtosis /
470	    peak prominence" style check, not a magnitude-only threshold -- a loud
471	    but broadband-noisy spectrum won't false-positive.
472	    """
473	    freqs = np.asarray(freqs)
474	    magnitude = np.asarray(magnitude)
475	    band = (freqs >= target_hz - tolerance_hz) & (freqs <= target_hz + tolerance_hz)
476	    guard = (freqs >= target_hz - 5 * tolerance_hz) & (freqs <= target_hz + 5 * tolerance_hz)
477	
478	    if not np.any(band) or np.sum(~guard) < 10:
479	        return DefectPeakResult(label, target_hz, False, None, None, 0.0, 0.0)
480	
481	    noise_pool = magnitude[~guard]
482	    noise_floor = float(np.mean(noise_pool))
483	    noise_sigma = float(np.std(noise_pool)) or 1e-9
484	
485	    idx_in_band = np.where(band)[0]
486	    peak_idx = idx_in_band[np.argmax(magnitude[idx_in_band])]
487	    peak_mag = float(magnitude[peak_idx])
488	    peak_hz = float(freqs[peak_idx])
489	    sigma_above = (peak_mag - noise_floor) / noise_sigma
490	
491	    found = sigma_above >= sigma_threshold
492	    return DefectPeakResult(
493	        label=label,
494	        target_hz=target_hz,
495	        found=found,
496	        peak_hz=peak_hz,
497	        peak_magnitude=peak_mag,
498	        noise_floor=noise_floor,
499	        sigma_above_noise=float(sigma_above),
500	    )

"""
AxiomDynamics physics engine.

Three independent, named-physical-law analysis modules. Each one is a
deliberate upgrade over a specific legacy practice in freight rail wayside
monitoring, and each is implemented as plain, auditable math (no black-box
model) so a railroad's own engineers can verify every number by hand.

1. thermodynamics  Rate-of-change anomaly detection on wheel-bearing
                    temperature. Legacy hot-box detectors alarm on a fixed
                    absolute threshold (e.g. 170F). That misses a bearing
                    that is heating rapidly but hasn't crossed the line yet.
                    Here we track dT/dt (Newton's-law-of-cooling-consistent)
                    and flag when the *rate* is a statistical outlier
                    (z-score) against that axle's own recent baseline.

2. kinematics       Coasting distance/energy prediction from first
                    principles: KE = 1/2 m v^2, plus grade (gravity) and
                    resistance (rolling + aerodynamic drag) work terms,
                    integrated numerically.

3. acoustics        FFT-based bearing defect detection using the standard
                    rolling-element bearing defect-frequency equations
                    (BPFO, BPFI, BSF, FTF) from vibration analysis, not a
                    generic "listen for weird noise" model.

None of this is mystical. Every function below names the textbook equation
it implements.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List, Dict, Optional, Tuple

import numpy as np

# ===========================================================================
# 1. THERMODYNAMICS: rate-of-change (z-score) bearing temperature alerting
# ===========================================================================


def rolling_rate_of_change(temps_f: np.ndarray, times_s: np.ndarray, window: int = 5) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    dT/dt in degrees F per minute, via backward finite difference over a
    trailing `window` of samples. First `window` samples are NaN (no history
    yet).
    """
    temps_f = np.asarray(temps_f, dtype=float)
    times_s = np.asarray(times_s, dtype=float)
    n = len(temps_f)
    rates = np.full(n, np.nan)
    for i in range(window, n):
        dt_s = times_s[i] - times_s[i - window]
        if dt_s <= 0:
            continue
        dtemp = temps_f[i] - temps_f[i - window]
        rates[i] = dtemp / (dt_s / 60.0)
    return rates


@dataclass
class ThermoAlert:
    index: int
    time_s: float
    temp_f: float
    rate_f_per_min: float
    zscore: float
    severity: str  # "watch" | "warning" | "critical"


def zscore_sweep(
    temps_f: np.ndarray,
    times_s: np.ndarray,
    window: int = 10,
    baseline_window: int = 36,
    z_watch: float = 2.5,
    z_warning: float = 3.5,
    z_critical: float = 5.0,
    min_rate_f_per_min: float = 0.4,
) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, List[ThermoAlert]]:
    """
    Compute rolling rate-of-change, then a rolling z-score of that rate
    against its own trailing baseline (mean/std over `baseline_window`
    prior samples). Flags a point when the current rate is an outlier
    relative to *that axle's own recent behavior* -- this is what lets the
    same logic work on a cold Montana morning and a hot Arizona afternoon
    without separate hand-tuned thresholds.

    `min_rate_f_per_min` suppresses alerts on essentially-flat traces where
    the z-score is mathematically large but physically meaningless (e.g.
    std is near zero so any tiny wobble looks like infinity sigma).

    Returns (rates, zscores, alerts).
    """
    rates = rolling_rate_of_change(temps_f, times_s, window=window)
    n = len(rates)
    zscores = np.full(n, np.nan)
    alerts: List[ThermoAlert] = []

    for i in range(window + baseline_window, n):
        baseline = rates[i - baseline_window:i]
        baseline = baseline[~np.isnan(baseline)]
        if len(baseline) < max(5, baseline_window // 2):
            continue
        mu = float(np.mean(baseline))
        sigma = float(np.std(baseline))
        if sigma < 1e-6:
            sigma = 1e-6
        z = (rates[i] - mu) / sigma
        zscores[i] = z

        if rates[i] < min_rate_f_per_min:
            continue
        if z >= z_critical:
            severity = "critical"
        elif z >= z_warning:
            severity = "warning"
        elif z >= z_watch:
            severity = "watch"
        else:
            continue
        alerts.append(
            ThermoAlert(
                index=i,
                time_s=float(times_s[i]),
                temp_f=float(temps_f[i]),
                rate_f_per_min=float(rates[i]),
                zscore=float(z),
                severity=severity,
            )
        )
    return rates, zscores, alerts


def ambient_relative_alarm(
    temp_f: float,
    ambient_f: float,
    warning_delta_f: float = 115.0,
    critical_delta_f: float = 170.0,
) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Legacy hot-bearing detector (HBD) logic, modeled as actually deployed:
    alarms are set on temperature ABOVE AMBIENT, not an absolute number.
    This matches the real-world mechanism in the NTSB account of the
    February 3, 2023 East Palestine, OH derailment -- the bearing that
    failed read 253F above an ambient of 10F at the final detector before
    critical alarm, i.e. the absolute temperature (~263F) is not the
    number the system was actually checking; the DELTA against that
    night's cold ambient is.

    This function exists specifically so the dashboard can show, side by
    side, what a legacy point-in-time absolute/delta check would have said
    versus what the z-score rate-of-change sweep (above) says from the
    same data -- the core of the product's argument.
    """
    delta_f = temp_f - ambient_f
    if delta_f >= critical_delta_f:
        legacy_status = "critical"
    elif delta_f >= warning_delta_f:
        legacy_status = "warning"
    else:
        legacy_status = "normal"
    return {
        "temp_f": temp_f,
        "ambient_f": ambient_f,
        "delta_f": delta_f,
        "critical_delta_f": critical_delta_f,
        "legacy_status": legacy_status,
    }


@dataclass
class PeerZScoreResult:
    index: int
    time_s: float
    value: float
    median_peer: float
    mad_peer: float
    robust_z: float
    severity: str  # "normal" | "watch" | "warning" | "critical"


def robust_mad_zscore(
    value: float,
    peer_population: np.ndarray,
    z_watch: float = 2.5,
    z_warning: float = 3.5,
    z_critical: float = 5.0,
) -> PeerZScoreResult:
    """
    Robust (outlier-resistant) z-score of a single reading against a peer
    population, using median and MAD (median absolute deviation) instead
    of mean/std:

        Z = (x - median(P)) / (1.4826 * MAD(P))

    The 1.4826 constant scales MAD to be a consistent estimator of the
    standard deviation under a normal distribution, so this Z is
    comparable to an ordinary z-score but isn't dragged around by one or
    two extreme peer readings the way mean/std would be.

    `peer_population` can be ANY comparable population -- this same axle's
    history across past detector passes, a fleet-wide cohort of the same
    bearing type, or a route/environmental cohort (same line, similar
    ambient conditions) -- the math doesn't care which; the caller decides
    what "peer" means for a given comparison.
    """
    peer_population = np.asarray(peer_population, dtype=float)
    peer_population = peer_population[~np.isnan(peer_population)]
    if len(peer_population) == 0:
        return PeerZScoreResult(0, 0.0, value, value, 0.0, 0.0, "normal")

    median_p = float(np.median(peer_population))
    mad_p = float(np.median(np.abs(peer_population - median_p)))
    scaled_mad = 1.4826 * mad_p
    if scaled_mad < 1e-6:
        scaled_mad = 1e-6
    z = (value - median_p) / scaled_mad

    az = abs(z)
    if az >= z_critical:
        severity = "critical"
    elif az >= z_warning:
        severity = "warning"
    elif az >= z_watch:
        severity = "watch"
    else:
        severity = "normal"

    return PeerZScoreResult(
        index=0, time_s=0.0, value=float(value),
        median_peer=median_p, mad_peer=mad_p, robust_z=float(z), severity=severity,
    )


def same_axle_differential_alarm(
    temp_left_f: float,
    temp_right_f: float,
    critical_diff_f: float = 95.0,
) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Same-axle left/right journal temperature differential check, standard
    industry hot-bearing practice alongside the ambient-relative check
    above: the two journals on one axle should run close to each other,
    since they share the same axle, same speed, same load path. A large
    gap between them points at ONE side failing specifically (e.g. a
    spalled race on just that journal), independent of what the ambient-
    relative absolute check says -- a bearing could be running hot on both
    sides from heavy load/high ambient (not necessarily a defect) while
    still showing a small, healthy differential; conversely a modest
    absolute temperature with a large differential is a red flag.

    This is deliberately a DIFFERENT signal from ambient_relative_alarm
    and zscore_sweep -- it's checking symmetry, not absolute level or
    trend -- which is why it's tracked as its own independent piece of
    evidence in the fusion/corroboration layer (see warrants.py).
    """
    diff_f = abs(temp_left_f - temp_right_f)
    status = "critical" if diff_f >= critical_diff_f else "normal"
    return {
        "temp_left_f": temp_left_f,
        "temp_right_f": temp_right_f,
        "diff_f": diff_f,
        "critical_diff_f": critical_diff_f,
        "status": status,
    }


# ===========================================================================
# 2. KINEMATICS: coasting distance / energy from E_k = 1/2 m v^2
# ===========================================================================

G = 9.80665  # m/s^2, standard gravity


def kinetic_energy_j(mass_kg: float, velocity_mps: float) -> float:
    """E_k = 1/2 m v^2, in joules."""
    return 0.5 * mass_kg * velocity_mps**2


@dataclass
class CoastResult:
    times_s: List[float]
    velocities_mps: List[float]
    distances_m: List[float]
    kinetic_energy_j: List[float]
    stop_distance_m: Optional[float]
    stop_time_s: Optional[float]
    will_accelerate_on_grade: bool


def coasting_profile(
    mass_kg: float,
    velocity0_mps: float,
    grade_percent: float,
    rolling_resistance_coeff: float = 0.0020,
    drag_coeff_area_m2: float = 6.0,
    air_density_kgm3: float = 1.225,
    dt_s: float = 0.5,
    max_time_s: float = 1800.0,
) -> CoastResult:
    """
    Numerically integrates the equation of motion for a coasting (throttle
    off, no braking) train on a constant grade:

        m * dv/dt = F_grade - F_roll - F_drag

        F_grade = m * G * sin(theta)              (positive = downgrade helps)
        F_roll  = rolling_resistance_coeff * m * G  (Davis-equation style term)
        F_drag  = 0.5 * air_density * drag_coeff_area_m2 * v^2

    grade_percent follows railroad convention (feet of rise per 100 feet of
    track, e.g. 1.0 = a 1% grade). Positive = climbing, negative = descending.

    This answers the dispatcher-relevant question "if this train goes to
    idle right now, how far does it roll and does it need to brake, or will
    the grade make it accelerate instead" -- useful for both fuel strategy
    and for flagging a car that is coasting abnormally short/far versus its
    predicted profile (which can itself be an early mechanical signal, e.g.
    excess rolling resistance from a dragging brake shoe).
    """
    theta = math.atan(grade_percent / 100.0)
    # Signed so that a positive result ACCELERATES the train: climbing
    # (theta > 0) decelerates it (gravity pulls back), descending
    # (theta < 0) accelerates it (gravity pulls forward).
    a_grade_signed = -G * math.sin(theta)
    f_roll_per_kg = rolling_resistance_coeff * G  # always opposes motion

    v = velocity0_mps
    d = 0.0
    t = 0.0
    times, vels, dists, kes = [0.0], [v], [0.0], [kinetic_energy_j(mass_kg, v)]

    # At v=0, drag is zero, so this tells us whether gravity alone (on a
    # descending grade) already beats rolling resistance: if so the train
    # will speed up while coasting rather than need braking, converging on
    # a terminal velocity once drag grows enough to balance it.
    will_accelerate = a_grade_signed > f_roll_per_kg

    stop_distance_m = None
    stop_time_s = None

    while t < max_time_s:
        drag_per_kg = 0.5 * air_density_kgm3 * drag_coeff_area_m2 * v * v / mass_kg
        a = a_grade_signed - f_roll_per_kg - drag_per_kg
        v_new = v + a * dt_s
        if v_new <= 0 and not will_accelerate:
            # Linear interpolation to the exact stop instant within this step.
            frac = v / (v - v_new) if (v - v_new) != 0 else 1.0
            d += v * (frac * dt_s) + 0.5 * a * (frac * dt_s) ** 2
            t += frac * dt_s
            v = 0.0
            stop_distance_m = d
            stop_time_s = t
            times.append(t)
            vels.append(v)
            dists.append(d)
            kes.append(0.0)
            break

        d += v * dt_s + 0.5 * a * dt_s**2
        v = max(v_new, 0.0) if not will_accelerate else v_new
        t += dt_s
        times.append(t)
        vels.append(v)
        dists.append(d)
        kes.append(kinetic_energy_j(mass_kg, v))

        if will_accelerate and v > velocity0_mps * 3:
            # Safety cutoff: profile has clearly diverged (runaway on grade),
            # stop simulating further -- the point (needs intervention) is made.
            break

    return CoastResult(
        times_s=times,
        velocities_mps=vels,
        distances_m=dists,
        kinetic_energy_j=kes,
        stop_distance_m=stop_distance_m,
        stop_time_s=stop_time_s,
        will_accelerate_on_grade=will_accelerate,
    )


# ===========================================================================
# 3. ACOUSTICS: FFT bearing-defect detection
# ===========================================================================


def bearing_defect_frequencies(
    shaft_hz: float,
    n_balls: int,
    ball_diameter_mm: float,
    pitch_diameter_mm: float,
    contact_angle_deg: float = 0.0,
) -> Dict[str, float]:
    """
    Standard rolling-element bearing characteristic defect frequencies
    (Hz), as used throughout industrial vibration analysis (see e.g. SKF /
    Timken bearing diagnostics literature):

        BPFO = (n/2) * f_r * (1 - (d/D) cos(theta))   outer race defect
        BPFI = (n/2) * f_r * (1 + (d/D) cos(theta))   inner race defect
        BSF  = (D/2d) * f_r * (1 - (d/D)^2 cos^2(theta))  ball (rolling element) defect
        FTF  = (f_r/2) * (1 - (d/D) cos(theta))        cage (fundamental train) frequency

    where f_r is the shaft rotation frequency (Hz), n is the number of
    rolling elements, d is ball diameter, D is pitch diameter, theta is the
    contact angle.

    shaft_hz for a rail axle is derived from train speed and wheel diameter:
    f_r = v / (pi * wheel_diameter).
    """
    d_over_D = ball_diameter_mm / pitch_diameter_mm
    cos_t = math.cos(math.radians(contact_angle_deg))
    bpfo = (n_balls / 2.0) * shaft_hz * (1 - d_over_D * cos_t)
    bpfi = (n_balls / 2.0) * shaft_hz * (1 + d_over_D * cos_t)
    bsf = (pitch_diameter_mm / (2.0 * ball_diameter_mm)) * shaft_hz * (1 - (d_over_D * cos_t) ** 2)
    ftf = (shaft_hz / 2.0) * (1 - d_over_D * cos_t)
    return {"BPFO": bpfo, "BPFI": bpfi, "BSF": bsf, "FTF": ftf}


def axle_shaft_hz(speed_mps: float, wheel_diameter_m: float) -> float:
    """Shaft rotation frequency f_r = v / (pi * wheel_diameter)."""
    if wheel_diameter_m <= 0:
        return 0.0
    return speed_mps / (math.pi * wheel_diameter_m)


def fft_spectrum(signal: np.ndarray, sample_rate_hz: float) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """
    One-sided amplitude spectrum via real FFT. Returns (freqs_hz, magnitude).
    """
    signal = np.asarray(signal, dtype=float)
    n = len(signal)
    window = np.hanning(n)
    spectrum = np.fft.rfft(signal * window)
    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(n, d=1.0 / sample_rate_hz)
    magnitude = np.abs(spectrum) / n
    return freqs, magnitude


@dataclass
class DefectPeakResult:
    label: str
    target_hz: float
    found: bool
    peak_hz: Optional[float]
    peak_magnitude: Optional[float]
    noise_floor: float
    sigma_above_noise: float


def detect_defect_peak(
    freqs: np.ndarray,
    magnitude: np.ndarray,
    target_hz: float,
    label: str,
    tolerance_hz: float = 3.0,
    sigma_threshold: float = 4.0,
) -> DefectPeakResult:
    """
    Looks for a spectral peak within `tolerance_hz` of a theoretical defect
    frequency (BPFO/BPFI/BSF/FTF, or a harmonic of one) and checks whether
    it stands `sigma_threshold` standard deviations above the broadband
    noise floor (noise floor estimated from the whole spectrum excluding a
    guard band around the target). This is a standard "spectral kurtosis /
    peak prominence" style check, not a magnitude-only threshold -- a loud
    but broadband-noisy spectrum won't false-positive.
    """
    freqs = np.asarray(freqs)
    magnitude = np.asarray(magnitude)
    band = (freqs >= target_hz - tolerance_hz) & (freqs <= target_hz + tolerance_hz)
    guard = (freqs >= target_hz - 5 * tolerance_hz) & (freqs <= target_hz + 5 * tolerance_hz)

    if not np.any(band) or np.sum(~guard) < 10:
        return DefectPeakResult(label, target_hz, False, None, None, 0.0, 0.0)

    noise_pool = magnitude[~guard]
    noise_floor = float(np.mean(noise_pool))
    noise_sigma = float(np.std(noise_pool)) or 1e-9

    idx_in_band = np.where(band)[0]
    peak_idx = idx_in_band[np.argmax(magnitude[idx_in_band])]
    peak_mag = float(magnitude[peak_idx])
    peak_hz = float(freqs[peak_idx])
    sigma_above = (peak_mag - noise_floor) / noise_sigma

    found = sigma_above >= sigma_threshold
    return DefectPeakResult(
        label=label,
        target_hz=target_hz,
        found=found,
        peak_hz=peak_hz,
        peak_magnitude=peak_mag,
        noise_floor=noise_floor,
        sigma_above_noise=float(sigma_above),
    )

199	    The 1.4826 constant scales MAD to be a consistent estimator of the
200	    standard deviation under a normal distribution, so this Z is
201	    comparable to an ordinary z-score but isn't dragged around by one or
202	    two extreme peer readings the way mean/std would be.
203	
204	    `peer_population` can be ANY comparable population -- this same axle's
205	    history across past detector passes, a fleet-wide cohort of the same
206	    bearing type, or a route/environmental cohort (same line, similar
207	    ambient conditions) -- the math doesn't care which; the caller decides
208	    what "peer" means for a given comparison.
209	    """
210	    peer_population = np.asarray(peer_population, dtype=float)
211	    peer_population = peer_population[~np.isnan(peer_population)]
212	    if len(peer_population) == 0:
213	        return PeerZScoreResult(0, 0.0, value, value, 0.0, 0.0, "normal")
214	
215	    median_p = float(np.median(peer_population))
216	    mad_p = float(np.median(np.abs(peer_population - median_p)))
217	    scaled_mad = 1.4826 * mad_p
218	    if scaled_mad < 1e-6:
219	        scaled_mad = 1e-6
220	    z = (value - median_p) / scaled_mad
221	
222	    az = abs(z)
223	    if az >= z_critical:
224	        severity = "critical"
225	    elif az >= z_warning:
226	        severity = "warning"
227	    elif az >= z_watch:
228	        severity = "watch"
229	    else:
230	        severity = "normal"
231	
232	    return PeerZScoreResult(
233	        index=0, time_s=0.0, value=float(value),
234	        median_peer=median_p, mad_peer=mad_p, robust_z=float(z), severity=severity,
235	    )
236	
237	
238	def same_axle_differential_alarm(
239	    temp_left_f: float,
240	    temp_right_f: float,
241	    critical_diff_f: float = 95.0,
242	) -> Dict[str, object]:
243	    """
244	    Same-axle left/right journal temperature differential check, standard
245	    industry hot-bearing practice alongside the ambient-relative check
246	    above: the two journals on one axle should run close to each other,
247	    since they share the same axle, same speed, same load path. A large
248	    gap between them points at ONE side failing specifically (e.g. a
249	    spalled race on just that journal), independent of what the ambient-
250	    relative absolute check says -- a bearing could be running hot on both
251	    sides from heavy load/high ambient (not necessarily a defect) while
252	    still showing a small, healthy differential; conversely a modest
253	    absolute temperature with a large differential is a red flag.
254	
255	    This is deliberately a DIFFERENT signal from ambient_relative_alarm
256	    and zscore_sweep -- it's checking symmetry, not absolute level or
257	    trend -- which is why it's tracked as its own independent piece of
258	    evidence in the fusion/corroboration layer (see warrants.py).
259	    """
260	    diff_f = abs(temp_left_f - temp_right_f)
261	    status = "critical" if diff_f >= critical_diff_f else "normal"
262	    return {
263	        "temp_left_f": temp_left_f,
264	        "temp_right_f": temp_right_f,
265	        "diff_f": diff_f,
266	        "critical_diff_f": critical_diff_f,
267	        "status": status,
268	    }
269	
270	
271	# ===========================================================================
272	# 2. KINEMATICS: coasting distance / energy from E_k = 1/2 m v^2
273	# ===========================================================================
274	
275	G = 9.80665  # m/s^2, standard gravity
276	
277	
278	def kinetic_energy_j(mass_kg: float, velocity_mps: float) -> float:
279	    """E_k = 1/2 m v^2, in joules."""
280	    return 0.5 * mass_kg * velocity_mps**2
281	
282	
283	@dataclass
284	class CoastResult:
285	    times_s: List[float]
286	    velocities_mps: List[float]
287	    distances_m: List[float]
288	    kinetic_energy_j: List[float]
289	    stop_distance_m: Optional[float]
290	    stop_time_s: Optional[float]
291	    will_accelerate_on_grade: bool
292	
293	
294	def coasting_profile(
295	    mass_kg: float,
296	    velocity0_mps: float,
297	    grade_percent: float,
298	    rolling_resistance_coeff: float = 0.0020,
299	    drag_coeff_area_m2: float = 6.0,
300	    air_density_kgm3: float = 1.225,
301	    dt_s: float = 0.5,
302	    max_time_s: float = 1800.0,
303	) -> CoastResult:
304	    """
305	    Numerically integrates the equation of motion for a coasting (throttle
306	    off, no braking) train on a constant grade:
307	
308	        m * dv/dt = F_grade - F_roll - F_drag
309	
310	        F_grade = m * G * sin(theta)              (positive = downgrade helps)
311	        F_roll  = rolling_resistance_coeff * m * G  (Davis-equation style term)
312	        F_drag  = 0.5 * air_density * drag_coeff_area_m2 * v^2
313	
314	    grade_percent follows railroad convention (feet of rise per 100 feet of
315	    track, e.g. 1.0 = a 1% grade). Positive = climbing, negative = descending.
316	
317	    This answers the dispatcher-relevant question "if this train goes to
318	    idle right now, how far does it roll and does it need to brake, or will
319	    the grade make it accelerate instead" -- useful for both fuel strategy
320	    and for flagging a car that is coasting abnormally short/far versus its
321	    predicted profile (which can itself be an early mechanical signal, e.g.
322	    excess rolling resistance from a dragging brake shoe).
323	    """
324	    theta = math.atan(grade_percent / 100.0)
325	    # Signed so that a positive result ACCELERATES the train: climbing
326	    # (theta > 0) decelerates it (gravity pulls back), descending
327	    # (theta < 0) accelerates it (gravity pulls forward).
328	    a_grade_signed = -G * math.sin(theta)
329	    f_roll_per_kg = rolling_resistance_coeff * G  # always opposes motion
330	
331	    v = velocity0_mps
332	    d = 0.0
333	    t = 0.0
334	    times, vels, dists, kes = [0.0], [v], [0.0], [kinetic_energy_j(mass_kg, v)]
335	
336	    # At v=0, drag is zero, so this tells us whether gravity alone (on a
337	    # descending grade) already beats rolling resistance: if so the train
338	    # will speed up while coasting rather than need braking, converging on
339	    # a terminal velocity once drag grows enough to balance it.
340	    will_accelerate = a_grade_signed > f_roll_per_kg
341	
342	    stop_distance_m = None
343	    stop_time_s = None
344	
345	    while t < max_time_s:
346	        drag_per_kg = 0.5 * air_density_kgm3 * drag_coeff_area_m2 * v * v / mass_kg
347	        a = a_grade_signed - f_roll_per_kg - drag_per_kg
348	        v_new = v + a * dt_s
349	        if v_new <= 0 and not will_accelerate:
350	            # Linear interpolation to the exact stop instant within this step.
351	            frac = v / (v - v_new) if (v - v_new) != 0 else 1.0
352	            d += v * (frac * dt_s) + 0.5 * a * (frac * dt_s) ** 2
353	            t += frac * dt_s
354	            v = 0.0
355	            stop_distance_m = d
356	            stop_time_s = t
357	            times.append(t)
358	            vels.append(v)
359	            dists.append(d)
360	            kes.append(0.0)
361	            break
362	
363	        d += v * dt_s + 0.5 * a * dt_s**2
364	        v = max(v_new, 0.0) if not will_accelerate else v_new
365	        t += dt_s
366	        times.append(t)
367	        vels.append(v)
368	        dists.append(d)
369	        kes.append(kinetic_energy_j(mass_kg, v))
370	
371	        if will_accelerate and v > velocity0_mps * 3:
372	            # Safety cutoff: profile has clearly diverged (runaway on grade),
373	            # stop simulating further -- the point (needs intervention) is made.
374	            break
375	
376	    return CoastResult(
377	        times_s=times,
378	        velocities_mps=vels,
379	        distances_m=dists,
380	        kinetic_energy_j=kes,
381	        stop_distance_m=stop_distance_m,
382	        stop_time_s=stop_time_s,
383	        will_accelerate_on_grade=will_accelerate,
384	    )
385	
386	
387	# ===========================================================================
388	# 3. ACOUSTICS: FFT bearing-defect detection
389	# ===========================================================================
390	
391	
392	def bearing_defect_frequencies(
393	    shaft_hz: float,
394	    n_balls: int,
395	    ball_diameter_mm: float,
396	    pitch_diameter_mm: float,
397	    contact_angle_deg: float = 0.0,
398	) -> Dict[str, float]:
399	    """
400	    Standard rolling-element bearing characteristic defect frequencies
401	    (Hz), as used throughout industrial vibration analysis (see e.g. SKF /
402	    Timken bearing diagnostics literature):
403	
404	        BPFO = (n/2) * f_r * (1 - (d/D) cos(theta))   outer race defect
405	        BPFI = (n/2) * f_r * (1 + (d/D) cos(theta))   inner race defect
406	        BSF  = (D/2d) * f_r * (1 - (d/D)^2 cos^2(theta))  ball (rolling element) defect
407	        FTF  = (f_r/2) * (1 - (d/D) cos(theta))        cage (fundamental train) frequency
408	
409	    where f_r is the shaft rotation frequency (Hz), n is the number of
410	    rolling elements, d is ball diameter, D is pitch diameter, theta is the
411	    contact angle.
412	
413	    shaft_hz for a rail axle is derived from train speed and wheel diameter:
414	    f_r = v / (pi * wheel_diameter).
415	    """
416	    d_over_D = ball_diameter_mm / pitch_diameter_mm
417	    cos_t = math.cos(math.radians(contact_angle_deg))
418	    bpfo = (n_balls / 2.0) * shaft_hz * (1 - d_over_D * cos_t)
419	    bpfi = (n_balls / 2.0) * shaft_hz * (1 + d_over_D * cos_t)
420	    bsf = (pitch_diameter_mm / (2.0 * ball_diameter_mm)) * shaft_hz * (1 - (d_over_D * cos_t) ** 2)
421	    ftf = (shaft_hz / 2.0) * (1 - d_over_D * cos_t)
422	    return {"BPFO": bpfo, "BPFI": bpfi, "BSF": bsf, "FTF": ftf}
423	
424	
425	def axle_shaft_hz(speed_mps: float, wheel_diameter_m: float) -> float:
426	    """Shaft rotation frequency f_r = v / (pi * wheel_diameter)."""
427	    if wheel_diameter_m <= 0:
428	        return 0.0
429	    return speed_mps / (math.pi * wheel_diameter_m)
430	
431	
432	def fft_spectrum(signal: np.ndarray, sample_rate_hz: float) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
433	    """
434	    One-sided amplitude spectrum via real FFT. Returns (freqs_hz, magnitude).
435	    """
436	    signal = np.asarray(signal, dtype=float)
437	    n = len(signal)
438	    window = np.hanning(n)
439	    spectrum = np.fft.rfft(signal * window)
440	    freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(n, d=1.0 / sample_rate_hz)
441	    magnitude = np.abs(spectrum) / n
442	    return freqs, magnitude
443	
444	
445	@dataclass
446	class DefectPeakResult:
447	    label: str
448	    target_hz: float
449	    found: bool
450	    peak_hz: Optional[float]
451	    peak_magnitude: Optional[float]
452	    noise_floor: float
453	    sigma_above_noise: float
454	
455	
456	def detect_defect_peak(
457	    freqs: np.ndarray,
458	    magnitude: np.ndarray,
459	    target_hz: float,
460	    label: str,
461	    tolerance_hz: float = 3.0,
462	    sigma_threshold: float = 4.0,
463	) -> DefectPeakResult:
464	    """
465	    Looks for a spectral peak within `tolerance_hz` of a theoretical defect
466	    frequency (BPFO/BPFI/BSF/FTF, or a harmonic of one) and checks whether
467	    it stands `sigma_threshold` standard deviations above the broadband
468	    noise floor (noise floor estimated from the whole spectrum excluding a
469	    guard band around the target). This is a standard "spectral kurtosis /
470	    peak prominence" style check, not a magnitude-only threshold -- a loud
471	    but broadband-noisy spectrum won't false-positive.
472	    """
473	    freqs = np.asarray(freqs)
474	    magnitude = np.asarray(magnitude)
475	    band = (freqs >= target_hz - tolerance_hz) & (freqs <= target_hz + tolerance_hz)
476	    guard = (freqs >= target_hz - 5 * tolerance_hz) & (freqs <= target_hz + 5 * tolerance_hz)
477	
478	    if not np.any(band) or np.sum(~guard) < 10:
479	        return DefectPeakResult(label, target_hz, False, None, None, 0.0, 0.0)
480	
481	    noise_pool = magnitude[~guard]
482	    noise_floor = float(np.mean(noise_pool))
483	    noise_sigma = float(np.std(noise_pool)) or 1e-9
484	
485	    idx_in_band = np.where(band)[0]
486	    peak_idx = idx_in_band[np.argmax(magnitude[idx_in_band])]
487	    peak_mag = float(magnitude[peak_idx])
488	    peak_hz = float(freqs[peak_idx])
489	    sigma_above = (peak_mag - noise_floor) / noise_sigma
490	
491	    found = sigma_above >= sigma_threshold
492	    return DefectPeakResult(
493	        label=label,
494	        target_hz=target_hz,
495	        found=found,
496	        peak_hz=peak_hz,
497	        peak_magnitude=peak_mag,
498	        noise_floor=noise_floor,
499	        sigma_above_noise=float(sigma_above),
500	    )

"""
Predictive Ghost Warrant construction.

A "Ghost Warrant" is this product's name for a single traceable evidence
packet: one axle, one point in time, every signal that fired on it, a
severity tier, and a cryptographic hash binding the record so it can't be
quietly edited after the fact. This is the audit/evidence-trail layer that
turns "the dashboard said critical" into something a railroad's safety and
legal team can actually stand behind.

Two design choices worth calling out explicitly:

1. Severity tiers are named INFORMATIONAL / REVIEW / URGENT REVIEW, not
   "watch/warning/critical" -- the point of the rename is to make it
   impossible to mistake these for operational alarm levels. See the
   CRITICAL SAFETY GUARDRAIL note below and in the README: this system
   never issues a stop-train or braking instruction. It produces evidence
   for a human to review. Existing railroad operating rules, detector
   logic, and authorized personnel remain the sole authority over any
   train-movement decision.

2. Escalation to URGENT REVIEW requires CORROBORATION: at least two
   independent signal types (e.g. thermal rate-of-change AND a peer-group
   outlier, or thermal AND acoustic) must agree. A single signal, even one
   that is itself severe, is capped at REVIEW. This directly implements
   the infographic's "acoustic detection requires corroboration before
   fracture classification" rule, generalized across all signal types, so
   one noisy sensor can't single-handedly manufacture a false urgent case.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
from typing import Dict, List, Optional

# Internal physics-module severities ("watch"/"warning"/"critical") map
# onto a 0..3 ordinal so independent signals can be compared and combined.
_SEVERITY_ORDINAL = {None: 0, "normal": 0, "watch": 1, "warning": 2, "critical": 3}

TIER_INFORMATIONAL = "INFORMATIONAL"
TIER_REVIEW = "REVIEW"
TIER_URGENT_REVIEW = "URGENT REVIEW"

RECOMMENDED_RESPONSE = {
    TIER_INFORMATIONAL: "Record in audit ledger. No operational action required.",
    TIER_REVIEW: "Authorized analyst examination and prioritization.",
    TIER_URGENT_REVIEW: "Escalate to authorized railroad personnel per carrier-approved procedures.",
}


@dataclass
class SignalEvidence:
    """One independent signal's reading on this axle at this pass."""
    signal_type: str          # "thermal_rate_of_change" | "ambient_relative_legacy" | "peer_historical" | "peer_cross_fleet" | "acoustic_bearing_defect"
    severity: str             # "normal" | "watch" | "warning" | "critical"
    detail: str
    confidence_note: str = ""


@dataclass
class GhostWarrant:
    advisory_id: str
    asset_id: str
    train_consist: str
    detector_location: str
    component_position: str
    timestamp_s: float
    severity_tier: str
    corroborated: bool
    evidence: List[SignalEvidence]
    reference_population_version: str
    model_version: str
    confidence: str
    recommended_response: str
    reviewer_disposition: str
    ground_truth_status: str
    cryptographic_hash: str


REFERENCE_POPULATION_VERSION = "v1.4.2"   # stands in for a real versioned baseline dataset
MODEL_VERSION = "0.97"                     # stands in for a real model/ruleset version


def _severity_to_tier(worst_ordinal: int, corroborated: bool) -> str:
    if worst_ordinal <= 0:
        return TIER_INFORMATIONAL
    if worst_ordinal >= 3 and corroborated:
        return TIER_URGENT_REVIEW
    if worst_ordinal >= 2 and corroborated:
        return TIER_URGENT_REVIEW
    # Severe-but-uncorroborated, or merely moderate: held at REVIEW, not
    # escalated further, until a second independent signal agrees.
    return TIER_REVIEW


def build_warrant(
    advisory_seq: int,
    asset_id: str,
    train_consist: str,
    detector_location: str,
    component_position: str,
    timestamp_s: float,
    evidence: List[SignalEvidence],
    confidence: Optional[str] = None,
    reviewer_disposition: str = "Pending",
    ground_truth_status: str = "Not available",

    Fuses a set of independent signal readings for one axle/pass into a

    flagged = [e for e in evidence if _SEVERITY_ORDINAL.get(e.severity, 0) > 0]

        "evidence": [asdict(e) for e in evidence],
        "model_version": MODEL_VERSION,
        "reference_population_version": REFERENCE_POPULATION_VERSION,
    }, sort_keys=True)
    crypto_hash = hashlib.sha256(canonical.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    return GhostWarrant(
        advisory_id=advisory_id,
        asset_id=asset_id,
        train_consist=train_consist,
        detector_location=detector_location,
        component_position=component_position,
        timestamp_s=timestamp_s,
        severity_tier=tier,
        corroborated=corroborated,
        evidence=evidence,

        model_version=MODEL_VERSION,
        confidence=confidence,
        recommended_response=RECOMMENDED_RESPONSE[tier],
        reviewer_disposition=reviewer_disposition,
        ground_truth_status=ground_truth_status,
        cryptographic_hash=crypto_hash,
    )

"""
SQLite-backed persistence for reviewer dispositions.

Deliberately the stdlib `sqlite3` module -- no new dependency, no server
process, one file (`axiom.db`) that lives next to the app and survives a
restart. This replaces an earlier in-memory dict: a disposition is an
audit-relevant record (who reviewed what, and what they decided), and
losing it on every restart undercuts the whole "human-in-the-loop" story.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import os
import sqlite3
from contextlib import contextmanager
from typing import Dict, Optional

DB_PATH = os.environ.get("AXIOM_DB_PATH", os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))), "axiom.db"))


@contextmanager
def _connect():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    try:
        yield conn
        conn.commit()
    finally:
        conn.close()


def init_db():
    with _connect() as conn:
        conn.execute("""
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS dispositions (
                advisory_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                reviewer_name TEXT NOT NULL,
                cert_id TEXT NOT NULL,
                disposition TEXT NOT NULL,
                recorded_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
            )
        """)


def save_disposition(advisory_id: str, reviewer_name: str, cert_id: str, disposition: str):
    with _connect() as conn:
        conn.execute(
            """
            INSERT INTO dispositions (advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, recorded_at)
            VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, datetime('now'))
            ON CONFLICT(advisory_id) DO UPDATE SET
                reviewer_name=excluded.reviewer_name,
                cert_id=excluded.cert_id,
                disposition=excluded.disposition,
                recorded_at=excluded.recorded_at
            """,
            (advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition),
        )


def get_disposition(advisory_id: str) -> Optional[Dict[str, str]]:
    with _connect() as conn:
        row = conn.execute(
            "SELECT reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, recorded_at FROM dispositions WHERE advisory_id = ?",
            (advisory_id,),
        ).fetchone()
    if row is None:
        return None
    return {"reviewer_name": row[0], "cert_id": row[1], "disposition": row[2], "recorded_at": row[3]}


def all_dispositions() -> Dict[str, Dict[str, str]]:
    with _connect() as conn:
        rows = conn.execute(
            "SELECT advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, recorded_at FROM dispositions"
        ).fetchall()
    return {
        r[0]: {"reviewer_name": r[1], "cert_id": r[2], "disposition": r[3], "recorded_at": r[4]}
        for r in rows
    }

3	
4	A "Ghost Warrant" is this product's name for a single traceable evidence
5	packet: one axle, one point in time, every signal that fired on it, a
6	severity tier, and a cryptographic hash binding the record so it can't be
7	quietly edited after the fact. This is the audit/evidence-trail layer that
8	turns "the dashboard said critical" into something a railroad's safety and
9	legal team can actually stand behind.
10	
11	Two design choices worth calling out explicitly:
12	
13	1. Severity tiers are named INFORMATIONAL / REVIEW / URGENT REVIEW, not
14	   "watch/warning/critical" -- the point of the rename is to make it
15	   impossible to mistake these for operational alarm levels. See the
16	   CRITICAL SAFETY GUARDRAIL note below and in the README: this system
17	   never issues a stop-train or braking instruction. It produces evidence
18	   for a human to review. Existing railroad operating rules, detector
19	   logic, and authorized personnel remain the sole authority over any
20	   train-movement decision.
21	
22	2. Escalation to URGENT REVIEW requires CORROBORATION: at least two
23	   independent signal types (e.g. thermal rate-of-change AND a peer-group
24	   outlier, or thermal AND acoustic) must agree. A single signal, even one
25	   that is itself severe, is capped at REVIEW. This directly implements
26	   the infographic's "acoustic detection requires corroboration before
27	   fracture classification" rule, generalized across all signal types, so
28	   one noisy sensor can't single-handedly manufacture a false urgent case.
29	"""

57	    severity: str             # "normal" | "watch" | "warning" | "critical"

1	# B01 — System Blueprint & Architecture
2	
3	**Docket position:** B01. Descriptive annex to D07. B-series documents create no warranty unless D07 expressly incorporates them (Docket Index, Part IV, rule 5).
4	
5	**Written against:** the production architecture, not the demonstration build. §7 lists every point where the two currently differ. Nothing in this document should be treated as describing the demo.
6	
7	**Governing architectural decisions:**
8	
9	- **AD-1 — Deployment: fully on-premise edge, zero outbound network.** No licence server, no telemetry, no update callback, no third-party cloud. The platform never initiates a network connection to anything outside the Railroad's network. Ever.
10	- **AD-2 — Reviewer identity: local accounts plus a signed certification registry**, administered by the Railroad. No dependency on Railroad directory services, no cloud identity provider.
11	- **AD-3 — The disposition ledger is append-only.** A disposition can be superseded but never overwritten, and never deleted.
12	
13	AD-1 and AD-2 were chosen specifically so the platform remains deployable on an air-gapped network. Both have costs, stated in §8.
14	
15	---
16	
17	## 1. Purpose and boundary
18	
19	The platform ingests wayside sensor signals from the Railroad's existing detector infrastructure, applies deterministic physics models to derive bearing and running-gear condition, and presents ranked advisory warrants to a certified reviewer who records a disposition.
20	
21	**The platform does not decide anything.** It does not issue stop orders, does not communicate with train crews, does not influence signal systems, and does not actuate any equipment. It produces advisories for a qualified human being, who retains sole operating authority. This framing is deliberate and must be identical in B01, C02, D02, D07, D08 and D12. See D00 §III.1.
22	
23	**In scope:** sensor ingestion, physics inference, warrant generation and ranking, reviewer disposition recording, audit export, ROI reporting.
24	
25	**Out of scope:** detector hardware, network infrastructure, train control, crew communication, regulatory reporting to FRA/TC/ARTF on the Railroad's behalf.
26	
27	## 2. Component inventory
28	
29	| Component | Function | Technology |
30	|---|---|---|
31	| Signal ingest | Accepts wayside detector payloads in a defined schema | Python, file/socket ingest |
32	| Physics engine | Thermo, kinematic, acoustic models; deterministic, no learned parameters | Python + numpy |
33	| Warrant builder | Converts model output into ranked, cited advisories | Python |
34	| Identity & certification | **Local accounts, admin-issued credentials — operational today.** Signed certification registry: **designed, not built** (§7 item 1) | Python + SQLite |
35	| Disposition ledger | Record of reviewer decisions. **Append-only is the design; the current write path overwrites** (§7 item 2) | SQLite, WAL mode |
36	| API layer | Read APIs for fleet/alerts/ROI; write API for disposition | Python stdlib HTTP server |
37	| Presentation | Single-page dashboard, no external assets | HTML/CSS/JS, served locally |
38	| Audit export | Timestamped export with content hashes. **Not cryptographically signed** (§7 item 8) | Python |
39	
40	**Total external dependency count: one** (numpy). Everything else is Python standard library. This is an architectural property, not an accident, and it is the platform's principal security argument — see B04.
41	
42	## 3. Data flow
43	
44	```
45	Wayside detector (HBD / WILD / ABD)
46	        │  sensor payload
47	        ▼
48	┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
49	│  RAILROAD EDGE BOX  —  no outbound network   │
50	│                                              │
51	│  ingest ──► physics engine ──► warrant       │
52	│              (deterministic)     builder     │
53	│                                    │         │
54	│                                    ▼         │
55	│                            reviewer queue    │
56	│                                    │         │
57	│                        [certified human]     │
58	│                                    │         │
59	│                                    ▼         │
60	│                        disposition ledger    │
61	│                         (append-only, WAL)   │
62	│                                    │         │
63	│                                    ▼         │
64	│                          audit export        │
65	└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
66	        │
67	        ▼
68	Railroad's own reporting / regulatory process
69	```
70	
71	**There is no line leaving the box.** That is AD-1 stated as a diagram.
72	
73	## 4. The disposition ledger
74	
75	The single most important component, because it is the artifact our regulatory argument rests on.
76	
77	**Requirements (production):**
78	
79	1. **Append-only.** Each disposition is a new row. Supersede-and-insert, never `UPDATE`. The current demo uses an upsert that silently overwrites — that is a defect against AD-3, not a design choice.
80	2. **Authenticated identity.** A disposition is only accepted from an authenticated session bound to an issued, unexpired, unrevoked certification record. Free-text name and cert ID are not acceptable in production.
81	3. **Immutable timestamps**, server-generated, not client-supplied.
82	4. **Retention** per the Railroad's records policy, specified in D09.
83	5. **Export** produces a signed bundle: partition boundary, record count, and a hash over the contents, so a regulator can verify nothing was removed.
84	6. **Hash chaining** (recommended, not required at v1): each record carries the hash of its predecessor, making retroactive alteration detectable.
85	
86	**Why this matters commercially:** the Canadian pitch rests on producing auditable evidence that a flagged bearing was reviewed and acted upon. A ledger that can be silently rewritten produces no such evidence. Until the ledger meets §4.1–4.3, the certification story in C02 cannot be told, and the demo must not describe it as certification.
87	
88	## 5. Failure modes
89	
90	| Failure | Behavior | Consequence |
91	|---|---|---|
92	| Detector feed stops | Platform flags data staleness; advisories marked stale | No false reassurance — staleness is surfaced, not hidden |
93	| Physics engine error | Request fails, logged; no advisory emitted | Fails closed on that unit, not silently degraded |
94	| Edge box loses power | SQLite WAL recovers committed dispositions | Committed audit records survive |
95	| Disk full | Ingest rejects; dashboard alarms | Fails visibly |
96	| Clock drift | Timestamps become unreliable | **Requires NTP against Railroad's own time source — see §7** |
97	| Cert registry unavailable | New dispositions rejected | Fails closed — no unauthenticated decisions |
98	
99	**Fails closed everywhere.** Where the choice exists, the platform refuses to act rather than acting unverified.
100	
101	## 6. Scale envelope
102	
103	Per edge box, designed for: one to six detector feeds, up to ~5,000 monitored axles, sub-second inference per unit, disposition volume in the low hundreds per day. Beyond that, additional boxes — which is exactly what the per-site platform fee in D08/A2 prices.
104	
105	## 7. Production decisions required — where the code differs today
106	
107	**This section is the honest gap list. It must be emptied before any contract cites B01.**
108	
109	| # | Item | Current state | Required for production |
110	|---|---|---|---|
111	| 1 | Reviewer authentication | Free-text name + cert ID, unverified | AD-2: local accounts + signed cert registry |
112	| 2 | Ledger append-only | `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` — overwrites | Append-only with supersede semantics |
113	| 3 | Timestamps | SQLite `datetime('now')` default | Server-generated with NTP-synced clock |
114	| 4 | Storage durability | The demonstration environment's storage is ephemeral — the demo database is lost on spin-down | Persistent volume on Railroad hardware |
