# A2 / D08 Arithmetic Pass — 2026-11-09 (chat-3)

**Scope.** Every fee figure, band rate, cumulative total, performance cap, and
modelled return in `A2-RATE-CARD-AND-BAND-DEFINITIONS.md` and
`D08-MASTER-LICENSING-AND-LIABILITY.md`, recomputed from its stated source
equation rather than re-read. Both documents were last touched at `cf2e6ba`;
this is the first figure-by-figure re-derivation since.

**Method.** `assets/a2-d08-arithmetic-pass.py` computes each figure independently
and compares it to the value as written. It exits non-zero on any mismatch, so
the pass is repeatable rather than a claim. Run it with:

```
python3 -I assets/a2-d08-arithmetic-pass.py
```

**Result: 78 of 78 computed figures agree with the documents.** No arithmetic
error was found in either document. Every band total, worked example, site-fee
product, payment split, conversion credit, three-year row, performance cap,
cumulative schedule, and five-percent escalation is correct as written.

Two claims did **not** reproduce. They are not arithmetic errors — the arithmetic
inside each is sound — but the model each rests on does not agree with the model
the rest of the docket uses. They are recorded below as open items and were
**not** silently rewritten, because correcting them means choosing which model
governs, and that is an owner decision.

---

## What was checked and confirmed

**A2 §3.1–§3.3 — the band structure.** Band 1 at $600 to $300,000; Band 2
cumulative at $1,050,000; Band 3 at $2,175,000 at 5,000 axles and $4,050,000 at
10,000. All three worked examples (A: $300,000; B: $550,000 + $90,000 =
$640,000; C: $2,175,000 + $855,000 = $3,030,000) recompute correctly. The
marginal structure is genuinely marginal — no band charges for axles already
priced in a lower band.

**A2 §3.3 — the corridor site count.** 2,200 miles at 40-mile spacing is 55
sites, at 64-mile spacing 34.4. Site fees at 55 sites are $2,430,000, correctly
described as roughly half the $2,175,000 licence. The claim holds.

**A2 §5.1 — the pilot.** The five components sum to $370,000. The 40/30/30 split
is $148,000 / $111,000 / $111,000 and sums back to $370,000 exactly. The
conversion credit is 50% × $180,000 = $90,000.

**A2 §9 and D08 §5 — the rollover.** Year 1 production at $300,000 less the
$90,000 credit is $210,000 net; three years at 210 + 300 + 300 = $810,000;
four-year commitment $1,180,000. Both documents agree.

**D08 §3.1 — the three-year cost table.** All four rows recompute, including the
cost-per-axle column. The stated finding — that holding axles constant and
spreading across eleven sites raises cost 114% and more than doubles unit cost
from $2,360 to $5,060 — is arithmetically exact. So is the $135,000 three-year
charge per additional site.

**D08 §4 — performance component.** 33% caps of $99,000 / $181,500 / $346,500 at
500 / 1,000 / 2,000 axles are correct. The 1,000-axle worked example is right:
3% of $1,390,000 is $41,700, below the $181,500 cap, total $591,700. The earlier
draft's "$41.8K" was indeed rounded the wrong way; the current text is correct.

**D08 §6 — cumulative and escalation.** $370,000 / $580,000 / $880,000 /
$1,180,000 cumulative correctly. Year 5 at 5% is $315,000 and Year 6 $330,750,
cumulative $1,495,000 and $1,825,750, so "~$1.83M" is right.

**D06 §6 — the quarterly fee.** ($1,050,000 + 12 × $45,000) ÷ 4 = $397,500, and a
5% credit is $19,875. Correct; no change needed there.

---

## Finding 1 — the modelled-return claim does not reproduce

A2 §3.2 states the customer's modelled return rises "approximately 2.0x at 500
axles, rising to about 4.1x at 10,000." D08 §3 repeats both figures verbatim.

Recomputed with A1's own default assumptions (0.05% catastrophic rate, $500,000
typical failure, $1.0B catastrophic, 2.1 vs 1.4 defects caught per 500 axles,
$1,500 per false alarm), the three-year return is:

| Axles | 3-yr benefit | A2/D08 cost basis | A1 workbook basis |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 500 | $2,090,025 | 1.77x | 2.36x |
| 1,000 | $4,180,050 | 2.17x | 3.02x |
| 2,000 | $8,360,100 | 2.44x | 3.51x |
| 5,000 | $20,900,250 | 3.07x | 4.51x |
| 10,000 | $41,800,500 | 3.36x | 4.99x |

Neither basis produces 2.0x at 500 and 4.1x at 10,000. A sweep across plausible
per-defect valuations found no parameter set in the repository that reproduces
both endpoints. The *direction* of the claim is correct — return does improve
monotonically with fleet size on either basis — but the two anchor values are not
derivable from the model the docket ships.

**Why this matters and why it was not fixed here.** The sentences carrying these
numbers are also the document's defence against a "flat tier cliff" objection, and
D08 §3 already labels them "a pricing hypothesis validated only against modelled
return, not against a real procurement conversation." Replacing 2.0/4.1 with
1.77/3.36 would be defensible; so would restating the claim without anchor values.
Choosing between those is a commercial decision about what the first real
conversation opens with, and it changes a client-facing sentence in two documents.
It should be decided, not quietly edited.

**Recommended disposition:** strike the two anchor multiples from A2 §3.2 and D08 §3
and keep the monotonic claim, which is true on every basis tested. If anchors are
wanted, use values the shipped model actually produces and say which basis.

> **Update, same day — see `assets/a2-d08-model-decision-2026-11-09.md`.** The
> statement above that "no parameter set in the repository reproduces both
> endpoints" is correct only for the two cost bases tested here. A third basis —
> a four-year cost including the pilot and three full production years at list,
> with no conversion credit — reproduces both anchors from a single value of the
> catastrophic probability, **0.0714%**, to within 1.8%. So the anchors were not
> invented; they were computed on an unstated frame at an undisclosed third value
> of the parameter. That makes Finding 1 a disclosure defect rather than a
> fabrication, and the disposition above still stands: state the frame or strike
> the numbers. The decision paper carries the full table.

---

## Finding 2 — D08's modelled benefits exceed what A1 produces

D08 §5 says a 500-axle customer sees $6–8M of avoided damage in the pilot year
and $14–20M over four years; §6 says $40–60M over six years and a 20x–30x return.

A1 at 500 axles with default assumptions produces **$696,675 net annual benefit**.
The comparison:

| D08 claim | Period | A1 produces | Ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $6M–$8M | pilot year | $696,675 | 8.6x – 11.5x higher |
| $14M–$20M | 4 years | $2,786,700 | 5.0x – 7.2x higher |
| $40M–$60M | 6 years | $4,180,050 | 9.6x – 14.4x higher |

The returns quoted in D08 (16–22x for the pilot year) are internally consistent
with D08's own benefit figures divided by the $370,000 fee — that is checked and
passes. The problem is upstream: D08's benefit figures are roughly an order of
magnitude above the benefit A1 computes from the same fleet inputs. Any
per-defect valuation that would support D08's pilot figure lands near $8.6M–$11.4M
per prevented defect, against A1's $999,750.

D08 §9.1 already instructs: "Recalculate against the final A2 rate card before any
customer sees it." This is that check, and it does not pass.

**Why this matters.** These are the headline numbers in the document a CFO reads.
A1 is named as the instrument of record in both D08 §5 and §9, and D08 §5 states
that "A1 produces the customer's figure from the customer's data; this document
must never be used to present one." The two disagree by nearly an order of
magnitude at identical inputs, which is exactly the contradiction the sentence is
trying to prevent.

**Recommended disposition:** one of the two models is wrong and it needs a decision
on which. If A1 is the instrument of record — as D08 says twice — then §5 and §6
must be restated from A1's output. If D08's figures are right, A1's per-defect
valuation or defect-frequency assumption is too conservative and the workbook is
the thing to fix. Deciding this changes what the pilot pitch asks a customer to
believe, so it is left open deliberately.

---

## Corrections made in this pass

Three edits, all in `A1-ROI-MODEL/build_roi_calculator.py`, none altering any
figure in A2 or D08:

1. **Stale attribution corrected.** The assumptions note on sheet 5 still said
   "the 2% catastrophic escalation rate" while cell B17 has held 0.05% since the
   correction. The note now reads "the 0.05% catastrophic escalation rate (cell
   B17)". A reader reconciling the sheet against its own footnote would have
   found a ten-fold discrepancy that no longer exists.

2. **Sandbox output path removed.** Line 621 saved the workbook to
   `/sessions/ecstatic-gifted-bell/mnt/outputs/...` — a path inside a destroyed
   sandbox, from before the write-in-repo rule. Running the builder would have
   raised `FileNotFoundError`. It now writes beside the script via
   `os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))`.

3. **Import added** for the above (`import os`).

The committed workbook at `A1-ROI-MODEL/AxiomDynamics-ROI-Calculator.xlsx` was
**not** regenerated. Regenerating it would bake Finding 1 and Finding 2 into a new
file before the model question is settled. The workbook on disk still carries the
$180,000 pilot licence with no conversion credit and no site-fee line, which
disagrees with A2 §5.1 and §9 — that is a third instance of the same model
divergence and is covered by Finding 2's disposition.

---

## What to do next

1. Decide Finding 1 — strike or restate the 2.0x/4.1x anchors.
2. Decide Finding 2 — which model governs, A1 or D08 §5–§6.
3. Then regenerate the A1 workbook from the corrected builder and re-run this
   script; it will hold as long as no figure moves.
4. D07 §14.5 governing law and venue remains open, unchanged by this pass.

Nothing here is client-facing.*

### 4.4 The third divergence: the dashboard

`backend/roi.py` uses 2%. At an identical 500-axle fleet it produces
**$14,339,850** net annual benefit against A1's **$696,675** — **20.6x**. So the
live dashboard and the workbook disagree by more than A1 and D08 do. This is not
in the pass record's finding set and should be, because the dashboard is the

input.new_string:
### 4.4 The third divergence: the dashboard

`backend/roi.py` differs from A1 in **two** ways, not one, and the second is
larger than the first.

- **Probability.** `roi.py` uses 2%; A1 uses 0.05% — a 40× difference, and the
  divergence the README already discloses.
- **Contained-failure cost.** `roi.py` uses the **$9.25M midpoint** of the two
  sourced NTSB figures; A1 uses a **$500,000 typical** cost, deliberately, because
  A1's B14 note says the $5M/$13.5M bench figures are "an investigated,
  above-average event — do NOT use as your typical cost." So the two files
  disagree about which sourced number is the base case, not only about `p`.

The per-missed-defect values that result:

| Basis | Value per missed defect |
|---|---:|
| A1: contained $500k, p = 0.05% | $999,750 |
| A1's contained cost at roi.py's 2% | $20,490,000 |
| **`roi.py` as shipped: contained $9.25M, p = 2%** | **$29,065,000** |

So the live dashboard values a missed defect at **29.1×** A1's figure, and the
2% parameter alone accounts for only 20.5× of that — the rest is the contained-
cost disagreement. The dashboard is what a prospect actually sees in a demo, and
it is the artifact furthest from the workbook by a wide margin.

**An important limit on this comparison:** `roi.py` takes a list of warrants, not
an axle count, so it cannot be run "at 500 axles" directly — it prices whatever
warrants the current fleet snapshot produced. The figures above compare the two
files' *per-defect valuations*, which is the correct like-for-like comparison,
rather than pretending the dashboard produces an annual-fleet benefit number it
has no input for. Anyone quoting "the dashboard says $14.3M" has re-run A1's
formula at 2% and mislabelled it; that number appears in no file.

At **p = 0.0714%** the first basis produces **2.00x at 500 axles and 4.06x at
10,000** against stated claims of 2.0x and 4.1x. **That is consistent with the
anchors having been computed on this frame — but it is not proof that they were,
and the paper should not claim it.** The reason is in the next paragraph, and it
is the reason Finding 1 stays open rather than being closed as solved.

The cost ratio the anchors demand is a property of the *pricing*, not of the
benefit model, so it is fixed regardless of any probability: `cost(10,000) /
cost(500)` must equal 9.756. That is why the first row's two implied probabilities
agree — the ratio is doing the work, and any `p` on that basis fits both anchors
to within a few percent. But the *absolute level* of `p` depends on the benefit
horizon, which the document never states. Put three years of benefit against the
four-year cost and `p` = 0.0714%; put four years of benefit against it and
`p` = 0.0412%, which **also** satisfies both anchors (spread 2.3%). Both are
defensible readings of an undescribed frame.

So the honest finding is narrower than "this is where the numbers came from":

> The anchors are mutually consistent with a single linear model on a
> pilot-plus-three-years cost basis. They cannot be reproduced to a stated frame
> because no frame is stated, and the undisclosed parameter that fits them is
> between 0.04% and 0.07% — an order of magnitude below the 2% `roi.py` uses and
> close to A1's 0.05%, but not the value A1 ships.

That is still a disclosure defect, and it still needs fixing. It is not a
fabrication, and the paper should not accuse the earlier drafter of one.

input.old_string:
### 4.1 D08 contradicts itself, before A1 is involved

Section 4, immediately above, works a transparent example: at 1,000 axles the
corroborated prevented cost is **$1,390,000**, and the performance fee is 3% of
it. At 1.4 missed defects per 1,000 axles that is **$992,857 per prevented
failure**.

Section 5 then prices the same kind of prevented failure at $6M/$0.7 =
**$8,571,429** to $8M/$0.7 = **$11,428,571**. A ratio of **8.6x to 11.5x**
between two adjacent sections of one document.

This matters more than the A1 comparison, for three reasons. It cannot be
resolved by arguing A1's assumptions. It is visible to any reader who reads D08
in order, without access to the workbook. And it is load-bearing in the wrong
way: **§4's performance fee — 3% of corroborated prevented cost — is computed on
the low valuation, while §5's headline benefit is computed on the high one.** A
customer who elects the performance component is agreeing to a fee calculated on
a prevented failure worth about $993,000, having been sold the product by a
section that values the same prevented failure at $8.6M–$11.4M. Those two
numbers sit four pages apart in one document.
input.new_string:
### 4.1 D08 is internally inconsistent, before A1 is involved

Section 4, immediately above, works a transparent example: at 1,000 axles the
corroborated prevented cost is **$1,390,000**, and the performance fee is 3% of
it. At 1.4 missed defects per 1,000 axles that is **$992,857 per prevented
failure**.

Section 5 then prices the same kind of prevented failure at $6M/$0.7 =
**$8,571,429** to $8M/$0.7 = **$11,428,571**. A ratio of **8.6x to 11.5x**.

**One honest qualification first.** §4's figures are *corroborated* prevented
cost — a subset gated by the customer's own root-cause analysis — while §5's are
*modelled* avoided damage across the whole fleet. Those are not strictly the same
quantity, and a careful reader could argue §4 prices the subset that got
proven while §5 prices the expected total. So the word "contradiction" slightly
overstates it.

But the objection does not rescue the document, for three reasons. The ratio
survives the comparison per axle rather than per defect ($1,390 per axle against
$12,000–$16,000 per axle, still 8.6x–11.5x), so it is not an artefact of the
defect rate. It is visible to any reader who reads D08 in order, without the
workbook. And it is load-bearing in the wrong direction: **§4's performance fee
is computed on the low valuation while §5's headline benefit is computed on the
high one.** A customer who elects the component agrees to a fee calculated on a
prevented failure worth about $993,000, having been sold the product by a section
that values the same failure at $8.6M–$11.4M. If §4's $993,000 is right, §5 is
roughly ten times too high; if §5 is right, the performance fee is roughly a
tenth of what the customer's own act of corroboration is worth.

**And §4's number is essentially A1's.** $992,857 against A1's $999,750 at
0.05% — a 0.7% difference, well inside the rounding of an illustrative example.
That is the most useful fact in this document: **D08 already contains an
A1-consistent valuation, in §4, four pages before the section that abandons it.**

Three different numbers for the probability that a missed bearing defect becomes
a catastrophic event — **0.05%** in the A1 workbook, **2%** in `backend/roi.py`,
and an implied **≈0.07%** behind A2's 2.0x/4.1x anchors — are all in circulation,

in the pass record traces to that one parameter or to the cost basis it is
applied to. Choose the number, choose the basis, and Findings 1 and 2 both close
in a single edit pass across four files.

`roi.py` is brought into line.** The reasoning is in §6. The case against it is
in §6.3 and it is not weak — read it before agreeing.

## 1. The decision in one paragraph

Four different numbers for the probability that a missed bearing defect becomes a
catastrophic event are in circulation. **0.05%** in the A1 workbook, whose own
note calls 2% physically impossible. **2%** in `backend/roi.py`, whose own note
calls that value conservatively low. An implied **0.04%–0.07%** behind A2's
2.0x/4.1x anchors, on a frame the documents never state. And **0.8%–1.4%** implied
by D08's headline benefit figures. On top of that, the two files disagree about
the contained-failure base cost — $500,000 in A1, a $9.25M midpoint in `roi.py` —
so `roi.py` values a missed defect at **29×** A1's figure.

Every finding in the pass record traces to those two choices: which probability,
applied to which cost. Choose them and Findings 1 and 2 close in one edit pass
across four files.

**Recommendation: A1's 0.05% governs, the contained cost stays at A1's $500,000,
the anchors are restated from that model, and `roi.py` is brought into line.** The
reasoning is in §7. The case against it is in §7 and it is not weak — read it
before agreeing. One thing should happen first: value the cost components A1
omits, which may raise the benefit figure honestly and make the choice easier
(§7, final paragraph).

272	### 4.4 The third divergence: the dashboard
273	
274	`backend/roi.py` differs from A1 in **two** ways, not one, and the second is
275	larger than the first.
276	
277	- **Probability.** `roi.py` uses 2%; A1 uses 0.05% — a 40× difference, and the
278	  divergence the README already discloses.
279	- **Contained-failure cost.** `roi.py` uses the **$9.25M midpoint** of the two
280	  sourced NTSB figures; A1 uses a **$500,000 typical** cost, deliberately, because
281	  A1's B14 note says the $5M/$13.5M bench figures are "an investigated,
282	  above-average event — do NOT use as your typical cost." So the two files
283	  disagree about which sourced number is the base case, not only about `p`.
284	
285	The per-missed-defect values that result:
286	
287	| Basis | Value per missed defect |
288	|---|---:|
289	| A1: contained $500k, p = 0.05% | $999,750 |
290	| A1's contained cost at roi.py's 2% | $20,490,000 |
291	| **`roi.py` as shipped: contained $9.25M, p = 2%** | **$29,065,000** |
292	
293	So the live dashboard values a missed defect at **29.1×** A1's figure, and the
294	2% parameter alone accounts for only 20.5× of that — the rest is the contained-
295	cost disagreement. The dashboard is what a prospect actually sees in a demo, and
296	it is the artifact furthest from the workbook by a wide margin.
297	
298	**An important limit on this comparison:** `roi.py` takes a list of warrants, not
299	an axle count, so it cannot be run "at 500 axles" directly — it prices whatever
300	warrants the current fleet snapshot produced. The figures above compare the two
301	files' *per-defect valuations*, which is the correct like-for-like comparison,
302	rather than pretending the dashboard produces an annual-fleet benefit number it
303	has no input for. Anyone quoting "the dashboard says $14.3M" has re-run A1's

## Phase 3 — the A2/D08 model decision, priced (committed `b23d0c7`)

Chosen ahead of the signed ledger export, and the reason is worth recording:
the ledger phase fixed a document claiming more than the code did, and these two
findings are the same defect class — except they sit in the money documents a
customer's procurement team will run, and D14 §8 names the gap between the sales
description and the contract as the product's largest liability. A missing
signature on a ledger is a production requirement. A rate card that contradicts
its own ROI model cannot be sent out at all.

**What was built.** No code changed in the product. `assets/a2-d08-model-decision-2026-11-09.md`
plus `a2-d08-model-decision.py` (65 reproducible checks) price both answers so the
owner's decision is a comparison rather than more research.

**Three findings the arithmetic pass did not have.**

1. **The 2.0x/4.1x anchors are recoverable.** The pass record tested two cost
   bases and concluded no parameter set reproduces both. On a third — pilot plus
   three full years at list, no conversion credit — one value of the catastrophic
   probability fits both, because the ratio the anchors demand
   (cost(10k)/cost(500) = 9.756) is a property of the *pricing*, not the benefit
   model. So this is a disclosure defect, not a fabrication. The level of p is
   not unique — a four-year benefit horizon gives 0.0412% and also fits — which is
   why the finding stays open.
2. **D08 contradicts itself.** §4 prices a prevented failure at ~$993,000; §5 at
   $8.6M–$11.4M. Holds per axle as well as per defect. And §4's figure is within
   0.7% of A1's $999,750 — the document already contains an A1-consistent
   valuation four pages before abandoning it.
3. **`roi.py` is further from A1 than the README says.** Two disagreements, not
   one: 2% vs 0.05%, and a $9.25M contained cost vs A1's $500,000. Per-missed-
   defect values are $29,065,000 vs $999,750 — 29×, of which probability accounts
   for 20.5×.

**What the independent audit caught, and this is the part worth keeping.** I wrote
the paper and then wrote its checker, which is exactly the arrangement where a
shared assumption passes unnoticed. A separate agent with no stake in it found
four errors:

- **The dashboard figure was not roi.py's output.** I had computed $14,339,850 by
  re-running A1's formula at 2% and labelled it as the dashboard. `roi.py` takes
  warrants, not axles — "at 500 axles" was never computable. Corrected to a
  per-defect comparison, which is the right like-for-like and a *larger* gap.
- "D08 repeats it verbatim" — it does not; two sentences are reworded. Corrected.
- "That is where the numbers came from" — overstated derivation from consistency.
  Corrected, with the horizon ambiguity shown rather than buried.
- "no site-fee line" in the stale workbook — wrong, the row exists and is inert at
  one site. Corrected, and the real disagreement (a $285,000 pilot built from
  hardware + training against A2's $370,000 with no hardware at all) stated.

Lesson for the next phase: when I produce both an analysis and the script that
checks it, a second reader is not optional. The checker validated my mistake
because I wrote it to.

## Next

1. Decide Finding 1 and Finding 2 — options priced in the decision paper §6,
   recommendation in §7. **This is the only blocking item that needs the owner.**
2. Worth pricing before locking Option A: adding the cost components A1 omits
   (service disruption, lading loss, regulatory penalty) to B14 at 0.05%, which
   may raise the benefit figure honestly.
3. Then regenerate the A1 workbook from the corrected builder and re-run both
   check scripts and the unit suite.
4. D07 §14.5 governing law and venue remains open, unchanged.
5. Signed, off-box ledger export — the next *build*, now unblocked by priority
   but not by dependency; it does not touch any of the above.
EOF

---
name: independent-audit-before-closing
description: "When Claude writes both an analysis and the script that verifies it, a separate agent must audit the result before it is treated as done"
type: feedback
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
---

When I produce an analysis **and** the script that checks it, I must run an independent audit before calling the work done. A second agent with no stake in the result, prompted to try to falsify the claims.

**Why:** On 2026-11-09 (chat-3) I wrote `assets/a2-d08-model-decision-2026-11-09.md` and its checker `a2-d08-model-decision.py`, which reported "all checks passed". An independent audit found **four material errors** — and the checker had validated one of them, because I wrote it to encode the same mislabelling. Specifically: a dashboard figure ($14,339,850) I presented as `backend/roi.py`'s output was actually A1's formula re-run at 2%; `roi.py` takes warrants, not axles, so "at 500 axles" was never computable from it. Also "repeats verbatim" (it didn't), "where the numbers came from" (overstated derivation from consistency), and a claim that a spreadsheet line was missing when it existed and was merely inert.

**How to apply:**
- A green self-check proves internal consistency, not correctness. It cannot catch a wrong premise I also encoded in the check.
- Use the `Agent` tool with `subagent_type: general-purpose`, and tell it explicitly to **falsify**, not confirm — "try hard to falsify this, it's the strongest claim". Ask it to write its own arithmetic rather than running my script.
- Ask it to verify *quotes against source files*, not just numbers. Two of the four errors were prose attributions.
- Budget for it: it took ~10 minutes and found real defects. That is a good trade.
- This generalises to any phase where I author both the artifact and its acceptance test — docket figures, test suites for my own code, verification passes.

content.text:
I picked Findings 1 and 2, and built the thing that was actually missing: the decision itself, costed.

**Why this over the signed ledger export.** The ledger phase closed a gap where a document claimed more than the code did. These two findings are the same defect — except they sit in the money documents a procurement team will actually run. D14 §8 names the gap between the sales description and the contract as the product's largest liability and calls it "fully controllable, and therefore inexcusable if it occurs." A missing signature on a ledger is a production requirement. A rate card that contradicts its own ROI model can't be sent to anyone.

**Three things the earlier pass didn't have.**

The 2.0x/4.1x anchors turn out to be *recoverable*, not invented. The pass record tested two cost bases and concluded no parameter fit both. On a third — pilot plus three full years at list, no conversion credit — a single value of the catastrophic probability fits both, because the ratio the anchors demand is a property of the pricing, not the benefit model. That makes Finding 1 a disclosure defect, not a fabrication. The level of that probability still isn't unique, though, which is why it stays open rather than being closed as solved.

D08 contradicts **itself**, with no assistance from A1. §4 prices a prevented failure at about $993,000; §5 prices the same failure at $8.6M–$11.4M. The ratio holds per axle as well as per defect, so it isn't an artifact of the defect rate. And §4's figure is within 0.7% of A1's — the document already contains the answer, four pages before abandoning it.

`roi.py` is further from A1 than the README says: two disagreements, not one. It uses 2% *and* a $9.25M contained cost, against A1's 0.05% and $500,000. Per-defect values are $29M against $1.0M — a 29× gap, of which probability accounts for 20.5×.

**One thing worth flagging about my own process.** I wrote the paper, then wrote the script that checks it, and it reported all-green. An independent audit found four errors — and the checker had validated one of them, because I'd encoded the same mistake in both. The worst: I presented $14,339,850 as the dashboard's output, but `roi.py` takes warrants, not axles, so "at 500 axles" was never computable from it. That number was A1's formula re-run at 2%, mislabelled. All four are corrected, and the real gap turned out larger than the one I'd overstated. I've noted the lesson: a green self-check proves internal consistency, not correctness.

**The decision you actually face.** A1 governs — 0.05%, $500,000, anchors restated to 1.77x/3.36x, D08 restated, `roi.py` fixed. It makes every number reconcile, and it changes the pitch from "20x–30x" to "~2.3x over six years." That is a large cost and I've stated it at full strength rather than burying it. The one thing I'd do before locking it: price the cost components A1 omits — service disruption, lading loss, regulatory penalty — against B14 at 0.05%. If the real economics are better than A1 models, that reaches a higher figure honestly, without the indefensible 2%.

[Read the decision paper](computer://C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics\assets\a2-d08-model-decision-2026-11-09.md)

Four commits waiting on `PUSH-TO-GITHUB.bat`. Everything is in the repo and committed — `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` is empty apart from the line-ending noise.

content.text:
Two different answers depending on whether you mean "next thing to build" or "next thing that's blocking."

**Blocking, and only you can clear it:** the A2/D08 model decision (open item 1). Until you pick, three things stay stuck — the anchors in A2 §3.2 and D08 §3, D08 §5–§6, and the A1 workbook regeneration (item 3), which can't run without baking the unresolved choice into a new file. That's a decision, not a build, and I've costed both answers so it's a comparison rather than more analysis.

**Next phase to build: the signed, off-box ledger export** (item 5). That's the real remaining work. The append-only ledger landed last phase, but the chain only proves integrity to someone who trusts the machine holding the database file — and if that machine's disk dies, the ledger is gone. Two gaps: the export isn't cryptographically signed, and nothing replicates off-box. Closing it means generating a signed digest bundle (partition boundary, record count, hash over contents) plus a replication path, so a regulator can verify nothing was removed without trusting the host. That's B01 §7 items 6 and 8, D09 §4.4.

It has a dependency worth stating: in an air-gapped deployment there's no external timestamping authority, so signing needs a key the Railroad controls — which loops back to AD-2, the certification registry that isn't built. So the honest sequencing is signing and replication first (self-contained, testable now), with the trust anchor documented as depending on AD-2.

The other open items aren't phases: D07 §14.5 is a counsel decision, and the D09 §4.4 supply-chain gaps are dated commitments (Q1–Q2 2027) already disclosed rather than work to do today.

If you want me to start, say which — I'd take the ledger export while you work through the model decision, since the two touch nothing in common and neither blocks the other.

# project-logs/transcripts — the conversation record

## What is here

```
transcripts/
├── README.md                        this file
├── 2026-11-09-chat-2.md             readable extract, chat-2
├── 2026-11-09-chat-3.md             readable extract, chat-3
└── raw/
    ├── 2026-11-09-chat-2.jsonl      raw session log, chat-2
    ├── chat-2-final.jsonl           later snapshot of the same session
    ├── chat-2-close.jsonl           snapshot taken at chat-2 close
    └── 2026-11-09-chat-3-snapshot.jsonl
                                     raw session log, chat-3 (mid-session)
```

## Why both a readable extract and the raw log

The `.md` extract is what a person reads: user and assistant prose verbatim, tool
calls recorded as one line each, tool output omitted because it is large and
reconstructible from the repository.

The raw `.jsonl` is what makes the extract falsifiable. It holds every event
including tool results, streaming partials and injected context. If an extract
ever looks wrong, or a decision needs to be traced to the exact thing that was
said, the raw log is the authority. **Committing only the extract would be a
summary pretending to be a record.**

## The rule

**Every session is extracted and committed in the same pass that produces its
work, raw log included.** This is not housekeeping. Chat-1 extracted three
readable transcripts and wrote them into a sandbox whose storage was destroyed at
session end; they never reached this repository and the raw logs went with them.
There is no copy anywhere. What survives of chat-1 is a distillation, which is a
judgement about what mattered rather than the conversation itself.

## How the extract is produced

A small Python script reads the session `.jsonl` and writes the `.md`. It is
deliberately not committed as a tool, because it is fifteen lines of `json.loads`
and a formatter, and a stale copy of it is worse than rewriting it. If you need to
regenerate:

1. Locate the session log — the live file is outside the repository, under the
   app's session directory, named `<session-id>.jsonl`.
2. Read each line as JSON. Keep `d["message"]` where `d["isSidechain"]` is false
   and the role is `user` or `assistant`.
3. De-duplicate assistant messages by `message["id"]` and tool calls by the
   content block's `id` — the log appends a message several times as it streams,
   so without this every paragraph appears three or four times.
4. Drop user-role messages that are machine injections rather than things the user
   typed: skill bodies (they begin `Base directory for this skill:`), compaction
   summaries (they begin `This session is being continued from a previous
   conversation`), and slash-command wrappers.
5. Flatten `content` arrays: keep `text` blocks, render `tool_use` as one line
   with the tool name and its most identifying argument, render `tool_result` as
   the literal `[tool result]`.
6. Copy the raw `.jsonl` into `raw/` alongside it.

**Chat-3's raw log is a mid-session snapshot.** It captures the session as of the
moment the transcript phase began, not the final state, because the session is
still running when the snapshot is taken. Later work in that session is covered by
`chat-3/SUMMARY.md`, and the raw log can be re-snapshotted at close.

derived from, so if the extraction ever looks wrong, the raw file is the answer.

moment the transcript was taken, not the final state, because the session was
still running. Later work in that session is covered by `chat-3/SUMMARY.md`, and
the raw log can be re-snapshotted at close.

**Chat-1 — the original build conversation — is lost.**

It ran from 2026-11-08 04:24 to 2026-11-10 03:00 and covered 2,527 turns across
three raw session logs. Chat-1 did extract those into readable transcripts. They
were written into a sandbox whose storage was destroyed when the session ended,
and they never reached this repository. The raw logs they came from were in the
same place and went with them.

There is no copy. No archive, no mirror, no cache. `project-logs/chat-1/SUMMARY.md`
is the only surviving record of that conversation, and it is a distillation — a
judgement about what mattered, not the conversation itself.

**This is why it will not happen again:** every session from chat-2 forward is
extracted and committed in the same pass that produces its work, raw log included.
Nothing is left in temporary storage to be lost.

The raw log lives at
`.claude/projects/session/<session-id>.jsonl` inside the session's mounted
folder. The extractor keeps only `user` and `assistant` events, drops sidechains

   session is being continued from a previous conversation`) and slash-command
   wrappers arrive with `role: user` but were not typed by anyone. Leaving them in
   makes the transcript unreadable and misrepresents what the user said.
3. **Verify the user turns against what you remember.** The extract is only
   trustworthy if you can read the user's actual messages back and recognise
   every one. If a message is missing or a prompt appears that nobody typed, the
   filter is wrong.

The extractor is a small script and easy to rewrite if needed; the point is that
the **raw file is committed**, so the conversation survives even if the extractor
does not.

# AxiomDynamics — Project Logs

This folder is the memory of the project. It exists because the work outgrew a
single conversation, and a fresh thread with no record of what was decided
rebuilds the same mistakes.

## Structure

```
project-logs/
├── README.md               this file — structure, purpose, order of authority
├── CURRENT-STATE.md        authoritative project state, updated as work lands
├── AxiomDynamics-Build-History-and-Working-Summary.docx
│                           the long-form account of the whole build (29 pp)
├── build-history-summary.js  generator for the above; re-run after a change
├── chat-1/
│   ├── SUMMARY.md          what chat-1 did, decided, caught, and left open
│   └── CARRY-FORWARD.md    the handoff document for chat-2
├── chat-2/
│   ├── SUMMARY.md          what chat-2 did; closed 2026-11-09
│   └── CARRY-FORWARD.md    the handoff document for chat-3
├── chat-3/
│   └── SUMMARY.md          running record of chat-3
└── transcripts/            chat-2 onward, readable + raw jsonl (chat-1 is lost)
    └── raw/                the source logs, committed with each transcript
```

**Start with the build history if you are new to this project.** It is 29 pages
covering the product, every build stage and its corrections, the full docket, the
loss of chat-1's work, the internal strategy, and the open items — written to be
read cold, without the conversation it describes.

## Order of authority

Three layers, and they are not equal:

1. **The repository itself** — `client-assets/MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/` and `assets/`.
   Where a document says one thing and a summary says another, the document wins.
2. **`CURRENT-STATE.md`** — what is built, what is pushed, what is open.
3. **`chat-N/SUMMARY.md`** — conclusions drawn from the above. Useful, never
   authoritative.

If any summary in this folder contradicts a document in the docket, **the docket

# AxiomDynamics — Project Logs

This folder is the memory of the project. It exists because the work outgrew a
single conversation, and a fresh thread with no record of what was decided
rebuilds the same mistakes.

## Structure

```
project-logs/
├── README.md               this file — structure, purpose, order of authority
├── CURRENT-STATE.md        authoritative project state, updated as work lands
├── AxiomDynamics-Build-History-and-Working-Summary.docx
│                           the long-form account of the whole build (29 pp)
├── build-history-summary.js  generator for the above; re-run after a change
├── chat-1/
│   ├── SUMMARY.md          what chat-1 did, decided, caught, and left open
│   └── CARRY-FORWARD.md    the handoff document for chat-2
├── chat-2/
│   ├── SUMMARY.md          what chat-2 did; closed 2026-11-09
│   └── CARRY-FORWARD.md    the handoff document for chat-3
├── chat-3/
│   └── SUMMARY.md          running record of chat-3
└── transcripts/            chat-2 onward, readable + raw jsonl (chat-1 is lost)
    └── raw/                the source logs, committed with each transcript
```

**Start with the build history if you are new to this project.** It is 29 pages
covering the product, every build stage and its corrections, the full docket, the
loss of chat-1's work, the internal strategy, and the open items — written to be
read cold, without the conversation it describes.

## Order of authority

Three layers, and they are not equal:

1. **The repository itself** — `client-assets/MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/` and `assets/`.
   Where a document says one thing and a summary says another, the document wins.
2. **`CURRENT-STATE.md`** — what is built, what is pushed, what is open.
3. **`chat-N/SUMMARY.md`** — conclusions drawn from the above. Useful, never
   authoritative.

If any summary in this folder contradicts a document in the docket, **the docket
governs and the summary is corrected.**

## The record, and the gap in it

`transcripts/` holds the conversation logs. **`2026-11-09-chat-2.md` and its raw
`.jsonl` are here** — chat-2 was extracted and committed at the end of its
session, raw log included, and that is now the rule for every session.

**Chat-1 is lost.** It covered 2,527 turns across three raw session logs from
2026-11-08 04:24 to 2026-11-10 03:00. Chat-1 extracted readable transcripts from
them — `2026-11-08-847804b3.md`, `2026-11-08-d4e7e999.md`, `2026-11-08-2c574bc2.md`
— but wrote them into a sandbox whose storage was destroyed when the session
ended. They never reached this repository, and the raw logs went with them.

There is no copy anywhere. What survives is `chat-1/SUMMARY.md`, which is a
distillation — a judgement about what mattered, not the conversation.

**The lesson, stated where it will be read:** work that exists in one volatile
place is one failure away from not existing. From chat-2 forward every session is
extracted and committed in the same pass that produces the work, and the raw log
is committed with it.

## Standing instructions

Two, from the original build, still in force:

- **"We will keep this same concept throughout."** The physics-first framing, the
  document structure, and the numbering discipline are not to be varied between
  documents. Consistency is the product.
- **"Strictly goes in our assets folder."** Internal analysis belongs in
  `assets/`, never in `client-assets/`. Client-facing material is
  `client-assets/MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/` only.

A third, added 2026-11-09 after the loss described above:

- **"Drop all the entire project work directly in AxiomDynamics folder so we don't
  lose any data from sandbox."** Work is written into this repository on the first
  pass and committed in the same pass that produces it. No drafts parked anywhere
  else. The sandbox is scratch space and its storage does not survive a session;
  this repository does.

## The discipline that matters most

Chat-1's own summary records it, and the record confirms it: nearly every bad
citation in the project came from writing a claim from memory and checking
afterwards. The worst defect — the detector ingest path drawn as built when no
inbound route exists — came from the same habit applied to a diagram.

**So: verify against the file, then write. Not the reverse.**

1	"""
2	SQLite-backed, append-only persistence for reviewer dispositions.
3	
4	Implements AD-3 (B01 §2): a disposition may be superseded but never overwritten
5	and never deleted. Three layers enforce that, and each one is load-bearing:
6	
7	1. **No UPDATE or DELETE path in Python.** There is no function here that
8	   mutates a row. A correction is a new row carrying `supersedes_id`, which
9	   points at the row it corrects. Both rows survive.
10	
11	2. **Database-level triggers.** Even someone holding the sqlite3 CLI, or a
12	   future contributor who adds an innocent-looking UPDATE, is stopped:
13	   `BEFORE UPDATE` and `BEFORE DELETE` on the ledger raise ABORT. The Python
14	   layer is not the guarantee; the schema is.
15	
16	3. **A hash chain.** Each row carries `prev_hash` (the previous row's
17	   `record_hash`, or 64 zeros for the first) and `record_hash`, a SHA-256 over
18	   the row's own content plus `prev_hash`. Editing a row in place therefore
19	   breaks its own hash, and deleting one breaks the next row's `prev_hash`.
20	   `verify_chain()` recomputes the whole chain and reports the first row that
21	   fails.
22	
23	What this does and does not prove — state it plainly rather than implying more:
24	
25	- It **does** prove the ledger has not been altered *by anything that went
26	  through this database*. An attacker with write access to the file can drop the
27	  triggers, rewrite rows and recompute every hash; the chain is a tamper-*evident*
28	  control, not tamper-*proof*.
29	- It **does** make an accidental overwrite impossible rather than merely
30	  discouraged, which is what the old upsert allowed.
31	- It does **not** replicate off-box. A destroyed disk still destroys the
32	  ledger. Off-box replication and signed audit export remain separate gaps
33	  (D09 §4.4).
34	
35	Deliberately the stdlib `sqlite3` module — no new dependency, no server
36	process, one file that survives a restart.
37	"""
38

"""
SQLite-backed, append-only persistence for reviewer dispositions.

Implements AD-3 (B01 §2): a disposition may be superseded but never overwritten
and never deleted. Three layers enforce that, and each one is load-bearing:

1. **No UPDATE or DELETE path in Python.** There is no function here that
   mutates a row. A correction is a new row carrying `supersedes_id`, which
   points at the row it corrects. Both rows survive.

2. **Database-level triggers.** Even someone holding the sqlite3 CLI, or a
   future contributor who adds an innocent-looking UPDATE, is stopped:
   `BEFORE UPDATE` and `BEFORE DELETE` on the ledger raise ABORT. The Python
   layer is not the guarantee; the schema is.

3. **A hash chain.** Each row carries `prev_hash` (the previous row's
   `record_hash`, or 64 zeros for the first) and `record_hash`, a SHA-256 over
   the row's own content plus `prev_hash`. Editing a row in place therefore
   breaks its own hash, and deleting one breaks the next row's `prev_hash`.
   `verify_chain()` recomputes the whole chain and reports the first row that
   fails.

What this does and does not prove — state it plainly rather than implying more:

- It **does** prove the ledger has not been altered *by anything that went
  through this database*. An attacker with write access to the file can drop the
  triggers, rewrite rows and recompute every hash; the chain is a tamper-*evident*
  control, not tamper-*proof*.
- It **does** make an accidental overwrite impossible rather than merely
  discouraged, which is what the old upsert allowed.
- It does **not** replicate off-box. A destroyed disk still destroys the
  ledger. Off-box replication and signed audit export remain separate gaps
  (D09 §4.4).

Deliberately the stdlib `sqlite3` module — no new dependency, no server
process, one file that survives a restart.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import json
import os
import sqlite3
from contextlib import contextmanager
from typing import Dict, List, Optional

DB_PATH = os.environ.get("AXIOM_DB_PATH", os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))), "axiom.db"))

GENESIS_HASH = "0" * 64

SCHEMA_VERSION = 2


@contextmanager
def _connect():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    try:
        yield conn
        conn.commit()
    finally:
        conn.close()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Chain arithmetic
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def _row_payload(row: Dict[str, object]) -> str:
    """
    Canonical serialisation of the fields the hash covers.

    `sort_keys=True`, no whitespace, fixed separators — so the same row always
    hashes the same way and a verifier in another language can reproduce it
    from the documented field list. `record_hash` is excluded, obviously.
    """
    covered = {
        "advisory_id": row["advisory_id"],
        "reviewer_name": row["reviewer_name"],
        "cert_id": row["cert_id"],
        "disposition": row["disposition"],
        "note": row["note"],
        "recorded_at": row["recorded_at"],
        "supersedes_id": row["supersedes_id"],
        "prev_hash": row["prev_hash"],
    }
    return json.dumps(covered, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))


def _compute_hash(row: Dict[str, object]) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(_row_payload(row).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Schema
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def init_db():
    """
    Create the ledger and its guard triggers, and migrate a v1 table in place.

    The v1 schema was `dispositions(advisory_id PRIMARY KEY, ...)` — one row per
    advisory, overwritten on re-decision. A v1 row held the *latest* decision
    and nothing else. Migration keeps that decision, marks it as the first link
    in the chain, and cannot invent history it never had; the timestamps of any
    prior overwrites are already gone and are not fabricated.
    """
    with _connect() as conn:
        existing = conn.execute(
            "SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' AND name='dispositions'"
        ).fetchone()

        legacy = None
        if existing is not None:
            cols = {r["name"] for r in conn.execute("PRAGMA table_info(dispositions)").fetchall()}
            if "record_hash" not in cols:
                # Rename out of the way only; the new table is created below by
                # the same CREATE statement used for a fresh install, so there is
                # exactly one definition of the schema.
                conn.execute("ALTER TABLE dispositions RENAME TO dispositions_v1")
                legacy = "dispositions_v1"

        conn.execute("""
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS dispositions (
                id            INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
                advisory_id   TEXT NOT NULL,
                reviewer_name TEXT NOT NULL,
                cert_id       TEXT NOT NULL,
                disposition   TEXT NOT NULL,
                note          TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
                recorded_at   TEXT NOT NULL,
                supersedes_id INTEGER REFERENCES dispositions(id),
                prev_hash     TEXT NOT NULL,
                record_hash   TEXT NOT NULL
            )
        """)
        conn.execute("""
            CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_dispositions_advisory
            ON dispositions (advisory_id, id)
        """)

        if legacy is not None:
            _migrate_v1(conn, legacy)

        # Guard triggers. `IF NOT EXISTS` so re-running init_db is harmless.
        # DROP TRIGGER is itself possible for someone with file access — see the
        # module docstring on what the chain does and does not prove.
        conn.execute("""
            CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS dispositions_no_update
            BEFORE UPDATE ON dispositions
            BEGIN
                SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'disposition ledger is append-only: UPDATE is not permitted (AD-3)');
            END
        """)
        conn.execute("""
            CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS dispositions_no_delete
            BEFORE DELETE ON dispositions
            BEGIN
                SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'disposition ledger is append-only: DELETE is not permitted (AD-3)');
            END
        """)

        conn.execute("PRAGMA user_version = %d" % SCHEMA_VERSION)


def _migrate_v1(conn, legacy: str):
    """Convert the v1 one-row-per-advisory table into an append-only ledger."""
    rows = conn.execute(
        f"SELECT advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, recorded_at "
        f"FROM {legacy} ORDER BY recorded_at, advisory_id"
    ).fetchall()

    prev = GENESIS_HASH
    for r in rows:
        rec = {
            "advisory_id": r["advisory_id"],
            "reviewer_name": r["reviewer_name"],
            "cert_id": r["cert_id"],
            "disposition": r["disposition"],
            "note": "",
            "recorded_at": r["recorded_at"],
            "supersedes_id": None,
            "prev_hash": prev,
        }
        rec["record_hash"] = _compute_hash(rec)
        conn.execute(
            """
            INSERT INTO dispositions
                (advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, note,
                 recorded_at, supersedes_id, prev_hash, record_hash)
            VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
            """,
            (rec["advisory_id"], rec["reviewer_name"], rec["cert_id"],
             rec["disposition"], rec["note"], rec["recorded_at"],
             None, rec["prev_hash"], rec["record_hash"]),
        )
        prev = rec["record_hash"]

    conn.execute(f"DROP TABLE {legacy}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Writes — insert only
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def save_disposition(advisory_id: str, reviewer_name: str, cert_id: str,
                     disposition: str, note: str = "") -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Append a disposition. Never updates.

    A second decision on the same advisory becomes a new row whose
    `supersedes_id` names the row it replaces. The earlier row keeps its own
    timestamp and content and remains readable.

    Runs under BEGIN IMMEDIATE so two concurrent appends cannot both read the
    same `prev_hash` and fork the chain.
    """
    with _connect_atomic() as conn:
        prev = conn.execute(
            "SELECT record_hash FROM dispositions ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1"
        ).fetchone()
        prev_hash = prev["record_hash"] if prev else GENESIS_HASH

        prior = conn.execute(
            "SELECT id FROM dispositions WHERE advisory_id = ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1",
            (advisory_id,),
        ).fetchone()

        recorded_at = conn.execute("SELECT datetime('now') AS t").fetchone()["t"]

        rec = {
            "advisory_id": advisory_id,
            "reviewer_name": reviewer_name,
            "cert_id": cert_id,
            "disposition": disposition,
            "note": note,
            "recorded_at": recorded_at,
            "supersedes_id": prior["id"] if prior else None,
            "prev_hash": prev_hash,
        }
        rec["record_hash"] = _compute_hash(rec)

        cur = conn.execute(
            """
            INSERT INTO dispositions
                (advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, note,
                 recorded_at, supersedes_id, prev_hash, record_hash)
            VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
            """,
            (rec["advisory_id"], rec["reviewer_name"], rec["cert_id"],
             rec["disposition"], rec["note"], rec["recorded_at"],
             rec["supersedes_id"], rec["prev_hash"], rec["record_hash"]),
        )
        rec["id"] = cur.lastrowid
        return dict(rec)


@contextmanager
def _connect_atomic():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH, isolation_level=None)
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    try:
        conn.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
        yield conn
        conn.execute("COMMIT")
    except Exception:
        conn.execute("ROLLBACK")
        raise
    finally:
        conn.close()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reads
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def get_disposition(advisory_id: str) -> Optional[Dict[str, object]]:
    """The current (latest) disposition for one advisory, or None."""
    with _connect() as conn:
        row = conn.execute(
            """
            SELECT id, advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, note,
                   recorded_at, supersedes_id, prev_hash, record_hash
            FROM dispositions WHERE advisory_id = ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1
            """,
            (advisory_id,),
        ).fetchone()
    return dict(row) if row else None


def disposition_history(advisory_id: str) -> List[Dict[str, object]]:
    """Every disposition ever recorded for one advisory, oldest first."""
    with _connect() as conn:
        rows = conn.execute(
            """
            SELECT id, advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, note,
                   recorded_at, supersedes_id, prev_hash, record_hash
            FROM dispositions WHERE advisory_id = ? ORDER BY id ASC
            """,
            (advisory_id,),
        ).fetchall()
    return [dict(r) for r in rows]


def all_dispositions() -> Dict[str, Dict[str, object]]:
    """Current disposition per advisory — the shape callers already expect."""
    out: Dict[str, Dict[str, object]] = {}
    with _connect() as conn:
        rows = conn.execute(
            """
            SELECT id, advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, note,
                   recorded_at, supersedes_id, prev_hash, record_hash
            FROM dispositions ORDER BY id ASC
            """
        ).fetchall()
    for r in rows:
        out[r["advisory_id"]] = dict(r)
    return out


def ledger_size() -> int:
    with _connect() as conn:
        return conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM dispositions").fetchone()["n"]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Verification
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def verify_chain() -> Dict[str, object]:
    """
    Recompute the whole chain. Returns
        {"ok": bool, "rows": n, "broken_at_id": int|None, "reason": str|None}

    Detects: a row whose content was changed (its own hash stops matching), a
    row removed from the middle (the next row's prev_hash no longer matches),
    and a chain whose links point at nothing.
    """
    with _connect() as conn:
        rows = conn.execute(
            """
            SELECT id, advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, note,
                   recorded_at, supersedes_id, prev_hash, record_hash
            FROM dispositions ORDER BY id ASC
            """
        ).fetchall()

    expected_prev = GENESIS_HASH
    for r in rows:
        rec = dict(r)
        if rec["prev_hash"] != expected_prev:
            return {"ok": False, "rows": len(rows), "broken_at_id": rec["id"],
                    "reason": "prev_hash does not match the preceding row "
                              "(a row was inserted, removed or reordered)"}
        if _compute_hash(rec) != rec["record_hash"]:
            return {"ok": False, "rows": len(rows), "broken_at_id": rec["id"],
                    "reason": "record_hash does not match the row content "
                              "(the row was altered)"}
        expected_prev = rec["record_hash"]

    return {"ok": True, "rows": len(rows), "broken_at_id": None, "reason": None}

5	and never deleted. Three layers enforce that, and each one is load-bearing:
6	
7	1. **No UPDATE or DELETE path in Python.** There is no function here that
8	   mutates a row. A correction is a new row carrying `supersedes_id`, which
9	   points at the row it corrects. Both rows survive.
10	
11	2. **Database-level triggers.** Even someone holding the sqlite3 CLI, or a
12	   future contributor who adds an innocent-looking UPDATE, is stopped:
13	   `BEFORE UPDATE` and `BEFORE DELETE` on the ledger raise ABORT. The Python
14	   layer is not the guarantee; the schema is.
15	
16	3. **A hash chain.** Each row carries `prev_hash` (the previous row's
17	   `record_hash`, or 64 zeros for the first) and `record_hash`, a SHA-256 over
18	   the row's own content plus `prev_hash`. Editing a row in place therefore
19	   breaks its own hash, and deleting one breaks the next row's `prev_hash`.
20	   `verify_chain()` recomputes the whole chain and reports the first row that
21	   fails.
22	
23	What this does and does not prove — state it plainly rather than implying more:
24	
25	- It **does** prove the ledger has not been altered *by anything that went
26	  through this database*. An attacker with write access to the file can drop the
27	  triggers, rewrite rows and recompute every hash; the chain is a tamper-*evident*
28	  control, not tamper-*proof*.
29	- It **does** make an accidental overwrite impossible rather than merely
30	  discouraged, which is what the old upsert allowed.
31	- It does **not** replicate off-box. A destroyed disk still destroys the
32	  ledger. Off-box replication and signed audit export remain separate gaps
33	  (D09 §4.4).
34	
35	Deliberately the stdlib `sqlite3` module — no new dependency, no server
36	process, one file that survives a restart.
37	"""
38	
39	from __future__ import annotations
40	
41	import hashlib
42	import json
43	import os
44	import sqlite3
45	from contextlib import contextmanager
46	from typing import Dict, List, Optional
47	
48	DB_PATH = os.environ.get("AXIOM_DB_PATH", os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))), "axiom.db"))
49	
50	GENESIS_HASH = "0" * 64
51	
52	SCHEMA_VERSION = 2
53	
54	
55	@contextmanager
56	def _connect():
57	    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
58	    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
59	    try:
60	        yield conn
61	        conn.commit()
62	    finally:
63	        conn.close()
64	
65	
66	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
67	# Chain arithmetic
68	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
69	def _row_payload(row: Dict[str, object]) -> str:
70	    """
71	    Canonical serialisation of the fields the hash covers.
72	
73	    `sort_keys=True`, no whitespace, fixed separators — so the same row always
74	    hashes the same way and a verifier in another language can reproduce it
75	    from the documented field list. `record_hash` is excluded, obviously.
76	    """
77	    covered = {
78	        "advisory_id": row["advisory_id"],
79	        "reviewer_name": row["reviewer_name"],
80	        "cert_id": row["cert_id"],
81	        "disposition": row["disposition"],
82	        "note": row["note"],
83	        "recorded_at": row["recorded_at"],
84	        "supersedes_id": row["supersedes_id"],
85	        "prev_hash": row["prev_hash"],
86	    }
87	    return json.dumps(covered, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
88	
89	
90	def _compute_hash(row: Dict[str, object]) -> str:
91	    return hashlib.sha256(_row_payload(row).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
92	
93	
94	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
95	# Schema
96	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
97	def init_db():
98	    """
99	    Create the ledger and its guard triggers, and migrate a v1 table in place.
100	
101	    The v1 schema was `dispositions(advisory_id PRIMARY KEY, ...)` — one row per
102	    advisory, overwritten on re-decision. A v1 row held the *latest* decision
103	    and nothing else. Migration keeps that decision, marks it as the first link
104	    in the chain, and cannot invent history it never had; the timestamps of any
105	    prior overwrites are already gone and are not fabricated.
106	    """
107	    with _connect() as conn:
108	        existing = conn.execute(
109	            "SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' AND name='dispositions'"
110	        ).fetchone()
111	
112	        legacy = None
113	        if existing is not None:
114	            cols = {r["name"] for r in conn.execute("PRAGMA table_info(dispositions)").fetchall()}
115	            if "record_hash" not in cols:
116	                # Rename out of the way only; the new table is created below by
117	                # the same CREATE statement used for a fresh install, so there is
118	                # exactly one definition of the schema.
119	                conn.execute("ALTER TABLE dispositions RENAME TO dispositions_v1")
120	                legacy = "dispositions_v1"
121	
122	        conn.execute("""
123	            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS dispositions (
124	                id            INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
125	                advisory_id   TEXT NOT NULL,
126	                reviewer_name TEXT NOT NULL,
127	                cert_id       TEXT NOT NULL,
128	                disposition   TEXT NOT NULL,
129	                note          TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
130	                recorded_at   TEXT NOT NULL,
131	                supersedes_id INTEGER REFERENCES dispositions(id),
132	                prev_hash     TEXT NOT NULL,
133	                record_hash   TEXT NOT NULL
134	            )
135	        """)
136	        conn.execute("""
137	            CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_dispositions_advisory
138	            ON dispositions (advisory_id, id)
139	        """)
140	
141	        if legacy is not None:
142	            _migrate_v1(conn, legacy)
143	
144	        # Guard triggers. `IF NOT EXISTS` so re-running init_db is harmless.
145	        # DROP TRIGGER is itself possible for someone with file access — see the
146	        # module docstring on what the chain does and does not prove.
147	        conn.execute("""
148	            CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS dispositions_no_update
149	            BEFORE UPDATE ON dispositions
150	            BEGIN
151	                SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'disposition ledger is append-only: UPDATE is not permitted (AD-3)');
152	            END
153	        """)
154	        conn.execute("""
155	            CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS dispositions_no_delete
156	            BEFORE DELETE ON dispositions
157	            BEGIN
158	                SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'disposition ledger is append-only: DELETE is not permitted (AD-3)');
159	            END
160	        """)
161	
162	        conn.execute("PRAGMA user_version = %d" % SCHEMA_VERSION)
163	
164	
165	def _migrate_v1(conn, legacy: str):
166	    """Convert the v1 one-row-per-advisory table into an append-only ledger."""
167	    rows = conn.execute(
168	        f"SELECT advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, recorded_at "
169	        f"FROM {legacy} ORDER BY recorded_at, advisory_id"
170	    ).fetchall()
171	
172	    prev = GENESIS_HASH
173	    for r in rows:
174	        rec = {
175	            "advisory_id": r["advisory_id"],
176	            "reviewer_name": r["reviewer_name"],
177	            "cert_id": r["cert_id"],
178	            "disposition": r["disposition"],
179	            "note": "",
180	            "recorded_at": r["recorded_at"],
181	            "supersedes_id": None,
182	            "prev_hash": prev,
183	        }
184	        rec["record_hash"] = _compute_hash(rec)
185	        conn.execute(
186	            """
187	            INSERT INTO dispositions
188	                (advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, note,
189	                 recorded_at, supersedes_id, prev_hash, record_hash)
190	            VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
191	            """,
192	            (rec["advisory_id"], rec["reviewer_name"], rec["cert_id"],
193	             rec["disposition"], rec["note"], rec["recorded_at"],
194	             None, rec["prev_hash"], rec["record_hash"]),
195	        )
196	        prev = rec["record_hash"]
197	
198	    conn.execute(f"DROP TABLE {legacy}")
199	
200	
201	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
202	# Writes — insert only
203	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
204	def save_disposition(advisory_id: str, reviewer_name: str, cert_id: str,
205	                     disposition: str, note: str = "") -> Dict[str, object]:
206	    """
207	    Append a disposition. Never updates.
208	
209	    A second decision on the same advisory becomes a new row whose
210	    `supersedes_id` names the row it replaces. The earlier row keeps its own
211	    timestamp and content and remains readable.
212	
213	    Runs under BEGIN IMMEDIATE so two concurrent appends cannot both read the
214	    same `prev_hash` and fork the chain.
215	    """
216	    with _connect_atomic() as conn:
217	        prev = conn.execute(
218	            "SELECT record_hash FROM dispositions ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1"
219	        ).fetchone()
220	        prev_hash = prev["record_hash"] if prev else GENESIS_HASH
221	
222	        prior = conn.execute(
223	            "SELECT id FROM dispositions WHERE advisory_id = ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1",
224	            (advisory_id,),
225	        ).fetchone()
226	
227	        recorded_at = conn.execute("SELECT datetime('now') AS t").fetchone()["t"]
228	
229	        rec = {
230	            "advisory_id": advisory_id,
231	            "reviewer_name": reviewer_name,
232	            "cert_id": cert_id,
233	            "disposition": disposition,
234	            "note": note,
235	            "recorded_at": recorded_at,
236	            "supersedes_id": prior["id"] if prior else None,
237	            "prev_hash": prev_hash,
238	        }
239	        rec["record_hash"] = _compute_hash(rec)
240	
241	        cur = conn.execute(
242	            """
243	            INSERT INTO dispositions
244	                (advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, note,
245	                 recorded_at, supersedes_id, prev_hash, record_hash)
246	            VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
247	            """,
248	            (rec["advisory_id"], rec["reviewer_name"], rec["cert_id"],
249	             rec["disposition"], rec["note"], rec["recorded_at"],
250	             rec["supersedes_id"], rec["prev_hash"], rec["record_hash"]),
251	        )
252	        rec["id"] = cur.lastrowid
253	        return dict(rec)
254	
255	
256	@contextmanager
257	def _connect_atomic():
258	    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH, isolation_level=None)
259	    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
260	    try:
261	        conn.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
262	        yield conn
263	        conn.execute("COMMIT")
264	    except Exception:
265	        conn.execute("ROLLBACK")
266	        raise
267	    finally:
268	        conn.close()
269	
270	
271	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
272	# Reads
273	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
274	def get_disposition(advisory_id: str) -> Optional[Dict[str, object]]:
275	    """The current (latest) disposition for one advisory, or None."""
276	    with _connect() as conn:
277	        row = conn.execute(
278	            """
279	            SELECT id, advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, note,
280	                   recorded_at, supersedes_id, prev_hash, record_hash
281	            FROM dispositions WHERE advisory_id = ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1
282	            """,
283	            (advisory_id,),
284	        ).fetchone()
285	    return dict(row) if row else None
286	
287	
288	def disposition_history(advisory_id: str) -> List[Dict[str, object]]:
289	    """Every disposition ever recorded for one advisory, oldest first."""
290	    with _connect() as conn:
291	        rows = conn.execute(
292	            """
293	            SELECT id, advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, note,
294	                   recorded_at, supersedes_id, prev_hash, record_hash
295	            FROM dispositions WHERE advisory_id = ? ORDER BY id ASC
296	            """,
297	            (advisory_id,),
298	        ).fetchall()
299	    return [dict(r) for r in rows]
300	
301	
302	def all_dispositions() -> Dict[str, Dict[str, object]]:
303	    """Current disposition per advisory — the shape callers already expect."""
304	    out: Dict[str, Dict[str, object]] = {}
305	    with _connect() as conn:
306	        rows = conn.execute(
307	            """
308	            SELECT id, advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, note,
309	                   recorded_at, supersedes_id, prev_hash, record_hash
310	            FROM dispositions ORDER BY id ASC
311	            """
312	        ).fetchall()
313	    for r in rows:
314	        out[r["advisory_id"]] = dict(r)
315	    return out
316	
317	
318	def ledger_size() -> int:
319	    with _connect() as conn:
320	        return conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM dispositions").fetchone()["n"]
321	
322	
323	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
324	# Verification
325	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
326	def verify_chain() -> Dict[str, object]:
327	    """
328	    Recompute the whole chain. Returns
329	        {"ok": bool, "rows": n, "broken_at_id": int|None, "reason": str|None}
330	
331	    Detects: a row whose content was changed (its own hash stops matching), a
332	    row removed from the middle (the next row's prev_hash no longer matches),
333	    and a chain whose links point at nothing.
334	    """
335	    with _connect() as conn:
336	        rows = conn.execute(
337	            """
338	            SELECT id, advisory_id, reviewer_name, cert_id, disposition, note,
339	                   recorded_at, supersedes_id, prev_hash, record_hash
340	            FROM dispositions ORDER BY id ASC
341	            """
342	        ).fetchall()
343	
344	    expected_prev = GENESIS_HASH
345	    for r in rows:
346	        rec = dict(r)
347	        if rec["prev_hash"] != expected_prev:
348	            return {"ok": False, "rows": len(rows), "broken_at_id": rec["id"],
349	                    "reason": "prev_hash does not match the preceding row "
350	                              "(a row was inserted, removed or reordered)"}
351	        if _compute_hash(rec) != rec["record_hash"]:
352	            return {"ok": False, "rows": len(rows), "broken_at_id": rec["id"],
353	                    "reason": "record_hash does not match the row content "
354	                              "(the row was altered)"}
355	        expected_prev = rec["record_hash"]
356	
357	    return {"ok": True, "rows": len(rows), "broken_at_id": None, "reason": None}

=== D09 §4.4 ===
91:| **Authentication** | The Platform currently uses local user accounts with passwords. **AD-2 (B01) recommends signed certification registry with issued credentials.** This is a gap; see §4.4. | Partial — authentication is local, not cryptographically registered |
92-| **Authorization** | Role-based access (Operator, Reviewer, Administrator) per C02. Enforced by the Platform. | Implemented per role model |
93:| **Audit logging** | All disposition writes, user login/logout, configuration changes, and patch applications are logged. Logs are not editable or deletable by any Platform user and are exportable by an Admin. The disposition ledger is insert-only, guarded by `BEFORE UPDATE`/`BEFORE DELETE` triggers and chained by SHA-256; the chain is verifiable on demand and a break is reported with the failing record. **Not yet signed or replicated off-box — see §4.4.** | **Partial — append-only and hash-chained built 2026-11-09; signed export and off-box replication outstanding** |
94-| **Data validation** | Input validation on disposition fields (reviewer name, cert ID, disposition text). Malformed data is rejected. | Implemented; schema incomplete (see B01 §7 gap register) |
95-| **Backup** | The Railroad performs nightly backups of the SQLite database (daily full, hourly WAL). Supplier does not hold backups. | Railroad responsibility |
96-| **Time synchronization** | The Platform relies on the host's system time. The Railroad must configure NTP for accurate timestamps in the disposition ledger. | Railroad responsibility |
97-
98-### 4.3 Operational controls
99-
100-**Supplier commits to:**
101-- **No unauthorized access:** Supplier personnel access the Platform only with explicit Railroad authorization and per §3.4.
102-- **Vulnerability management:** Supplier scans dependencies for known vulnerabilities before each release and notifies the Railroad of security patches per D06 §3.2.
103-- **Secure development:** Code review before merge; no committing secrets (API keys, credentials) to the repository.
104:- **SBOM:** Supplier is **building** SBOM generation and will provide a Software Bill of Materials with each release **once implemented (target Q1 2027)**. **Not provided today** — see §4.4 and D10 Part 5.
105:- **Supply chain:** Supplier documents the source of each component in **D10**. **Hash verification of dependency downloads is not yet implemented** (target Q1 2027) — see §4.4. Where the Railroad uses the sealed-archive method (C01 Part B), a SHA-256 manifest of the transferred set is provided for the Railroad's own verification.
106-
107:> **Why this section was corrected.** It previously stated as present commitments that an SBOM is provided with each release and that dependency integrity is verified by SHA-256. **Both were untrue, and both were listed as gaps six lines further down in §4.4.** A security schedule that lists a control as committed in §4.3 and unimplemented in §4.4 is worse than one that admits the gap once: it tells the reviewer what they want to hear and then contradicts itself, which is exactly the pattern that destroys a vendor's credibility in a CISO review.
108-
109:### 4.4 Known gaps and remediation roadmap
110-
111-The following controls are **not yet implemented** but are on the remediation roadmap:
112-
113-| Gap | Impact | Remediation | Target |
114-|---|---|---|---|
115-| **Authentication is local, not cryptographically registered** | A malicious insider with database access could potentially forge a disposition record. | Implement signed certification registry (AD-2 per B01 §7) | Q2 2027 |
116-| **No signed, off-box export of the disposition ledger** | The ledger cannot be silently altered through the application or by ordinary database access (insert-only, guard triggers, SHA-256 chain — built 2026-11-09), but it is not cryptographically **signed** and is not replicated off-box. A party with write access to the database file could drop the triggers, rewrite rows and recompute the chain. A lost disk loses the ledger. | Sign the export bundle and replicate it to a second host; see B01 §4.5, §7 items 6 and 8 | Q2 2027 |
117-| **No SBOM artifact in releases** | The Railroad cannot independently verify the dependency chain. | Generate SBOM (SPDX or CycloneDX) per release | Q1 2027 |
118-| **No hash verification of dependency downloads** | A compromised PyPI could serve malware as a dependency. | Require SHA-256 pinning of all dependencies in requirements.txt | Q1 2027 |
119-| **No signed release artifacts** | A malicious actor could replace a release archive with a trojan. | Sign releases with GPG; provide public key | Q2 2027 |
120-
121-**These gaps are disclosed proactively.** The Railroad should assess whether they are acceptable for its risk tolerance. If not, the Railroad may delay production deployment until the remediation is complete (escrow of current version per D13 remains available).
122-
123----
124-
125-## 5. Data retention and deletion
126-
127-### 5.1 Retention period
128-
129-**Default:** Railroad Data is retained indefinitely in the Platform database, subject to the Railroad's retention policy.
130-
