# AxiomDynamics — Project Logs

This folder is the memory of the project. It exists because the work outgrew a
single conversation, and a fresh thread with no record of what was decided
rebuilds the same mistakes.

## Structure

```
project-logs/
├── README.md               this file — structure, purpose, order of authority
├── CURRENT-STATE.md        authoritative project state, updated as work lands
├── AxiomDynamics-Build-History-and-Working-Summary.docx
│                           the long-form account of the whole build (29 pp)
├── build-history-summary.js  generator for the above; re-run after a change
├── chat-1/
│   ├── SUMMARY.md          what chat-1 did, decided, caught, and left open
│   └── CARRY-FORWARD.md    the handoff document for chat-2
├── chat-2/
│   ├── SUMMARY.md          what chat-2 did; closed 2026-11-09
│   └── CARRY-FORWARD.md    the handoff document for chat-3
├── chat-3/
│   └── SUMMARY.md          running record of chat-3
└── transcripts/            chat-2 onward, readable + raw jsonl (chat-1 is lost)
    ├── 2026-11-09-chat-2.md   readable extract
    ├── 2026-11-09-chat-3.md   readable extract
    └── raw/                the source logs, committed with each transcript
```

**Start with the build history if you are new to this project.** It is 29 pages
covering the product, every build stage and its corrections, the full docket, the
loss of chat-1's work, the internal strategy, and the open items — written to be
read cold, without the conversation it describes.

## Order of authority

Three layers, and they are not equal:

1. **The repository itself** — `client-assets/MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/` and `assets/`.
   Where a document says one thing and a summary says another, the document wins.
2. **`CURRENT-STATE.md`** — what is built, what is pushed, what is open.
3. **`chat-N/SUMMARY.md`** — conclusions drawn from the above. Useful, never
   authoritative.

If any summary in this folder contradicts a document in the docket, **the docket
governs and the summary is corrected.**

## The record, and the gap in it

`transcripts/` holds the conversation logs. **`2026-11-09-chat-2.md` and its raw
`.jsonl` are here** — chat-2 was extracted and committed at the end of its
session, raw log included, and that is now the rule for every session.

**Chat-1 is lost.** It covered 2,527 turns across three raw session logs from
2026-11-08 04:24 to 2026-11-10 03:00. Chat-1 extracted readable transcripts from
them — `2026-11-08-847804b3.md`, `2026-11-08-d4e7e999.md`, `2026-11-08-2c574bc2.md`
— but wrote them into a sandbox whose storage was destroyed when the session
ended. They never reached this repository, and the raw logs went with them.

There is no copy anywhere. What survives is `chat-1/SUMMARY.md`, which is a
distillation — a judgement about what mattered, not the conversation.

**The lesson, stated where it will be read:** work that exists in one volatile
place is one failure away from not existing. From chat-2 forward every session is
extracted and committed in the same pass that produces the work, and the raw log
is committed with it.

## Standing instructions

Two, from the original build, still in force:

- **"We will keep this same concept throughout."** The physics-first framing, the
  document structure, and the numbering discipline are not to be varied between
  documents. Consistency is the product.
- **"Strictly goes in our assets folder."** Internal analysis belongs in
  `assets/`, never in `client-assets/`. Client-facing material is
  `client-assets/MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/` only.

A third, added 2026-11-09 after the loss described above:

- **"Drop all the entire project work directly in AxiomDynamics folder so we don't
  lose any data from sandbox."** Work is written into this repository on the first
  pass and committed in the same pass that produces it. No drafts parked anywhere
  else. The sandbox is scratch space and its storage does not survive a session;
  this repository does.

## The discipline that matters most

Chat-1's own summary records it, and the record confirms it: nearly every bad
citation in the project came from writing a claim from memory and checking
afterwards. The worst defect — the detector ingest path drawn as built when no
inbound route exists — came from the same habit applied to a diagram.

**So: verify against the file, then write. Not the reverse.**

# Transcripts

Conversation records for the project.

## What is here

| File | Turns | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| `2026-11-09-chat-2.md` | 256 | chat-2, from the first line to the point of extraction |
| `2026-11-09-chat-3.md` | 582 | chat-3, from the first line to the transcript phase |
| `raw/2026-11-09-chat-2.jsonl` | 780 events | the unprocessed chat-2 log, 1.6 MB |
| `raw/chat-2-final.jsonl`, `raw/chat-2-close.jsonl` | — | later snapshots of the same chat-2 session |
| `raw/2026-11-09-chat-3-snapshot.jsonl` | 3,385 events | the chat-3 log, 13.2 MB, valid JSONL |

The `.md` is the readable version: every user and assistant turn in order. Tool
calls are recorded inline so you can see what was run; tool *output* — command
results, file listings, screenshots — is omitted, because it is bulk without
being conversation.

The `.jsonl` in `raw/` is the source. Don't edit it. It is what the `.md` was
derived from, so if the extraction ever looks wrong, the raw file is the answer.
Commit both: an extract alone is a summary pretending to be a record.

**Chat-3's raw log is a mid-session snapshot.** It captures the session as of the
moment the transcript was taken, not the final state, because the session was
still running. Later work in that session is covered by `chat-3/SUMMARY.md`, and
the raw log can be re-snapshotted at close.

## What is NOT here, and cannot be

**Chat-1 — the original build conversation — is lost.**

It ran from 2026-11-08 04:24 to 2026-11-10 03:00 and covered 2,527 turns across
three raw session logs. Chat-1 did extract those into readable transcripts. They
were written into a sandbox whose storage was destroyed when the session ended,
and they never reached this repository. The raw logs they came from were in the
same place and went with them.

There is no copy. No archive, no mirror, no cache. `project-logs/chat-1/SUMMARY.md`
is the only surviving record of that conversation, and it is a distillation — a
judgement about what mattered, not the conversation itself.

**This is why it will not happen again:** every session from chat-2 forward is
extracted and committed in the same pass that produces its work, raw log included.
Nothing is left in temporary storage to be lost.

## Reproducing an extraction

The raw log lives at
`.claude/projects/session/<session-id>.jsonl` inside the session's mounted
folder. The extractor keeps only `user` and `assistant` events, drops sidechains
and system reminders, and writes them in order.

Three things it must do, learned the hard way on chat-3:

1. **De-duplicate before writing anything.** The log appends each assistant
   message several times while it streams. Without de-duplication by
   `message["id"]` and by tool-call block `id`, every paragraph and every tool
   call appears three or four times. The first chat-3 extract was 1,062 turns and
   contained duplicates; the correct count is 582.
2. **Drop machine-injected `user` messages.** Skill bodies (they begin
   `Base directory for this skill:`), compaction summaries (they begin `This
   session is being continued from a previous conversation`) and slash-command
   wrappers arrive with `role: user` but were not typed by anyone. Leaving them in
   makes the transcript unreadable and misrepresents what the user said.
3. **Verify the user turns against what you remember.** The extract is only
   trustworthy if you can read the user's actual messages back and recognise
   every one. If a message is missing or a prompt appears that nobody typed, the
   filter is wrong.

The extractor is a small script and easy to rewrite if needed; the point is that
the **raw file is committed**, so the conversation survives even if the extractor
does not.

21	derived from, so if the extraction ever looks wrong, the raw file is the answer.
22	Commit both: an extract alone is a summary pretending to be a record.

25	moment the transcript was taken, not the final state, because the session was

40	is the only surviving record of that conversation, and it is a distillation — a

45	Nothing is left in temporary storage to be lost.

metadata:

---

When I produce an analysis **and** the script that checks it, I must run an independent audit before calling the work done. A second agent with no stake in the result, prompted to try to falsify the claims.

**Why:** On 2026-11-09 (chat-3) I wrote `assets/a2-d08-model-decision-2026-11-09.md` and its checker `a2-d08-model-decision.py`, which reported "all checks passed". An independent audit found **four material errors** — and the checker had validated one of them, because I wrote it to encode the same mislabelling. Specifically: a dashboard figure ($14,339,850) I presented as `backend/roi.py`'s output was actually A1's formula re-run at 2%; `roi.py` takes warrants, not axles, so "at 500 axles" was never computable from it. Also "repeats verbatim" (it didn't), "where the numbers came from" (overstated derivation from consistency), and a claim that a spreadsheet line was missing when it existed and was merely inert.

**How to apply:**
- A green self-check proves internal consistency, not correctness. It cannot catch a wrong premise I also encoded in the check.
- Use the `Agent` tool with `subagent_type: general-purpose`, and tell it explicitly to **falsify**, not confirm — "try hard to falsify this, it's the strongest claim". Ask it to write its own arithmetic rather than running my script.
- Ask it to verify *quotes against source files*, not just numbers. Two of the four errors were prose attributions.
- Budget for it: it took ~10 minutes and found real defects. That is a good trade.
- This generalises to any phase where I author both the artifact and its acceptance test — docket figures, test suites for my own code, verification passes.

# Chat-3 — Running Summary

Status: **in progress** as of 2026-11-09.
Opened with the chat-2 carry-forward. Its first act was to verify the inherited
state against the repository rather than trust the handoff, per the standing rule.

## Verification of inherited state (start of chat-3)

Read `CURRENT-STATE.md`, `chat-2/SUMMARY.md` and `project-logs/README.md`, then
checked the repo directly. Four things did not match the written record:

1. **Push state was stale in the carry-forward.** It named `785f335` and
   `ee9800c` as unpushed; both were already in `origin/main`, with `ee9800c` as
   the remote top. What was actually unpushed was the later transcript and
   handoff work — `3d773ac`, `36b43bd`, `d6f25ac`, `05b161d`.
2. **`chat-2/SUMMARY.md` still read "in progress"** and still claimed "Neither is
   pushed" about `f58b07c`/`c9b32bd`. Finalized and corrected.
3. **57 "modified" files were a line-ending artifact.** CRLF working tree against
   LF blobs; `--ignore-cr-at-eol` returned empty. Not content. Recorded in
   `CURRENT-STATE.md` so the next session does not re-investigate it.
4. Everything else was intact: 37 docket documents, `assets/`, and the chat-2
   transcript with three raw `.jsonl` files (5.8 MB).

## Work done in chat-3

### A2 / D08 arithmetic pass — complete

The highest-value item from both the carry-forward and `CURRENT-STATE.md`, and
untouched since `cf2e6ba`.

Built `assets/a2-d08-arithmetic-pass.py`: it recomputes every figure in A2 and D08
from its stated source equation and compares it to the document, exiting non-zero
on any mismatch. **78 of 78 computed figures agree.** No arithmetic error exists
in either document — every band total, worked example, site-fee product, payment
split, conversion credit, three-year row, performance cap, cumulative schedule and
the 5% escalation is correct as written.

Two *claims* did not reproduce. Both are model divergences rather than arithmetic
errors, and both are left open because fixing them means choosing which model
governs — an owner decision, not an editorial one:

- **Finding 1.** A2 §3.2 and D08 §3 claim ~2.0x at 500 axles rising to ~4.1x at
  10,000. The shipped models produce 1.77x/3.36x on the A2 cost basis, or
  2.36x/4.99x on A1's. No parameter set in the repository reproduces both anchors.
  The monotonic claim is true on every basis tested.
- **Finding 2.** D08 §5–§6 modelled benefits run 5x–14x above the $696,675 annual
  benefit A1 computes at identical inputs. D08 §5 states A1 must never be
  bypassed.

Full working, tables and recommended dispositions:
`assets/a2-d08-arithmetic-pass-2026-11-09.md`.

### A1 builder — two defects fixed

- The sheet-5 assumptions note attributed a **2%** catastrophic escalation rate to
  a model whose cell B17 has held **0.05%** since the correction. Corrected to
  name 0.05% and cite B17.
- The script saved to `/sessions/.../mnt/outputs/...`, a path inside the destroyed
  chat-1 sandbox, so running it raised `FileNotFoundError`. It now writes beside
  itself via `os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))`.

The committed workbook was **not** regenerated: doing so would bake both open
findings into a new file before the model question is settled.

### Project logs corrected

`CURRENT-STATE.md` updated (push state, open items, the line-ending trap, the A1
builder fixes). `chat-2/SUMMARY.md` finalized and its push claims corrected.
`chat-2/CARRY-FORWARD.md` push numbers and "work waiting" section corrected.
`project-logs/README.md` tree now lists `chat-2/CARRY-FORWARD.md`, `chat-3/` and
`transcripts/raw/`.

## Verification performed

- Arithmetic: 78 figures computed independently in `assets/a2-d08-arithmetic-pass.py`,
  all matching. Script re-run from the committed tree and exits 0.
- Every A1 figure cited in the pass record was read from the built workbook
  (`openpyxl`, `data_only=True`), not from the builder source — the two differ on
  the pilot cost line.
- A2 and D08 confirmed untouched: `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` on both returned
  empty after the pass.
- Commit inspected for line-ending churn. The first attempt rewrote the builder to
  CRLF and produced 1,248 changed lines for a 2-line fix; reset and recommitted so
  the commit shows 420 insertions and 2 deletions.

## The build history document

Requested by the owner because chat-1's conversation no longer exists and the
build needed a readable record of itself. Produced as
`project-logs/AxiomDynamics-Build-History-and-Working-Summary.docx` — 29 pages,
eight parts plus an appendix — with its generator committed beside it at
`project-logs/build-history-summary.js` so it can be rebuilt after a change.

Contents, in order: what the product is and why physics rather than ML; the six
models; the eight build stages across all 37 commits with every correction; the
38-artifact docket document by document plus the D00 Part IV precedence ladder;
the loss of chat-1's work, its mechanism and its cost; what chat-2 rebuilt and
how it verified it; internal strategy in `assets/`; the open items including both
chat-3 modelling findings; how to resume; and an appendix with the repository
map, the full commit chronology and a status table.

Written from the repository, not from recollection. Layout verified by rendering
to PDF and reading the pages: 29 pages, no overflow, tables within margins,
numbering restarting per list. Two defects were found and fixed in that pass —
all numbered lists shared one continuous sequence (Part VIII opened at "10."),
and the Word TOC field rendered empty in a converter that does not update
fields, so a static Parts table now carries the navigation.

## Commits

`ed78962` — the arithmetic pass, check script, pass record and builder fixes.
`a3ba43f` — the build history document and its generator.
`b3dcda4` — `CURRENT-STATE.md`: points at the summary, corrects the artifact
count, and replaces the hardcoded unpushed-hash list with an instruction to check
`git log origin/main..HEAD`.

**Push required.** Run `PUSH-TO-GITHUB.bat` in the repo root, then confirm with
`git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD` rather than trusting any hash written here.

## Phase 2 — append-only disposition ledger (AD-3), committed `209efe6`

Chosen as the next build because it was the one open code control that needed no
commercial decision from the owner, and because the docket's most legally
significant record was overstating what the code did.

**The defect, confirmed before touching it.** `backend/store.py` used
`advisory_id` as PRIMARY KEY with `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`. A second
disposition on the same advisory overwrote the first — its reviewer, its note
and its `recorded_at` all gone. F09 described an append-only record; the code
produced one row that could be rewritten. Six documents disclosed the gap.

**What was built.**

- Insert-only writes. A correction is a new row carrying `supersedes_id`; the
  corrected row keeps its own content and timestamp.
- `BEFORE UPDATE` / `BEFORE DELETE` triggers that `RAISE(ABORT)`, so the
  guarantee is in the schema rather than in application convention.
- SHA-256 chain: `prev_hash` (predecessor's hash, 64 zeros at the start) and
  `record_hash` over canonical content plus `prev_hash`. `verify_chain()`
  recomputes and names the first failing row.
- `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on writes, so two concurrent appends cannot both read the
  same `prev_hash` and fork the chain.
- Migration inside `init_db()` from the v1 table, preserving the surviving
  decision and its original timestamp without fabricating lost history.

**What it does not do, and the docket now says so in these words.** The chain is
tamper-*evident*, not tamper-*proof*. Whoever holds the database file can drop
the triggers, rewrite rows and recompute every hash. Signed, off-box export
stays open in D09 §4.4; the gap narrowed, it did not vanish. Recording that
distinction was the point — the failure mode this project keeps having is a
document claiming more than the code delivers.

**Verification.**

- 17 new adversarial tests in `tests/test_store.py`, each attempting to destroy
  an earlier decision: an `UPDATE`, a `DELETE`, a second disposition, a tampered
  row, a removed row, trigger survival across re-init, and two migration shapes.
- `tests/run_tests.py` was loading only `test_physics.py`, so the new module
  would never have run in CI. Rewritten to discover every `test_*.py`. Suite is
  now 38, all passing.
- End-to-end against a live server: two dispositions on one advisory produce
  two records, the second names the first as superseded, `/api/warrant/{id}/disposition`
  returns both with `chain_ok: true`, `/api/ledger/verify` returns
  `{ok: true, rows: 2}`, the alert carries "supersedes 1 earlier record", and
  empty reviewer input is rejected with 400.
- No headless browser in this environment, so the UI change was verified by
  `node --check` plus inspecting the served DOM construction rather than by
  screenshot. **The history panel has not been seen rendered.** Worth a look on
  first run.

**Docket corrected in the same commit** — the rule is that a gap closes only
when the code changes and the disclosing documents change with it: B01 §4.1,
§4.5, §4.6, §7 items 2 and 8 and the component table; D09 §4.4 and the
audit-logging row; F09 Parts 6 and 7 and its footer; F00; B02; C02; D12; D14 §5;
D00 Parts V and VI; and the root README.

**Two defects found in the root README while correcting it,** neither related to
the ledger: it opened "three named physical models" then listed seven; it had
two items numbered `7.`; and it described the 2% catastrophic-escalation
placeholder as current when `roi.py` uses 2% but the A1 workbook uses 0.05%.
All three fixed, and the 40× divergence now points at
`assets/a2-d08-arithmetic-pass-2026-11-09.md` instead of being restated as if
settled.

## Next

1. Decide Finding 1 — strike or restate the 2.0x/4.1x anchors.
2. Decide Finding 2 — which model governs, A1 or D08 §5–§6.
3. Then regenerate the A1 workbook and re-run the check script.
4. D07 §14.5 governing law and venue remains open, unchanged by this pass.
5. Signed, off-box ledger export — the natural successor to this phase, and the
   half of AD-3 that "tamper-evident" still does not cover.

## Phase 3 — the A2/D08 model decision, priced (committed `b23d0c7`)

Chosen ahead of the signed ledger export, and the reason is worth recording:
the ledger phase fixed a document claiming more than the code did, and these two
findings are the same defect class — except they sit in the money documents a
customer's procurement team will run, and D14 §8 names the gap between the sales
description and the contract as the product's largest liability. A missing
signature on a ledger is a production requirement. A rate card that contradicts
its own ROI model cannot be sent out at all.

**What was built.** No code changed in the product. `assets/a2-d08-model-decision-2026-11-09.md`
plus `a2-d08-model-decision.py` (65 reproducible checks) price both answers so the
owner's decision is a comparison rather than more research.

**Three findings the arithmetic pass did not have.**

1. **The 2.0x/4.1x anchors are recoverable.** The pass record tested two cost
   bases and concluded no parameter set reproduces both. On a third — pilot plus
   three full years at list, no conversion credit — one value of the catastrophic
   probability fits both, because the ratio the anchors demand
   (cost(10k)/cost(500) = 9.756) is a property of the *pricing*, not the benefit
   model. So this is a disclosure defect, not a fabrication. The level of p is
   not unique — a four-year benefit horizon gives 0.0412% and also fits — which is
   why the finding stays open.
2. **D08 contradicts itself.** §4 prices a prevented failure at ~$993,000; §5 at
   $8.6M–$11.4M. Holds per axle as well as per defect. And §4's figure is within
   0.7% of A1's $999,750 — the document already contains an A1-consistent
   valuation four pages before abandoning it.
3. **`roi.py` is further from A1 than the README says.** Two disagreements, not
   one: 2% vs 0.05%, and a $9.25M contained cost vs A1's $500,000. Per-missed-
   defect values are $29,065,000 vs $999,750 — 29×, of which probability accounts
   for 20.5×.

**What the independent audit caught, and this is the part worth keeping.** I wrote
the paper and then wrote its checker, which is exactly the arrangement where a
shared assumption passes unnoticed. A separate agent with no stake in it found
four errors:

- **The dashboard figure was not roi.py's output.** I had computed $14,339,850 by
  re-running A1's formula at 2% and labelled it as the dashboard. `roi.py` takes
  warrants, not axles — "at 500 axles" was never computable. Corrected to a
  per-defect comparison, which is the right like-for-like and a *larger* gap.
- "D08 repeats it verbatim" — it does not; two sentences are reworded. Corrected.
- "That is where the numbers came from" — overstated derivation from consistency.
  Corrected, with the horizon ambiguity shown rather than buried.
- "no site-fee line" in the stale workbook — wrong, the row exists and is inert at
  one site. Corrected, and the real disagreement (a $285,000 pilot built from
  hardware + training against A2's $370,000 with no hardware at all) stated.

Lesson for the next phase: when I produce both an analysis and the script that
checks it, a second reader is not optional. The checker validated my mistake
because I wrote it to.

## Next

1. Decide Finding 1 and Finding 2 — options priced in the decision paper §6,
   recommendation in §7. **This is the only blocking item that needs the owner.**
2. Worth pricing before locking Option A: adding the cost components A1 omits
   (service disruption, lading loss, regulatory penalty) to B14 at 0.05%, which
   may raise the benefit figure honestly.
3. Then regenerate the A1 workbook from the corrected builder and re-run both
   check scripts and the unit suite.
4. D07 §14.5 governing law and venue remains open, unchanged.
5. Signed, off-box ledger export — the next *build*, now unblocked by priority
   but not by dependency; it does not touch any of the above.

# AxiomDynamics — Current State

**Last updated:** 2026-11-09 (chat-3 — arithmetic pass, build history document,
then the append-only ledger rebuild)
**Repository:** `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics`
**Remote:** `github.com/kaanju19-lang/AxiomDynamics` (private)
**Push state:** run `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD`. As last confirmed the
local remote-tracking ref stood at `b946678`, with the build-history commit ahead
of it. Never trust a hash written in this file — check with git, because this
file's own commit moves the top of the branch every time it is edited. Run
`PUSH-TO-GITHUB.bat` in the repo root. The sandbox cannot reach GitHub: `git push`
and `git fetch` both fail with HTTP 403 from the proxy, so a local `origin/main`
ref is not proof of what the remote holds.

---

## What this project is

Physics-first predictive maintenance for freight rail. Six named physical models
— thermodynamics with per-axle rolling z-score, peer median/MAD comparison,
kinematics, acoustics (BPFO/BPFI/BSF/FTF), same-axle left/right differential, and
an executive ROI panel — instead of black-box ML or fixed alarm thresholds.

The Master Brief Docket is in `client-assets/MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/`: 38 artifacts
— 36 Markdown documents, the A1 Excel model (with its build script beside it) and
the B03 HTML infographic — across A (commercial), B (technical), C (deployment)
and D (contractual) series plus F (forms).

## Build status

**38 artifacts on disk; 37 docket IDs on disk (A1 is a folder holding the `.xlsx`
and the builder, so it counts as one ID and two files).** The docket index (D00)
carries 37 ID rows; 34 are marked `**Built**` in bold, and B02 (.md) and B03
(.html) carry plain "Built" with a format qualifier. D00 Part IV is the authority
on status, not this file.

A long-form account of the whole build — every stage, every document, every
correction, and the loss and rebuild — is at
`project-logs/AxiomDynamics-Build-History-and-Working-Summary.docx` (29 pages).
It is generated by `project-logs/build-history-summary.js`; re-run
`node project-logs/build-history-summary.js` after a material change.

Open docket items are tracked in **D00 Part IV** — that table is the authority,
not this file.

## The largest known gap

**There is no detector ingest path.** No endpoint accepts a Railroad payload.
Every demonstration signal is generated from the physics equations on synthetic
traces. This is disclosed in B01 §7 gap #5, B02 §2 and the B03 status block.

Every demonstration number demonstrates **the method**, not the Railroad's data.
The validation chain — schema, timestamp, plausibility — is designed and not built.

## Open items, in priority order

1. **Two A2/D08 model findings — need an owner decision, now priced.** The
   arithmetic pass of 2026-11-09 found **no arithmetic errors** in either document
   (78 of 78 figures recompute correctly). It did find that two *claims* do not
   reproduce from the shipped model. **Read
   `assets/a2-d08-model-decision-2026-11-09.md` first** — it costs both answers,
   corrects two points below, and is the shorter read. Checks:
   `python3 -I assets/a2-d08-arithmetic-pass.py` (78) and
   `python3 -I assets/a2-d08-model-decision.py` (65).
   - **Finding 1.** A2 §3.2 and D08 §3 claim ~2.0x return at 500 axles rising to
     ~4.1x at 10,000. *The decision paper refines this:* the anchors **are**
     recoverable on a pilot-plus-three-years cost basis at p ≈ 0.04%–0.07%, so
     this is a disclosure defect — an unstated frame — not an invention. They
     still cannot ship, because no frame is stated and the parameter is disclosed
     nowhere.
   - **Finding 2.** D08 §5–§6 modelled benefits ($6–8M pilot year, $14–20M
     four-year, $40–60M six-year) run 5x–14x above A1. *The decision paper adds:*
     D08 also contradicts **itself** — §4 prices a prevented failure at ~$993,000,
     §5 at $8.6M–$11.4M — and `backend/roi.py` values a missed defect at **29×**
     A1's figure (2% probability *and* a $9.25M contained cost, against A1's
     0.05% and $500,000).
   - **Recommended:** A1 governs (0.05%, $500,000), anchors restated to
     1.77x/3.36x, D08 §5–§6 restated from A1, `roi.py` corrected. Option B and the
     case against are in §6–§7 of the decision paper.
2. **D07 §14.5 — governing law and venue.** An open counsel decision, correctly
   labelled as open as of chat-2 (previously a blank pointing at an Order field
   that does not exist). Must be closed by signed addendum before first execution.
3. **A1 workbook regeneration.** Deliberately not regenerated during the
   arithmetic pass, because doing so would bake both open findings into a new
   file before the model question is settled. The builder is now fixed (see
   below) and will regenerate on demand once findings 1 and 2 are decided.
4. **D09 §4.4 supply-chain gaps** — SBOM (Q1 2027), hash verification of
   dependency downloads (Q1 2027), GPG-signed releases (Q2 2027). All disclosed.
5. **Signed, off-box ledger export** — the append-only ledger itself landed
   2026-11-09 (see below), which closed the overwrite gap. What remains is
   provability against a party holding the database file, and durability
   against disk loss: the export is not signed and the ledger is not
   replicated. D09 §4.4, B01 §7 items 6 and 8.

## Append-only disposition ledger — built 2026-11-09 (AD-3)

The gap that had been disclosed in six documents since `cf2e6ba` is closed at
the code level.

- `backend/store.py` rewritten. Records are inserted, never updated. A second
  decision on an advisory is a new row carrying `supersedes_id`; the earlier row
  keeps its content and timestamp. `BEFORE UPDATE` and `BEFORE DELETE` triggers
  `RAISE(ABORT)`, so the guarantee lives in the schema rather than in convention.
  Every row stores `prev_hash` and `record_hash` — a SHA-256 over its own
  canonical content plus the predecessor's hash — and `verify_chain()`
  recomputes the whole chain and names the first row that fails.
- Migration from the v1 one-row-per-advisory table runs inside `init_db()`,
  preserves the surviving decision and its original timestamp, and does not
  fabricate history that the old schema had already destroyed.
- 17 adversarial tests in `tests/test_store.py`: an UPDATE, a DELETE, a second
  disposition, a tampered row, a removed row, and two migration shapes. Each
  asserts the attempt fails or is detected. `tests/run_tests.py` now discovers
  every `test_*.py`, so the total suite is 38.
- New routes: `GET /api/warrant/{id}/disposition` (full trail, with `chain_ok`)
  and `GET /api/ledger/verify`. The dashboard shows the decision trail under the
  form and marks a corrected decision as superseding an earlier record.

**What it does not prove, and the docket now says so in these words:** the chain
is tamper-*evident*, not tamper-*proof*. A party with write access to the
database file can drop the triggers, rewrite rows and recompute every hash. That
is why items 6 and 8 above stay open.

Docket corrected in the same commit: B01 §4 and §7 items 2/8, D09 §4.4 and the
audit-logging row, F09 Part 6 and Part 7, F00, B02, C02, D12, D14 §5, D00 Part V
and Part VI, and the root README.

## A1 builder — fixed in chat-3

Two defects in `A1-ROI-MODEL/build_roi_calculator.py`, both cosmetic to the
workbook but both real if anyone runs it:

- The sheet-5 assumptions note attributed a **2% catastrophic escalation rate** to
  a model whose cell B17 has held **0.05%** since the correction. A reader
  reconciling the sheet against its own footnote would find a ten-fold conflict.
- The script saved to `/sessions/.../mnt/outputs/...`, a path inside the destroyed
  chat-1 sandbox, so running it raised `FileNotFoundError`. It now writes beside
  itself.


## Git state

The sandbox **cannot reach GitHub** — `git push` and `git fetch` both fail with
HTTP 403 from the proxy. Its `origin/main` ref therefore only advances when the
owner pushes and the sandbox is told the result. Do not trust it as evidence of
remote state without checking the commits page.

**Pushing is done by the owner**, with `PUSH-TO-GITHUB.bat` in the repo root. It
prints the commits waiting to go up and verifies afterwards.

**As of 2026-11-09, everything is pushed.** GitHub's top commit as last confirmed
by the owner against the commits page was `2ec168b`. Two commits are local and
waiting since then — `209efe6`, the append-only ledger rebuild, and the log entry
after it.

**The host repo at `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics` is authoritative for push state.**
Verify by opening the commits page.

**The line-ending trap.** `git status` in this repo lists nearly every tracked file
as modified on a fresh Windows checkout. It is CRLF working-tree content against
LF blobs, not a content change — `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` returns empty.
There is no `.gitattributes` and `core.autocrlf` is unset. **Always check with
`--ignore-cr-at-eol` before believing a diff stat**, and never let an editor
rewrite a whole file's endings into a commit: doing so once during chat-3 turned a
two-line fix into 1,248 changed lines, which had to be reset and recommitted.


## What was lost in the chat-1 → chat-2 transition

Recorded here so nobody goes looking for it:

- Three commits built at the end of chat-1 (`0b66d21`, `cb4f74d`, and the
  F00/D07/Q6 work) existed only in the old sandbox. **`F00` Rule 7, the D07 §14
  rewrite and Q6 were rebuilt into the repository in chat-2.** The project-logs
  structure was rebuilt. The transcripts were not and cannot be — see
  `README.md`.
- Because the rebuild is a reconstruction rather than a recovery, the wording may
  differ from what chat-1 wrote. The *decisions* are identical; the prose is not
  guaranteed to be. Do not treat the current text as a restoration of an earlier
  draft.

## Standing instructions

- **[WORK LOCATION] All project work is written directly into this repository, first pass, and committed in the same pass.** No drafts in sandbox scratch space — that is how chat-1's final phase was lost.
- Keep the same concept throughout — consistency of framing across every document.
- Internal analysis goes in `assets/`, never `client-assets/`.
- Verify against the file before writing the claim.

## Why chat-1's work was lost — the mechanism

Not a deletion. The work was never on the owner's machine.

Chat-1 built the repo inside a temporary sandbox container. To get anything out
it bundled the repo, embedded the bundle in a `.bat`, and the owner ran it once —
which is how `de9b245` reached GitHub. **Everything chat-1 did after that push
stayed in the container**, including the F00 Rule 7 work, the D07 §14 rewrite, Q6
and the transcripts. The bundle was never remade. When the session ended the
container was destroyed and took all of it.

The failure was treating "committed" as "safe." Inside that container it only
meant "saved somewhere that is about to be emptied."

**The rule that follows:** there is no automatic export. A commit in the sandbox
is not durable until it is in `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics` and pushed. Never tell
the owner work is saved without saying where it physically is.

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\RGV\AppData\Local\Claude-3p\local-agent-mode-sessions\skills-plugin\00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001\f8275f8d-c548-437b-92ff-9f01424b6b5d\skills\docx

# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis

If you are about to make a new document and this session offers Claude's own docs (a Docs connector, docs skill or Docs artifact type), and the user has neither named Word/.docx/.dotx, asked for tracked changes, nor supplied a .docx/.dotx file to change or use as a template, make the document there instead. It exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to make a Word file. A .docx/.dotx given only as source material does not count as supplied. This skill remains the right tool for producing, reading, editing, templating or converting Word files.

A `.docx` is a ZIP archive of XML files. Choose your approach by task:

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Create** a new document | Write a `docx` (npm) script — see gotchas below |
| **Edit** an existing document | `unzip` → edit `word/document.xml` → `zip` (docx-js cannot open existing files) |
| **Read** content | `pandoc -t markdown file.docx` |

> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.

## Creating with docx-js — gotchas

`docx` is preinstalled — do not run `npm install` first; write the script and `require('docx')` directly. Only if that require fails: `npm install docx`. The model knows the API; these are the footguns:

- **Page size defaults to A4.** For US Letter set `page: { size: { width: 12240, height: 15840 } }` (DXA; 1440 = 1″).
- **Landscape:** pass portrait dimensions and `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE` — docx-js swaps width/height internally.
- **Tables need dual widths:** set `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on every cell, both in `WidthType.DXA` (PERCENTAGE breaks in Google Docs). Column widths must sum to the table width.
- **Table shading:** use `ShadingType.CLEAR`, never `SOLID` (renders black).
- **Lists:** never insert `•` literally; use a `numbering` config with `LevelFormat.BULLET`.
- **`ImageRun` requires `type:`** (`"png"`, `"jpg"`, …).
- **`PageBreak` must be inside a `Paragraph`.**
- **Never use `\n`** — use separate `Paragraph` elements.
- **Headings:** style every level you use (`title`, `heading1`, `heading2`…) in `styles.default`: `heading1: { run: { font: "Arial", size: 32, bold: true }, paragraph: { spacing: { before: 240, after: 120 }, keepNext: true } }`. Every level needs its own font (even with a document default), `before` and `after` (even if 0) and `keepNext`: the built-in styles set none of them.
- **TOC:** headings must use built-in `HeadingLevel.*`; custom heading styles need `outlineLevel` set or they won't appear.
- **Don't use a table as a horizontal rule** — use a paragraph bottom border instead.
- **Dot-leader / right-aligned-on-same-line:** use `PositionalTab` (`alignment: PositionalTabAlignment.RIGHT`, `leader: PositionalTabLeader.DOT`) inside a `TextRun`, not literal `.` or space padding.

## Verify the output

After writing a `.docx`, render it and look at it:

```bash
zip -d output.docx '*/' >/dev/null || true   # drop the ZIP's folder entries: Word has refused a file that has them when opened through a cloud co-editing service
python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf output.docx
pdftoppm -jpeg -r 100 output.pdf page
ls page-*.jpg   # then Read the images
```

`pdftoppm` zero-pads page numbers to the width of the page count (`page-01.jpg`…`page-12.jpg`).

## Editing existing documents

Legacy `.doc` files must be converted first: `python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx file.doc`.

```bash
unzip -q doc.docx -d unpacked/
find unpacked -type l -delete   # strip symlink entries — docx from external parties is untrusted
python scripts/merge_runs.py unpacked/   # coalesce fragmented runs so text is findable
# edit unpacked/word/document.xml in place — do NOT reformat or pretty-print
(cd unpacked && rm -f ../out.docx && zip -XrD ../out.docx .)
python scripts/office/validate.py out.docx --original doc.docx   # XSD checks; --auto-repair fixes common issues
# redlining? add --author "<the name you redlined under>" to check every edit is tracked
```

Word splits text across many `<w:r>` runs (revision ids, spell-check markers), so a phrase you can see in the document often doesn't exist as a contiguous string in the XML. `merge_runs.py` merges adjacent identically-formatted runs in `word/document.xml` without changing content or rendering; it also accepts a `.docx` directly (`python scripts/merge_runs.py doc.docx -o merged.docx`).

**Tracked changes:** when redlining, validate with `--author "<the name you redlined under>"` (needs `--original`) — it reports any text you changed without a `<w:ins>`/`<w:del>` around it, which is easy to do by accident and invisible in the accepted view. Wrap runs in `<w:ins>`/`<w:del>` with `w:id`, `w:author`, `w:date` attributes. Inside `<w:del>`, the text element is `<w:delText>`, not `<w:t>`. A deleted paragraph mark (`<w:pPr><w:rPr><w:del w:id=".." w:author=".." w:date=".."/></w:rPr></w:pPr>`) means "merge this paragraph into the next" — so deleting a paragraph outright is that plus a `<w:del>` around every run. The `<w:del/>` must come before the rPr's other children; their order is schema-enforced.

To produce a clean copy with all tracked changes accepted: `python scripts/accept_changes.py in.docx out.docx`.

Accepting a deleted paragraph mark should join that paragraph to the one below it, so a paragraph whose runs are *all* deleted vanishes. Word does this; `accept_changes.py` and `pandoc --track-changes=accept` don't always. Both fail the same way — they strip the deleted text but leave the emptied paragraph behind, which reads as a stray empty bullet when it was auto-numbered:

- `pandoc --track-changes=accept` never joins the paragraphs.
- `accept_changes.py` (LibreOffice) joins them correctly, except when the deleted paragraph is followed by an empty spacer paragraph.

An empty bullet in either view is an artifact of that view, not a defect in the document. Check paragraph deletions in the XML.

## Comments

Comments require six cross-linked files. Use the helper — directory mode when you'll also be editing `document.xml` (saves an unzip/rezip cycle), `.docx`-direct mode otherwise:

```bash
# Against an already-unpacked directory (preferred when also placing markers)
python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ "Fees & expenses cap is too low"
python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ "Agreed" --parent 0

# Against a .docx directly
python scripts/comment.py contract.docx "This cap is too low" -o annotated.docx
```

The script writes `comments.xml`, `commentsExtended.xml`, `commentsIds.xml`, `commentsExtensible.xml`, the relationships, and the content-type overrides. Comment IDs are auto-assigned. It then prints the `<w:commentRangeStart>`/`<w:commentRangeEnd>`/`<w:commentReference>` snippet to add to `word/document.xml` so the comment anchors to specific text — until you place those markers, the comment exists but is not visible.

## Dependencies

`docx` (npm, preinstalled — install only if `require('docx')` fails) · `pandoc` · LibreOffice (`soffice`) · `pdftoppm` (Poppler)

## Scheduled tasks

The `mcp__scheduled-tasks__create_scheduled_task` tool sets up work that runs automatically — on a repeating schedule (every morning, weekly, hourly) or once at a specific future time (tomorrow at 3pm, in an hour).

**Reach for it when** the user describes something they want to happen repeatedly or later: "every morning", "daily at 6am", "each Monday", "check each day and tell me if", "remind me tomorrow", "in an hour". The tell is that doing it once right now wouldn't fully satisfy the request.

**Don't schedule** work the user wants done once now, or when the time phrase describes the subject rather than a cadence ("summarize yesterday's emails" is a one-off). When it could be read either way, do it once, then offer to schedule it.

**Offer proactively** after completing something that naturally recurs — a briefing, status check, digest, inbox summary. Many users don't know scheduling is possible.

To change an existing task's schedule or prompt, use `mcp__scheduled-tasks__update_scheduled_task`; `mcp__scheduled-tasks__list_scheduled_tasks` shows what's already set up.

**Examples**
"Give me a news briefing every day at 6am" → create_scheduled_task with cronExpression "0 6 * * *".
"Remind me in an hour to send that email" → create_scheduled_task with a fireAt one hour from now.
"Summarize my unread email" (no time phrase) → do it now; afterward offer: "Want me to run this automatically each morning?"


## Artifacts (live, persisted HTML views)

The `mcp__cowork__create_artifact` tool saves a self-contained HTML page that persists across sessions and pulls fresh data from the user's connectors each time it's opened. Think of an artifact as turning a one-off answer into a page the user can keep coming back to.

**What's available inside the page.**
- `window.cowork.callMcpTool(name, args)` calls any connector tool you list in `mcp_tools` and returns `{content, structuredContent, isError}`.
- `window.cowork.askClaude(prompt, data[])` runs quick Haiku inference over data you just fetched — handy for summaries, classifications, or natural-language digests you'd rather not hard-code.
- `window.cowork.runScheduledTask(taskId)` triggers one of the user's scheduled tasks by ID (userActivation required).

Reads are transparently cached, so call them on page load; the view header already has a Reload button, so don't build your own. You may load Chart.js, Grid.js, or Mermaid from CDN — those three only; anything else must be inline. `localStorage` persists across reloads and app restarts, so you can remember the user's filter and sort choices.

**Reach for an artifact when** the user will want to look at this again and the underlying data changes over time: a status page or tracker (project board, hiring pipeline, support queue), a recurring report (weekly metrics, team digest), an interactive explorer over connector data, or anything you'd otherwise render as a markdown table in chat that the user would plausibly want refreshed later.

**Probe before you build.** Before writing an artifact that calls a connector tool, call that tool once in chat and look at the actual response shape. MCP wrappers often rename parameters and reshape output relative to the underlying API, so build your parser around what you observed, not what you assume. Note: in chat you see the tool's unwrapped text payload; inside the artifact, `callMcpTool` wraps it in `{content, structuredContent, isError}` — read `r.structuredContent ?? JSON.parse(r.content[0].text)`.

**Offering without being asked.** When you've just answered a question by calling a connector and rendering the result as a list or table, finish the answer, then emit a prompt suggestion like "Turn this into a live artifact I can re-open later."

"What tasks are waiting on me?" → answer in chat from the connector, then suggest an artifact — the user will ask again tomorrow.

# auto memory
You have a persistent, file-based memory system at `C:\Users\RGV\AppData\Local\Claude-3p\local-agent-mode-sessions\f8275f8d\00000000\memory\memory`. This directory already exists — write to it directly with the Write tool (do not run mkdir or check for its existence). What you write here survives across sessions, interruptions and context compaction — a future session (or you, hours from now) can read it. Anything useful that exists only in your working context is one interruption away from being lost.

Build this memory up over time so that future conversations start with a picture of who the user is, how they like to collaborate, and the context behind their work. That includes more than facts: tone and formality, how much to hedge versus assert, how closely to stick to cited sources, and preferred output formats or tools (e.g. "always save financial reports as Excel, not markdown").

If the user explicitly asks you to remember something, save it immediately as whichever type fits best. If they ask you to forget something, find and remove the relevant entry.

## Types of memory

There are several discrete types of memory that you can store in your memory system:

For example, you should collaborate with a senior software engineer differently than a student who is coding for the very first time. Keep in mind, that the aim here is to be helpful to the user. ## What NOT to save in memory

- Facts you can re-derive from the filesystem (file locations, project structure you could just re-read) or re-fetch from a connected tool.
- Anything already documented in CLAUDE.md files.
- Ephemeral task details: analysis results, in-progress work, temporary state, current conversation context.

These exclusions apply even when the user explicitly asks you to save. If they ask you to save a meeting recap or an inbox summary, ask what was *surprising* or *non-obvious* about it — that is the part worth keeping.

## How to save memories

**Write early, write often.** Memory writes are cheap; rediscovery is expensive. Don't wait for a clean stopping point — there isn't one. Good moments to write include:
- figuring out why something was broken or behaving unexpectedly
- learning a fact, constraint, or config detail that wasn't obvious from the code/docs
- making a non-trivial decision (record the *why*, not just the what)
- discovering that an approach *doesn't* work — negative results save future time too
- finishing a sub-task or switching context
- noticing you've been working >15-20 min without saving anything
- finishing research (even partially)

**Err toward writing.** If you're unsure whether something is worth saving, save it — a slightly noisy memory is far better than an empty one.

Saving a memory is a two-step process:

**Step 1** — write the memory to its own file (e.g., `user_role.md`, `feedback_testing.md`) using this frontmatter format:

```markdown
---
name: {{memory name — other memories can reference this one inline as [[name]]}}
description: {{one-line description — used to decide relevance in future conversations, so be specific}}
type: {{user, feedback, project, reference}}
---

{{memory content — for feedback/project types, structure as: rule/fact, then **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. Use [[name]] to reference other memories by their name field. [[name]] should match filename.}}
```

**Step 2** — add a pointer to that file in `MEMORY.md`. `MEMORY.md` is an index, not a memory — each entry should be one line, under ~150 characters: `- [Title](file.md) — one-line hook`. It has no frontmatter. Never write memory content directly into `MEMORY.md`.

- `MEMORY.md` is the index and, when there is one, is loaded into your conversation context — lines after 200 will be truncated, so keep the index concise. If no index is loaded, `MEMORY.md` was missing or empty when this conversation started.
- Keep the name, description, and type fields in memory files up-to-date with the content
- Organize memory semantically by topic, not chronologically
- Update or remove memories that turn out to be wrong or outdated
- Do not write duplicate memories. First check if there is an existing memory you can update before writing a new one.

## When to access memories
- When memories seem relevant, or the user references prior-conversation work.
- You MUST access memory when the user explicitly asks you to check, recall, or remember.
- If the user says to *ignore* or *not use* memory: Do not apply remembered facts, cite, compare against, or mention memory content.
- **Maintain it.** If something in memory turns out to be wrong or outdated, correct it immediately — stale memory is worse than no memory.

## Before applying/recommending a memory

Check if the memory applies - some guidance is only specific to a particular type of workflow/deliverable, DO NOT extrapolate. When in doubt, ask the user.

Memory records what was true at write time. Docs get edited, tickets get reassigned, threads get new replies. When a memory points at something you can refetch, verify it before the user acts on it.

- **Doc or page** → open it. Content may have changed.
- **Ticket, task, or link** → re-read from the source when you can.

## Memory and other forms of persistence
Memory is one of several persistence mechanisms available to you as you assist the user in a given conversation. The distinction is often that memory can be recalled in future conversations and should not be used for persisting information that is only useful within the scope of the current conversation.
- When to use or update a plan instead of memory: If you are about to start a non-trivial implementation task and would like to reach alignment with the user on your approach you should use a Plan rather than saving this information to memory. Similarly, if you already have a plan within the conversation and you have changed your approach persist that change by updating the plan rather than saving a memory.
- When to use or update tasks instead of memory: When you need to break your work in current conversation into discrete steps or keep track of your progress use tasks instead of saving to memory. Tasks are great for persisting information about the work that needs to be done in the current conversation, but memory should be reserved for information that will be useful in future conversations.

## Sensitive personal information

Do not save the following to memory unless the user explicitly asks you to remember it:

- Protected attributes: race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, age, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, immigration status, disability, serious illness, union membership
- Government identifiers: Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, passport numbers, government ID numbers
- Financial account details: credit card numbers, bank account numbers
- Health information: medical conditions, diagnoses, lab results, mental health details, therapy or counseling
- Home or personal mailing addresses (work addresses are fine)

If any of the above appears in conversation context, complete the task but do not persist it to a memory file. If the user explicitly says "remember my address is X", saving it is acceptable — they've given consent.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## Usage notes

- Always include a short description summarizing what the agent will do
- When the agent is done, it will return a single message back to you. The result returned by the agent is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Trust but verify: an agent's summary describes what it intended to do, not necessarily what it did. When an agent writes or edits code, check the actual changes before reporting the work as done.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here. Every Agent call starts a fresh agent with no memory of prior runs (except subagent_type: "fork"), so the prompt must be self-contained.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tool access are set in its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter, or the SDK `agents` option); the `model` parameter here overrides the definition for this one call.
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since a fresh agent is not aware of the user's intent
- If the agent description mentions that it should be used proactively, then you should try your best to use it without the user having to ask for it first.
- If the user specifies that they want you to run agents "in parallel", you MUST send a single message with multiple Agent tool use content blocks. For example, if you need to launch both a build-validator agent and a test-runner agent in parallel, send a single message with both tool calls.
- With `isolation: "worktree"`, the worktree is automatically cleaned up if the agent makes no changes; otherwise the path and branch are returned in the result.

## When to fork

Fork yourself (pass `subagent_type: "fork"`) when the intermediate tool output isn't worth keeping in your context. The criterion is qualitative — "will I need this output again" — not task size. Fork open-ended questions. If research can be broken into independent questions, launch parallel forks in one message. A fork beats a fresh subagent for this — it inherits context and shares your cache.

Forks are cheap because they share your prompt cache.

**Don't peek.** The tool result includes an `output_file` path — do not Read or tail it. You get a completion notification; trust it. Reading the transcript mid-flight pulls the fork's tool noise into your context, which defeats the point of forking.

**Don't race.** After launching, you know nothing about what the fork found. Never fabricate or predict fork results in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. The notification arrives as a user-role message in a later turn; it is never something you write yourself. If the user asks a follow-up before the notification lands, tell them the fork is still running — give status, not a guess.

**Writing a fork prompt.** Since the fork inherits your context, the prompt is a *directive* — what to do, not what the situation is. Be specific about scope: what's in, what's out, what another agent is handling. Don't re-explain background.


## Writing the prompt

Any agent other than a fork starts with zero context. Brief the agent like a smart colleague who just walked into the room — it hasn't seen this conversation, doesn't know what you've tried, doesn't understand why this task matters.
- Explain what you're trying to accomplish and why.
- Describe what you've already learned or ruled out.
- Give enough context about the surrounding problem that the agent can make judgment calls rather than just following a narrow instruction.
- If you need a short response, say so ("report in under 200 words").
- Lookups: hand over the exact command. Investigations: hand over the question — prescribed steps become dead weight when the premise is wrong.

For fresh agents, terse command-style prompts produce shallow, generic work.

**Never delegate understanding.** Don't write "based on your findings, fix the bug" or "based on the research, implement it." Those phrases push synthesis onto the agent instead of doing it yourself. Write prompts that prove you understood: include file paths, line numbers, what specifically to change.

Example usage:

<example>
user: "What's left on this branch before we can ship?"
assistant: <thinking>Forking this — it's a survey question. I want the punch list, not the git output in my context.</thinking>
Agent({
  subagent_type: "fork",
  name: "ship-audit",
  description: "Branch ship-readiness audit",
  prompt: "Audit what's left before this branch can ship. Check: uncommitted changes, commits ahead of main, whether tests exist, whether the GrowthBook gate is wired up, whether CI-relevant files changed. Report a punch list — done vs. missing. Under 200 words."
})
assistant: Ship-readiness audit running.
<commentary>
Turn ends here. The coordinator knows nothing about the findings yet. What follows is a SEPARATE turn — the notification arrives from outside, as a user-role message. It is not something the coordinator writes.
</commentary>
[later turn — notification arrives as user message]
assistant: Audit's back. Three blockers: no tests for the new prompt path, GrowthBook gate wired but not in build_flags.yaml, and one uncommitted file.
</example>

<example>
user: "so is the gate wired up or not"
<commentary>
User asks mid-wait. The audit fork was launched to answer exactly this, and it hasn't returned. The coordinator does not have this answer. Give status, not a fabricated result.
</commentary>
assistant: Still waiting on the audit — that's one of the things it's checking. Should land shortly.
</example>

<example>
user: "Can you get a second opinion on whether this migration is safe?"
assistant: <thinking>I'll ask the code-reviewer agent — it won't see my analysis, so it can give an independent read.</thinking>
<commentary>
A non-fork subagent_type is specified, so the agent starts fresh. It needs full context in the prompt. The briefing explains what to assess and why.
</commentary>
Agent({
  name: "migration-review",
  description: "Independent migration review",
  subagent_type: "code-reviewer",
  prompt: "Review migration 0042_user_schema.sql for safety. Context: we're adding a NOT NULL column to a 50M-row table. Existing rows get a backfill default. I want a second opinion on whether the backfill approach is safe under concurrent writes — I've checked locking behavior but want independent verification. Report: is this safe, and if not, what specifically breaks?"
})
</example>
